Abiding is not just in the morning. Choose three moments in your day (your commute, a break, doing dishes) to say a sentence to Jesus. Little by little, the conversation becomes continuous.

pratique.titre: Keep the Fruit of These 7 Days
pratique.texte: Write the 7 "I Am" statements on a card and place it on your fridge or as your phone wallpaper. When a situation comes, ask: which "I Am" do I need today?

days.question: What disconnects me most often from Jesus during my day, and what simple habit could help me "abide" in him?
days.priere: Jesus, you are the true vine and I am a branch. Apart from you I can do nothing. I choose to abide in you, in your Word and in your love. Father, prune in me what needs to be pruned, so that I may bear much fruit, and that my joy may be complete. Amen.
days.aRetenir: My work is not to manufacture fruit, but to remain attached to Jesus.

items.title: Learn to Pray
items.subtitle: 10 days to discover the Lord's Prayer, phrase by phrase, and transform your prayer life.
items.summary: You may know the Lord's Prayer by heart… but have you ever truly prayed it? When the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, he didn't give them a magic formula, but a path. Over 10 days, we'll walk this path phrase by phrase: approaching God as a Father, worshiping him, seeking his kingdom, entrusting our needs to him, forgiving, standing firm in the battle, and persevering. By the end, you won't recite the Lord's Prayer anymore—you'll pray it. Biblical texts: Louis Segond 1910.

days.title: Lord, Teach Us to Pray
days.meditation:
## The Context

The disciples saw Jesus walk on water, multiply loaves, heal lepers, cast out demons, raise the dead. And yet, they never asked him, "Teach us to do miracles." The only thing they ever asked him to teach them was prayer.

"One day Jesus was praying in a certain place. When he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.'" (Luke 11:1)

Why? Because they understood where everything else came from. They saw Jesus disappear before dawn: "Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed." (Mark 1:35) They watched him withdraw after long days of ministry. They had noticed that the power he displayed in public came from what he lived in secret.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

The disciples' request should already reassure you: prayer is something you learn. No one is born knowing how to pray. Even those who had grown up in the synagogue, who knew the Psalms by heart, felt something was missing.

Think of a baby learning to talk. He says "da… da…," he mixes up words, he makes mistakes. Does his father laugh at him? Does he wait for the child to speak perfectly before listening? No—every little word melts him. God isn't waiting to catch you out for fumbling with your words. He rejoices that you come.

Jesus then gives them a model, what we call the Lord's Prayer. It's not a formula to recite mechanically: just before, in Matthew, he warns against those who "use many meaningless words." Rather, it's a framework, like the load-bearing walls of a house. Each phrase opens a room: worship, the kingdom, God's will, our needs, forgiveness, spiritual battle. Over ten days, we'll visit these rooms one by one.

Then Jesus tells the story of a friend who knocks on his neighbor's door at midnight to borrow bread, and who insists until he gets it. And he concludes: "So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened." (Luke 11:9-10)

Ask, seek, knock—three verbs of increasing intensity. Prayer is not religious politeness; it's an active, persevering, confident pursuit.

And he ends with a promise that reveals the Father's heart: What father would give his son a snake if he asked for a fish? How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! The greatest answer to prayer is not just something God gives—it's God himself giving himself.

Prayer is not learned from a book; it's learned on your knees.

## For Your Life

Many Christians live with silent guilt: "I don't pray enough. I don't know how to pray. I fall asleep, I get bored, I think of something else." If that's you, good news: you're exactly where the disciples were. And that's the best place to start.

For these ten days, I'm suggesting three very simple things. A time: choose a fixed slot, even ten minutes, rather than "a moment sometime" that never comes. A place: Jesus speaks of "going into your room and closing the door"; find your corner, your chair, your parked car, your walking route. An honest heart: start with the disciples' prayer: "Lord, teach me to pray."

It's not a small prayer. It's the beginning of a revolution.

pratique.texte: Choose a specific time slot for the next ten days: ten minutes when you wake up, at lunch or before bed. Set an alarm. A moment "when you have time" never comes.

Your armchair, your parked car, your bedroom with the door closed, a walk around the neighborhood. If you have young children and no quiet space, pray during their nap or while pushing the stroller—God hears you there too.
Start today with just one sentence, the disciples' prayer: "Lord, teach me to pray." Then tell him simply what keeps you from praying. That's already a prayer.

days.question: What keeps me from praying the most: lack of time, lack of motivation, or feeling like I don't know how to do it?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, like your disciples, I ask you: teach me to pray. Forgive me for rushed and distracted prayers. During these ten days, draw me into the secret place, and let my prayer life become a real encounter with you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Prayer is not learned from a book; it's learned on your knees.

days.title: Our Father
days.meditation:
## The Context

In the Old Testament, God is sometimes compared to a father, but almost no one addresses him directly by that name. He is called the Lord, the God of Abraham, the Most High, the Lord of Hosts. And now Jesus opens his prayer with two words that must have surprised everyone: "Our Father."

"This, then, is how you should pray: 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name'" (Matthew 6:9)

Jesus himself prayed by saying "Abba." It's a simple Aramaic word that a child uses when speaking to his father, with warmth and trust—something like "daddy," but with respect. And the most incredible thing is that he gives us the right to use it too: "The Spirit you received does not make you slaves, so that you live in fear again; rather, the Spirit you received brought about your adoption to sonship. And by him we cry, 'Abba, Father.'" (Romans 8:15)

## What Jesus Teaches Us

There's a famous photograph taken at the White House in the 1960s: President Kennedy is working in the Oval Office, one of the most powerful rooms in the world, and his little son is playing under his desk. Ministers and generals waited for hours to get a few minutes with this man. The child walked in without an appointment. Why? Not because he was important, but because he was his son.

That's exactly what Jesus offers you. You don't enter God's presence like an employee asking for a raise, and not like a defendant before a judge. You enter like a child into his Father's house. Your place is not based on how well you performed this week, but on what Jesus did for you.

Notice too the first word: "our." Jesus doesn't begin with "my Father." Even in the secret place, when you pray alone, you're part of a family. You pray with millions of brothers and sisters around the world and throughout the centuries. The Lord's Prayer teaches us that prayer is never selfish—it carries others.

Maybe the word "father" is hard for you. Your father was absent, harsh, violent, or you never knew him. And when you hear "God is your Father," you imagine someone distant, cold, or dangerous. I want to tell you gently: God is not your earthly father on a larger scale. He is the perfect Father your heart has always needed. David, who knew what it was to be forgotten by his family, wrote: "Though my father and mother forsake me, the Lord will receive me." (Psalm 27:10)

You don't have to fix your past to approach this Father. Let him—let him heal the picture you have of a father.

It's not your prayer that makes you God's child; because you are his child that you can pray.

## For Your Life

Today, before asking for anything, just take a moment to say: "Father." Repeat it slowly, without adding anything else. Let that word sink into your heart. You're not alone, you're not an orphan, you're not a number.

And if the word sticks, if it awakens pain, tell God honestly: "Father, I don't know what it means to have a real father. Teach me." That might be the most powerful prayer you pray this week.

Then think of "our": pray for a brother, a sister, someone in your faith family who is going through a hard time. You never pray alone.

pratique.texte: Today, before any request, say "Father" slowly several times, pausing silently between each one. Let that word do its work in you.
If your father hurt, abandoned, or disappointed you, say it to God without holding back. Ask him to show you what a real father is. You might also talk about it with a pastor or trusted friend.
Today, pray by name for three people in your faith family. Send a message to one of them: "I prayed for you this morning."

days.question: What image do I naturally have of God when I pray: a judge, a boss, a stranger, or a Father?
days.priere: Father, thank you for calling me your child. Thank you for Jesus, who opened the door of your house for me. Heal the picture I have of a father, and teach me to come to you with confidence, like a child, without an appointment. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I don't enter God's house like an employee—I enter like a child with his Father.

days.title: Who Is in Heaven
days.meditation:
## The Context

Yesterday, we saw that God is a close, tender, accessible Father. But Jesus doesn't stop at "Our Father." He immediately adds: "who is in heaven." These three words don't mean God is far away, somewhere above the clouds. In the Bible, "the heavens" refers to God's place, his reign, his sovereignty over all things.

"Our God is in heaven; he does all that he pleases." (Psalm 115:3)

Jesus holds together two truths that we tend to separate: God is close enough that I can call him Father, and great enough to govern the universe.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

In 1990, the spacecraft Voyager 1, billions of miles away, turned around one last time to photograph Earth. In the image, our planet is just a tiny pale blue dot, barely visible in a ray of light. Everything we know, all of human history, fits in that pixel.

David didn't have a spacecraft, but he had looked up at the starry sky and felt the same thing: "When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is mankind that you are mindful of them, human beings that you care for them?" (Psalm 8:3-4)

That's the wonderful tension of prayer. The God who created billions of galaxies knows the number of hairs on your head. The one who holds the universe holds your hand too.

If we forget that God is "in heaven," we turn him into a buddy, a personal assistant we call whenever we need something. Our prayer becomes small, centered on ourselves. If we forget he is "Father," we turn him into a distant, frightening being we don't dare speak to. Jesus keeps us from both mistakes.

Saying "who is in heaven" is also recognizing that God sees further than we do. "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the Lord. As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts." (Isaiah 55:8-9) When a prayer seems to go unanswered as you hoped, it's not that God isn't listening; it's that he sees the whole picture, while you only see one piece of the puzzle. A four-year-old who asks for candy at breakfast doesn't always understand his father's "no." Later, he understands that the "no" was love.

My Father is close enough for me to hear him, and great enough to change everything.

## For Your Life

Before you present your problems to God, lift your gaze. Problems look enormous when you're close to them; they return to their true size when you place them before a God who is in heaven.

Today, if you can, pray outside or by a window. Look at the sky. Think about the greatness of the one who created it, then remind yourself that this same God calls you by name. Tell him: "You are great, and you are my Father. What worries me today is not too great for you."

And when you don't understand his answers, choose trust. He is in heaven—he sees what you don't yet see.

pratique.titre: Pray While Looking at the Sky
pratique.texte: Go outside for a few minutes, or sit by a window. Look at the sky, then present your main concern to God by saying: "This is not too big for you."

pratique.titre: Put Your Problems in Their Right Size
pratique.texte: Write your biggest worry at the top of a page. Below it, write three things you know about God (he is all-powerful, he is faithful, he loves me). Read the list aloud.
If there's an answer from God you don't understand, write it down and tell him: "You see what I don't see. I choose to trust you." Psalm 8 can accompany you as you pray it.

days.question: Do I tend to make God a "buddy" who's too small, or a God who's too distant? How can I hold together both his closeness and his greatness?
days.priere: Our Father in heaven, you are greater than everything that worries me, and yet you remember me. Expand my vision. When I don't understand your ways, teach me to trust you, because you see what I don't yet see. Amen.
days.aRetenir: My Father is close enough to hear me, and great enough to change everything.

days.title: Hallowed Be Your Name
days.meditation:
## The Context

The first request of the Lord's Prayer is not about our needs. It's about God: "Hallowed be Your name." To hallow means to set apart, to recognize as holy, to honor as unique. In the Bible, a name is not just a label—it reveals who a person is.

The prophet Isaiah experienced what God's holiness means one day. In a vision, he sees the Lord on a throne, and seraphs crying out: "They were calling to one another: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory!'" (Isaiah 6:3) The foundations of the Temple shake. And Isaiah, overwhelmed, realizes his own smallness—before God purifies him and sends him out.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

Jesus teaches us to begin prayer with worship. Not because God needs compliments, but because we need to put things back in their proper place.

Have you ever tried to look at a tiny pebble held right in front of your eye? It hides the entire mountain. Our problems do the same thing: stuck in front of our eyes, they hide God. Worship moves the pebble and helps us see the mountain again.

In the Old Testament, God revealed his name through concrete situations. When Abraham saw God provide the sacrifice on Mount Moriah: "Abraham called that place 'The Lord Will Provide.' And to this day it is said, 'On the mountain of the Lord it will be provided.'" (Genesis 22:14) When Israel, thirsty in the desert, saw bitter waters become sweet, God said: "I am the Lord, who heals you." When Gideon, terrified, received God's peace, he built an altar and called it "The Lord Is Peace."

Each name of God is an answer to a human need. He provides, he heals, he gives peace, he is my shepherd, he fights for me. Hallowing his name means declaring: "You are all of this, and you are this for me today."

David understood this. He invited others to join him: "Glorify the Lord with me; let us exalt his name together!" (Psalms 34:4) He wrote this psalm during one of the worst times of his life—he was fleeing from King Saul and had to pretend to be insane before a foreign king to save his life. And that's when he begins with: "I will extol the Lord at all times." Worship is not reserved for easy days. It is often the key that unlocks difficult days.

When God becomes great, my problems find their true size.

pratique.texte: Begin your prayer with five minutes without any requests: simply tell God who he is. You can use a psalm (Psalm 103 or 145) by reading it aloud.

Take three names of God (the One who provides, the One who heals, my peace) and connect each one to a situation in your life: "You are the One who provides, for this rent. You are the One who heals, for this knee."

pratique.titre: Honor His Name in Your Life
pratique.texte: Choose one area where your life could better honor the name of Christ (the way you speak at work, your honesty, your patience at home) and take a concrete step today.

days.question: Which name of God (the One who provides, who heals, my peace, my shepherd) do I most need to proclaim in my current situation?
days.priere: Our Father, hallowed be Your name. You are holy, holy, holy. You are the One who provides, the One who heals, my peace and my shepherd. Before I ask you for anything else, I want to worship you for who you are. Let my entire life honor your name. Amen.
days.aRetenir: When God becomes great, my problems find their true size.

days.title: Your Kingdom Come
days.meditation:
## The Context

Jesus's very first message, at the beginning of his ministry, fits in one sentence: "The time has come," he said. "The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news." (Mark 1:15) The kingdom of God is the heart of all his preaching. And right after, Mark tells us that Jesus enters a synagogue, teaches with authority, and casts an unclean spirit out of a man. God's kingdom is not just an idea—it manifests.

When Jesus teaches us to pray "Your kingdom come," he invites us to ask that this kingdom expand: in our hearts, in our families, in our cities, and until the day it is fully established.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

God's kingdom is where God reigns, where his will is done, where his presence changes things. And this kingdom has something surprising about it: it is both here already and not yet complete.

It is already here. Jesus said so himself: "But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." (Luke 11:20) Every time someone is healed in the name of Jesus, every time a person is set free, every time a heart is restored, every time a sinner returns to the Father, God's kingdom breaks into the earth. Paul sums it up: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." (Romans 14:17)

And it is not yet fully here. There is still sickness, injustice, war, death. One day, the kingdom will be fully established, and the Bible describes that moment with splendor: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Messiah, and he will reign for ever and ever."

Think of an embassy. In a large foreign city, the embassy of a nation is a small territory where that nation's laws apply. You pass through the door, and you are, in a sense, "in that country." The Church is an embassy of God's kingdom on earth. And you are one of its representatives. Paul says we serve "as Christ's ambassadors." Wherever you go—at work, at school, in your family—the kingdom enters with you.

To pray "Your kingdom come" is therefore a dangerous prayer. It means saying: "Lord, reign first over me." You cannot ask God to reign over the world while refusing him the throne of your own heart.

Don't ask God to bless your kingdom; ask him to bring his.

## For Your Life

Jesus made a promise to those who put his kingdom first: "Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well." (Matthew 6:33) Notice the order: first. Not "also," not "when I have time left over." First.

Today, ask yourself: What areas of my life are still "my kingdom" instead of his? My money, my time, my relationships, my projects, my hobbies? Open them one by one in prayer: "Lord, may your kingdom come here too."

Then expand your prayer. Pray for your city, for the sick people you know, for those who don't yet know Jesus. Ask that the kingdom be manifested through conversions, healings, and deliverance. And be ready: often, God answers this prayer by sending you.

pratique.titre: Open Your Domains One by One
pratique.texte: List four areas: money, time, relationships, projects. For each one, pray: "Your kingdom come here too." Note which one resists the most—that's often where God wants to work.
Take five minutes to pray for your city: its leaders, the schools, the hospitals, broken families, those who don't yet know Jesus. If you can, do it while walking through your neighborhood.

pratique.titre: Let the Kingdom Flow Through You
pratique.texte: Ask God for one opportunity today: a sick person to pray for, someone to tell about Jesus, a chance to act justly. The kingdom comes through your hands too.

days.question: What area of my life is still "my kingdom" instead of God's reign, and am I ready to give it to him today?
days.priere: Our Father, Your kingdom come. Reign first over me: my heart, my time, my money, my projects. Make me an ambassador of your kingdom wherever you send me. Let lives be saved, healed, and set free in my city, for your glory. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Don't ask God to bless your kingdom; ask him to bring his.

days.title: Your Will Be Done
days.meditation:
## The Context

"Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven." In heaven, God's will is done perfectly, joyfully, immediately. Jesus teaches us to ask that earth resemble heaven.

But to understand what this phrase costs, you have to go to the Garden of Gethsemane, a few hours before the cross. Jesus knows what awaits him: betrayal, flogging, crucifixion, and above all the weight of the world's sin. He is so anguished that his sweat becomes like drops of blood. And he prays: "Then, going a little farther, he fell with his face to the ground and prayed, 'My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will.'" (Matthew 26:39)

## What Jesus Teaches Us

Jesus doesn't pretend. He tells the Father what he truly feels: "If it is possible, take this cup from me." Praying "your will be done" doesn't mean hiding your emotions or reciting a pious phrase through gritted teeth. You have the right to tell God what you want, what you fear, what hurts you.

But Jesus doesn't stop there. He adds: "Yet not as I will, but as you will." This is the most difficult and most liberating moment of prayer: when you place your will in the Father's hands.

And Luke tells what happens next: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done. An angel from heaven appeared to him and strengthened him." (Luke 22:42-43) God didn't remove the cup, but he gave strength to drink it. Sometimes God changes the situation. Sometimes he changes the one going through it. Both are answers to prayer.

Have you ever used a GPS? When you miss an exit, it doesn't yell at you. It simply says: "recalculating route." God's will is a bit like that. Even when you've taken the wrong road, he doesn't abandon you: he redirects you. But for the GPS to work, you have to let it decide the destination.

Watch out for a misunderstanding: praying "your will be done" doesn't mean giving up by saying "anyway, God will do what he wants." The Bible shows that prayer truly changes things: "The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective." God's will is often to heal, to save, to deliver, to provide. Praying his will is therefore also claiming it with faith where he has already revealed it in his Word.

How do you know it? Paul answers: "Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God's will is—his good, pleasing and perfect will." (Romans 12:2) The more you fill your mind with his Word, the more you recognize his will.

Prayer doesn't serve to bend God to my will, but to align my will with his.

## For Your Life

Is there a situation where you're struggling with God right now? A project, a relationship, a decision where your will and his seem to pull in two directions?

Do as Jesus did. First, be honest: tell him what you really want, without filter. Next, if your request aligns with what God has promised in his Word (the salvation of a loved one, healing, peace, provision), pray with faith and perseverance. And finally, let go: "Yet not as I will, but as you will."

It's not a defeat. It's trust. The One to whom you entrust your will is a Father who wants only your good.

pratique.texte: Write down the situation where your will and God's seem to oppose each other. Tell him without filter what you really want. Jesus did this in Gethsemane.
If your request matches a clear promise in the Bible (a loved one's salvation, peace, provision, wisdom), find a verse that carries it and pray it with perseverance this week.
End with Jesus' words: "Not as I will, but as you will." If it's too hard today, say: "Lord, help me be able to say this." That's a real beginning.

days.question: In what situation am I struggling to say "not as I will, but as you will," and why?
days.priere: Our Father, may your will be done on earth as it is in heaven, and first in my life. I tell you honestly what I want. I entrust it to you. Where your Word reveals your will, I claim it with faith; where I don't understand, I trust you. Strengthen me as you strengthened Jesus. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Prayer doesn't serve to bend God to my will, but to align my will with his.

days.title: Give Us Today Our Daily Bread
days.meditation:
## The Context

After speaking about God's glory, his kingdom, and his will, Jesus teaches us to speak about… bread. Nothing is too small for God. The same lips that worship the Creator of the universe can ask him for food today.

This phrase refers to a story that all of Jesus' listeners knew: the manna in the wilderness. Israel had just left Egypt, there was nothing to eat, and the people grumbled. God responds: "The Lord said to Moses, 'I will rain down bread from heaven for you. The people are to go out each day and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test them and see whether they will follow my instructions. On the sixth day they are to prepare what they bring in, and that is to be twice as much as they gather on the other days.'" (Exodus 16:4) Each morning, manna covered the ground. Everyone gathered enough for the day. Those who tried to save some for the next day discovered it was full of maggots.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

God wanted to teach his people an essential lesson: daily dependence. Not a confidence for the year, but for today. Not reserves to do without God, but a daily appointment with his faithfulness.

There is the story of George Müller, a pastor who in the nineteenth century in Bristol cared for thousands of orphans without ever asking anyone for money, only God. One morning there was nothing to eat for breakfast. Müller had the children sit at the table and thanked God for the food he would provide. A few moments later, a baker knocked on the door: he hadn't been able to sleep and felt he should bake them bread. Then a milkman, whose cart had just broken down right in front of the orphanage, offered his milk rather than let it spoil.

Whether or not the story was embellished by those who tell it, it illustrates what Jesus promises: "So do not worry, saying, 'What shall we eat?' or 'What shall we drink?' or 'What shall we wear?' For the pagans run after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them." (Matthew 6:31-32)

"Our daily bread" concerns not just food. It's everything you need to live today: a roof, a job, health, strength, wisdom for a decision, patience with your children, courage for a difficult appointment. Paul experienced this: "And my God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:19)

And notice again: "our" bread. It's not "my" bread. When I pray this phrase, I am also invited to think of those who have no bread today, and sometimes God will answer their prayer through me.

God doesn't give you the provision for your whole life all at once; he gives you the grace of today, and he waits for you tomorrow morning.

## For Your Life

What worries you right now materially? Bills, work, a project, your children's future? Worry tries to live tomorrow with today's strength. Jesus tells you: ask for today's bread.

Today, make a very concrete list of your needs for the day, and present them to God without shame, like a child to his Father. Then thank him for three things he has already given you this week. Gratitude is the best antidote to worry.

And ask yourself: is there someone around me who is lacking "bread" today, in the broad sense? Maybe you are the answer to their prayer.

pratique.texte: Write down the concrete needs of today (a bill, an appointment, strength for your day, patience with your children) and present them to God one by one, without shame.
Note three things God has given you this week, even small ones: a meal, a call, a moment of peace. Gratitude loosens the grip of worry.
Spot someone around you who is lacking something: food, presence, administrative help, encouragement. Make a concrete gesture for them by the end of the week.

days.question: Am I living with tomorrow's anxiety, or today's trust? What specific need am I going to entrust to God this morning?
days.priere: Our Father, give us today our daily bread. I entrust you with my needs for this day, without shame. Thank you for all you have already given me. Deliver me from tomorrow's anxiety, and make me an answer for those around me who are lacking. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God doesn't give me my whole life all at once; he gives me the grace of today.

days.title: Forgive Us as We Forgive
days.meditation:
## The Context

"Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." This is the only phrase of the Lord's Prayer that Jesus comments on right after teaching it: "For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins." (Matthew 6:14-15)

Jesus knew this would be the hardest point. Receiving forgiveness is wonderful. Giving it is often a battle.

One day, Peter asks the question many are asking: "Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother or sister who sins against me? Up to seven times?" He thinks he's being generous. Jesus answers: "up to seventy times seven," in other words, without counting. And he tells a parable.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

A servant owes his king ten thousand talents. It's an astronomical sum: a talent represented the wages of many years of work. This debt, he could never repay it, even in ten lives. The servant begs, and the king, moved with compassion, forgives him his entire debt. Then that same servant goes out, meets a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, a few months' wages, seizes him by the throat and has him thrown in prison.

When the king learns of it, he is angry: "Then the master called the servant in. 'You wicked servant,' he said, 'I canceled all that debt of yours because you begged me to. Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?'" (Matthew 18:32-33)

The lesson is clear: when I refuse to forgive, I forget how much I have been forgiven. The cross of Jesus erased a debt I could never repay. The offenses done to me, even serious ones, are "hundred denarii" compared to it.

I want to be very clear: forgiving doesn't mean what was done to you wasn't serious. It doesn't mean excusing, forgetting, or necessarily trusting again or returning to a dangerous relationship. Forgiveness means giving up making the other person pay, and putting justice in God's hands.

Corrie ten Boom, a Dutch Christian who had hidden Jews during World War II, was deported to the Ravensbrück camp, where her sister Betsie died. After the war, while preaching forgiveness in Germany, a man came up to shake her hand at the end of the meeting. She recognized him: he was one of the cruelest guards in the camp. He told her he had become a Christian and asked for her forgiveness. Corrie said she felt nothing but anger. So she prayed silently: "Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness." She reached out her hand, and she felt God's love flow through her arm.

Forgiveness is not first a feeling, it's a decision. The feelings usually follow later.

Forgiveness is opening the door of a prison… and discovering that the prisoner was me.

## For Your Life

Is there a name that comes to mind as you read these lines? A parent, an ex, a friend who betrayed you, a church leader who hurt you, yourself perhaps?

Today, don't force your emotions, but make an act of will before God. You can pray like this: "Lord, I choose to forgive [name] for [what he did]. I give up making him pay. I entrust my wound to you and put justice in your hands. Heal my heart." You may need to say this several times: it's not a failure, it's the way.

And don't forget the first part of the phrase: "forgive us." You too need forgiveness today. Simply confess to him what weighs on your conscience, and receive his grace. "Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you." (Ephesians 4:32)

pratique.texte: If a name comes to mind, pray out loud: "Lord, I choose to forgive... for... I give up making them pay. Heal my heart." You may need to say this again: that's normal.
Forgiveness does not mean staying in a situation of violence or pretending nothing happened. If you are in danger or seriously hurt, protect yourself and ask for help from a leader or professional.
Confess to God today what weighs on your conscience, simply, then read 1 John 1:9 out loud. If you have hurt someone, ask them for forgiveness this week.

days.question: What person do I still need to forgive, and what is holding me back from making this act of will before God?
days.priere: Our Father, forgive me my sins. Thank you for erasing a debt I could not pay. Today, by your grace, I choose to forgive those who have hurt me. I cannot do this alone: give me your forgiveness and heal my heart. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Forgiveness is opening the door of a prison and discovering that the prisoner was me.

days.title: Deliver Us from Evil
days.meditation:
## The Context

"Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." This phrase can be surprising: does God push us toward evil? James answers clearly: "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God'; for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire." (James 1:13-14) God tempts no one. But he allows us to go through trials, and in those trials, the enemy seeks to make us fall. Jesus teaches us to pray: "Keep me from falling, and deliver me from the hands of the enemy."

Jesus himself went through this. Right after his baptism, he is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where he fasts for forty days, and then he is tempted by the devil.

## What Jesus Teaches Us

Look at how the devil attacks Jesus: when he is hungry, the devil offers to turn stones into bread. He then tries to make him prove his identity: "If you are the Son of God..." Then he offers him all the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. The enemy always targets the same points: our needs, our identity, our ambition. And he often chooses our moments of weakness: tiredness, loneliness, discouragement.

And look at how Jesus responds. He does not argue, he does not negotiate. Three times, he says: "It is written." And the last time: "Jesus said to him, 'Away with you, Satan! For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.'" (Matthew 4:10) Jesus overcame temptation with the same weapon available to you: the Word of God, spoken with authority.

In Greek mythology, sirens attracted sailors with an irresistible song, and ships crashed on the rocks. Odysseus had himself tied to the mast so he would not give in. But Orpheus found another solution: when his ship passed by the sirens, he played music even more beautiful, and the sailors did not even hear their song. The best defense against temptation is not only to grit your teeth; it is to be filled with something more beautiful: God's presence, his Word, his love.

And God makes a promise to those who are tempted: "No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it." (1 Corinthians 10:13) There is always a way out. Always.

Finally, Jesus has given you real authority over the enemy. James says it in one sentence: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." (James 4:7) Notice the order: first submit to God, then resist the devil. It is not our strength that makes the enemy flee; it is the name of Jesus and our submission to him.

Temptation knocks at the door; it is you who decides whether to open it.

## For Your Life

Know your weak points. What are the times, places, screens, and relationships where you fall most often? To pray "lead us not into temptation" also means making concrete decisions: not voluntarily putting yourself on the path of the trap.

Fill yourself with God's Word. Choose today one or two verses that directly answer your main temptation, and memorize them. The day the enemy attacks, you will be able to say like Jesus: "It is written."

And if you have fallen, do not stay on the ground. Deliver us from evil also means: "Lift me up, cleanse me, set me free." The God who teaches you to pray this phrase is the one who has already defeated the enemy at the cross.

pratique.texte: Write down the times, places, screens, or relationships where you fall most often. Then make one concrete decision to avoid one of them (a filter, a rule, a schedule, an accountability partner).
Choose a verse that directly answers your main temptation and memorize it today. Write it on your phone so you have it on hand when the attack comes.
Do not stay on the ground. Confess, receive forgiveness, and get back up today. If it is a fall that keeps returning, talk to someone you trust: light sets free.

days.question: What is my main point of weakness when facing temptation, and what verse will I memorize to answer it?
days.priere: Our Father, do not lead me into temptation, and deliver me from evil. I submit myself to you. Fill me with your Word and your presence. In Jesus' name, I resist the enemy. Thank you for the way out you always give me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Temptation knocks at the door; it is me who decides whether to open it.

days.title: Persevere in Prayer
days.meditation:
## The Context

The Lord's Prayer ends, in Matthew's version, with an explosion of praise: "For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen!" You begin by worshiping, and you end by worshiping. In between, you have trusted everything to God.

But Jesus knew there would be a trap: becoming discouraged when the answer is delayed. That is why he tells a parable with a very clear intention: "And he told them a parable, to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart." (Luke 18:1)

## What Jesus Teaches Us

In a city, there is an unjust judge who does not fear God and does not care about people. And there is a widow, without power, without connections, without money, who comes to him repeatedly asking for justice. The judge refuses for a long time, then finally gives in, simply because she wears him out.

Attention: Jesus does not say that God resembles this judge. He says the opposite! If even an unjust judge eventually responds to persistence, how much more will your Father, who loves you, answer those who cry out to him day and night!

The prophet Elijah experienced this perseverance. After three and a half years of drought, God had promised rain. Elijah goes to the top of Mount Carmel, kneels down, his face between his knees, and prays. He sends his servant to look toward the sea. "There is nothing." He prays again. "There is nothing." Seven times. "And at the seventh time he said, 'Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising from the sea.' And Elijah said, 'Go up, say to Ahab, "Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you."'" (1 Kings 18:44)

Elijah did not stop praying at the sixth time. How many prayers are abandoned just before the little cloud?

Persevering does not mean that God is deaf or that you have to convince him by force of words. Perseverance works mainly in us: it deepens our faith, purifies our motivations, teaches us to depend on him. And sometimes there is also invisible spiritual warfare, as Daniel discovered when the angel explained to him that his prayer had been heard on the first day, but he had been held back.

Paul sums up this life of prayer in three verbs: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you." (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18) To pray without ceasing does not mean to stay on your knees twenty-four hours a day; it means to live in constant conversation with God, while driving, in the shower, at work, before sleeping.

God's delay is not a refusal; often, it is an appointment being prepared.

## For Your Life

During these ten days, you have gone through the entire Lord's Prayer: approaching God as a Father, contemplating his greatness, worshiping his name, seeking his kingdom, accepting his will, entrusting your needs to him, forgiving, resisting evil. You now have a framework for your entire life of prayer.

Today, I invite you to two things. First, go through the Lord's Prayer slowly, phrase by phrase, and at each phrase, add your own words, your own life. That is how it becomes your prayer.

Next, choose one or two prayers that you had stopped persevering in: a loved one who does not know God, a healing, a restoration, a calling. Write them down, date them, and take them up each day. And when you see the little cloud, do not forget to come back and give thanks.

Because to him belong the kingdom, the power, and the glory. Amen!

pratique.titre: Pray the Lord's Prayer in Your Own Words
pratique.texte: Go through the Lord's Prayer phrase by phrase and, after each phrase, add your own prayer: your loved ones, your concerns, your gratitude. It becomes your prayer.
Write down one or two prayers that you had stopped persevering in. Date them. Take them up each day this week, and note the answers when they come.
This plan ends, but your appointment with God continues. Keep the same time slot tomorrow. If you can, find someone to pray with once a week, even by phone.

days.question: What prayer have I abandoned too soon, and am I ready to take it up again with perseverance, like Elijah on Mount Carmel?
days.priere: Our Father, for yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory. Thank you for teaching me to pray. Give me Elijah's perseverance and the widow's faith. I take up again today the prayers I had abandoned, and I trust you for the time of your answer. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God's delay is not a refusal; often, it is an appointment being prepared.

items.title: 40 Days with Jesus
items.subtitle: 40 days to walk with Jesus, from Bethlehem to the empty tomb, and let his life transform yours.
items.summary: What if, for 40 days, you walked alongside Jesus as his disciples did? You'll see him born in a manger, call fishermen, touch lepers, calm a storm, weep at a tomb, wash feet, carry a cross… and walk out alive from the grave. Each day: a passage from the Gospels to read, a meditation full of stories and examples, a question to reflect on, a prayer, and a phrase to remember. The goal isn't to know more about Jesus, but to know him. Bible texts: based on the English Standard Version.

days.title: God Came in Person
days.meditation:
## Part 1: The King Arrives

For 40 days, you're going to walk with Jesus. Not study him from a distance, like a character in history: walk with him, like Peter, John, Mary, or Zacchaeus. You'll see him born, call, heal, weep, die, and rise again. And at the end, I'm praying that you'll be able to say, like those who met him: "I knew of him by name. Now I know him."

John doesn't begin his Gospel with a manger, but with eternity: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made." (John 1:1-3)

## When God Becomes One of Us

An old story tells of a farmer, one snowy winter evening. Frantic birds throw themselves against his windows, lost in the cold. He opens the barn door wide, lights the lamp, scatters seeds on the straw. Nothing works: the birds are afraid of him. He tries to shepherd them, but they flee. Then he sighs: "If only I could become a bird, for just a moment, I could speak to them in their language, and they'd follow me to the warmth." At that very moment, the bells of the nearby church ring out Christmas. And he understands.

That's exactly what God did: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth." (John 1:14)

God didn't send us a message. He came in person. He didn't shout from heaven: he took a body, a voice, carpenter's hands, feet that grew tired on the roads. He knew hunger, fatigue, tears, betrayal. The Creator of the universe lived in a neighborhood, with neighbors.

And if you want to know what God looks like, you no longer have to guess: "No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known." (John 1:18) Everything you'll see of Jesus over these 40 days—his tenderness with the wounded, his firmness with the hypocrites, his compassion for the crowds—that's the face of God.

## For Your Life

John also warns us: the light has come, and many haven't received it. But he adds an incredible promise: "But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God, who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God." (John 1:12)

Receiving Jesus isn't just believing that he existed. It's opening the door of your life to him, like the farmer opening his barn. Maybe you did that a long time ago, and you need to rekindle the flame. Maybe you've never really done it.

Today, before you begin this journey, just tell him: "Jesus, I want to know you, not just know things about you. Over these 40 days, show me who you are." He didn't come all the way from heaven to stay a stranger in your life.

pratique.texte: Tell Jesus, in your own words: "I want to know you, not just know things about you." If you've never received him into your life, do it today (John 1:12).
Choose a specific time and place for these 40 days: when you wake up, during a break, in the evening. Set an alarm. A fixed appointment is better than a good intention.
Invite someone to do this plan with you (using the "plan together" feature or just a simple message each evening). You'll stick with it longer with a companion.

days.question: Do I know Jesus personally, or only by name? What am I expecting from these 40 days with him?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, eternal Word, thank you for coming to me. You didn't send a message—you came in person. I open the door of my life to you. Over these 40 days, show me your face, and help me know you truly. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God didn't send us a message: he came in person.

days.title: No Room at the Inn
days.meditation:
## The Story

A decree from Emperor Augustus, a census, a journey of over a hundred kilometers for a pregnant woman, a town packed to the brim. And this sentence, which says it all: "And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn." (Luke 2:7)

The King of kings isn't born in a palace, but in a place where animals are fed. His first cradle is a manger. No one had reserved a room for the Son of God.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Look at who receives the first birth announcement. Not the emperor in Rome. Not the high priest in Jerusalem. Not the scholars. Shepherds, at night, in the fields. In those days, shepherds were looked down on: they were suspected of theft, their testimony wasn't worth much in court, and their work often kept them from going to the temple. Yet they're the ones God chooses: "And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.'" (Luke 2:10-11)

"For all the people." For the shepherds as for the kings. For the one who smells like the stable as for the one who smells like perfume. From his birth, Jesus announces the agenda: no one is too small, too dirty, or too far away to be invited.

The first birth announcement of the Son of God wasn't sent to the palace, but to the shepherds in the night.

## For Your Life

There's a question running through this story: Is there room for Jesus? The innkeeper of Bethlehem probably wasn't cruel. He was simply full. Too many people, too much noise, too much to manage. He didn't turn Jesus away: he just had no room.

What if that's your situation? Your life isn't closed to God—it's just full. Full of work, worries, screens, notifications, projects. Jesus never forces his way in. But he makes do with little: a manger was enough for him. He's not asking you for a perfect life, neat and decorated. He's asking you for room.

Notice also the shepherds' reaction. They don't sit around discussing it: they go see, they tell others, and they leave praising God (Luke 2:20). They came as shepherds, they left as witnesses. Nothing had changed in their job—their sheep were still waiting. But they had changed.

Today, ask yourself: what's cluttering my life so much that there's no room left for Jesus? And make room for him, concretely: a time, a place, a decision. Even a manger—he transforms it into a place of glory.

pratique.texte: Identify what fills your life so much that there's no room for Jesus (screens, work, busyness). Choose one thing to reduce this week and give that time to God.
Who's left out around you (a lonely person, a coworker people avoid, an elderly neighbor)? Reach out to them this week: the good news is for them too.
The shepherds left telling others. Share with someone today something God has done for you recently, even something simple.

days.question: What fills my life so much that I leave little room for Jesus? What will I change concretely?
days.priere: Jesus, King born in a manger, thank you for coming for the small, the forgotten, the night shepherds. Forgive me for sometimes being too full to make room for you. Today I open my heart, my time, and my priorities to you. Come and live in me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus doesn't ask for a perfect life—he asks for room.

days.title: Prepare the Way
days.meditation:
## The Story

Before Jesus begins his ministry, God sends a strange man: John the Baptist. He lives in the desert, wears a garment of camel's hair, and eats locusts and wild honey. Not exactly an influencer profile. Yet crowds come from everywhere to listen to him. His message fits in one sentence: "In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" (Matthew 3:2-3)

## What This Reveals

In ancient times, when a king was about to visit a region, a messenger was sent ahead. The inhabitants would repair the roads, fill in the holes, remove the stones, smooth out the bumps. You didn't receive a king on a torn-up road. Even today, when a head of state visits a city, sometimes they resurface the road the day before.

John is that messenger. And the way to be prepared isn't made of earth: it's the heart. The word "repent" frightens many people, but it's full of hope. To repent is to turn around. It's like your GPS saying "recalculating route": you took the wrong road, it's not the end of your journey, but you need to turn around.

John doesn't settle for fine words. To the religious people who come to be baptized as a habit, he says: "Bear fruit in keeping with repentance," (Matthew 3:8) In other words: don't show me your tears, show me your life. Real repentance shows: in the way you speak, spend money, forgive, love.

And John knows his place. He, the star of the moment, says about Jesus: "I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire." (Matthew 3:11) The greatest of the prophets calls himself unworthy to carry Jesus' sandals. That's the mark of a true servant: he prepares the way, then he steps aside.

## For Your Life

The King wants to come into every area of your life. But there may be holes to fill: wounds never healed, forgiveness never given. Mountains to level: pride, resentment, a habit you've been justifying for too long. Crooked paths to straighten: a lie, an unclear relationship, a deal that's not quite honest.

The good news is you're not preparing the way alone. John announces that Jesus will baptize "with the Holy Spirit and fire." The one asking you to turn around also gives you the strength to do it.

Today, take a moment of silence and ask: "Lord, what way should I prepare for you?" Then take one concrete step of repentance: an apology, a restitution, a decision. The King is just waiting for that to come in.

pratique.texte: Take a moment of silence and ask: "Lord, what way should I prepare for you?" Write down what comes to mind: a grudge, a lie, a habit.
Choose a visible act this week: apologize, repay a debt, stop a dishonest practice, call someone you're at odds with.
John told soldiers and tax collectors to change the way they worked (Luke 3:12-14). Is there anything to straighten out in the way you work or study?

days.question: What "crooked path" of my life is the Lord asking me to straighten this week?
days.priere: Lord, I want to prepare the way for you. Show me the holes to fill, the mountains to level, the crooked paths to straighten. I turn around from where I've drifted from you. Come and reign in every area of my life. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Repentance isn't the end of your journey—it's a recalculation of your route.

days.title: My Beloved Son
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus is about thirty years old. He leaves the carpenter's workshop in Nazareth, walks to the Jordan, and gets in line in the middle of sinners coming to confess their sins. John is astonished: surely he should be baptized by Jesus! But Jesus insists. The one who never sinned stands in the place of sinners. The whole Gospel is already there.

Then the sky opens: "As soon as Jesus was baptized, he came up out of the water. And behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him. And behold, a voice from heaven said, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'" (Matthew 3:16-17)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Pay careful attention to when the Father speaks these words. Jesus hasn't healed anyone yet. He hasn't preached a sermon, multiplied bread, or cast out a demon. For thirty years, he was a carpenter in a village nobody talked about. Yet the Father says: "I am proud of you. You are my beloved Son."

The Father's love comes before performance. Jesus didn't serve to be loved; he served because he was loved.

Imagine a father in the stands at his child's first game. The whistle hasn't even blown, and he's already shouting: "That's my son!" He doesn't wait to see the score to be proud. He's proud because it's his child.

And right after this moment, what happens? Jesus is led into the wilderness to be tempted, and the enemy's first attack is: "If you are the Son of God..." (Matthew 4:3). The enemy always attacks identity first. But Jesus holds firm, because he just heard his Father's voice.

## For Your Life

Many Christians live exhausted because they're trying to earn a love they already have. They serve, pray, give, commit... so God will love them a little more. But the Gospel turns it all around: in Christ, what the Father said about Jesus, he says about you. "He predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace, which he freely bestowed on us in the Beloved." (Ephesians 1:5-6)

You don't have to earn your place at the table: you're family. Before your first achievement and after your worst failure, the Father looks at you with the same affection.

So today, before you do anything for God, take five minutes to simply receive. Close your eyes and listen to the Father tell you: "You are my beloved child." Then go serve, not to be loved, but because you're already loved. That changes everything: you no longer serve in fear of disappointing, but in the joy of being like your Father.

pratique.texte: Before you do anything for God today, take five minutes to listen to the Father tell you: "You are my beloved child." Begin your day with that.
Choose a service you do often out of fear of disappointing. This week, do it remembering: I do this because I'm loved, not to be loved.
Tell your child today that you're proud of them for who they are, not for what they've achieved. You're giving them a glimpse of the Father's heart.

days.question: Am I serving God to be loved, or because I'm already loved? What does that change concretely?
days.priere: Father, thank you for loving me before I do anything for you. I receive today your word over my life: I am your beloved child. Free me from the need to earn your love, and let all my service flow from this assurance. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus didn't serve to be loved; he served because he was loved.

days.title: It Is Written
days.meditation:
## The Story

Right after the voice from heaven comes the wilderness. Forty days without food. And when Jesus is hungry, when he's at his weakest, the tempter approaches. Satan never attacks when you're strong; he waits until you're tired, alone, starving.

Three temptations, and three doors the enemy still tries to open in our lives.

The first targets appetite: "Command these stones to become bread." Satisfy your need, right now, your way. The second targets spectacle: "Throw yourself down from the temple," do something sensational, show everyone who you are. The third targets the shortcut: "All these kingdoms I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." The devil offers Jesus what the Father already promised him... but without the cross.

The devil always offers the crown without the cross.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Each time, Jesus responds the same way: "It is written." He doesn't argue, doesn't debate, doesn't do a miracle to prove anything. He draws his sword: the Word. "Jesus answered, 'It is written: Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.'" (Matthew 4:4)

Notice that all three of Jesus' answers come from the book of Deuteronomy. Jesus isn't quoting verses picked at random for the occasion: he knows Scripture because he's read it, meditated on it, memorized it long before the wilderness. You don't reach for your sword when the enemy strikes; you already have it in hand.

And Satan, he also knows how to quote the Bible (Matthew 4:6). But he quotes it by cutting, twisting, taking it out of context. That's why Jesus responds: "Jesus said to him, 'It is also written: Do not put the Lord your God to the test.'" (Matthew 4:7) A single sentence of the Bible ripped from its context can become a trap; the whole Scripture is a light.

## For Your Life

Jesus wasn't tempted so you'd admire his strength, but so he could understand you and come to your aid: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin." (Hebrews 4:15)

He knows what it's like to be hungry, to be tired, to hear a small voice saying: "Take the shortcut, nobody will know." And he won because you could win in him.

What's your most frequent temptation? Appetite (sex, food, money, screens)? Spectacle (image, likes, the need to be seen)? The shortcut (lying, cheating, compromising)? Today, choose a verse that specifically answers that temptation. Write it down, memorize it, and the next time that voice comes, respond like your Master: "It is written."

pratique.texte: Appetite, spectacle, or shortcut: which of these temptations touches you most? Write it down honestly.
Choose a verse that directly answers this temptation, memorize it, and make it your phone wallpaper. In the moment of attack, respond like Jesus: "It is written."
Identify when you're most vulnerable (tired, alone, late at night) and make a concrete decision for those times: go to bed earlier, call someone, leave your phone out of the bedroom.

days.question: What is my most frequent temptation, and what verse will I memorize to answer it?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for conquering temptation for me. You know what I'm going through; you understand me. Give me a love for your Word so it's in my heart before the battle. When the voice of the shortcut comes, make me answer like you: it is written. Amen.
days.aRetenir: You don't reach for your sword when the enemy strikes: you already have it in hand.

days.title: Come and See
days.meditation:
## Part 2: The Calling

Jesus begins his ministry. And the first thing he does isn't organize a campaign or build a building: he calls people. All of church history begins with a few encounters on the banks of a river.

## The Story

Two of John the Baptist's disciples start following Jesus. He turns around and asks them a question—the very first words Jesus speaks in the Gospel of John: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' And they said to him, 'Rabbi (which means Teacher), where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and you will see.' So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour." (John 1:38-39)

"What are you seeking?" Jesus doesn't start with a sermon but with a question. He's interested in what's in your heart. And his answer isn't an address or a program; it's an invitation: "Come and see."

Then faith spreads person to person. Andrew finds his brother Simon. Philip finds Nathanael. But Nathanael is skeptical: "Nathanael said to him, 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?' Philip said to him, 'Come and see.'" (John 1:46)

Nazareth was a village with no reputation. Nathanael has a prejudice, and Philip doesn't launch into a big debate. He simply says: come see for yourself.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

When Nathanael arrives, Jesus tells him: "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you." (John 1:48). Nathanael is stunned. What had happened under that fig tree? We don't know. A secret prayer, maybe, a question, a struggle. But Jesus knew.

Before you even sought him, Jesus saw you. Before anyone told you about him, he knew your fig tree: your questions, your doubts, your prayers that no one else heard.

Notice too what Jesus does with Simon: he gives him a new name, Cephas, which means Peter, "the rock." Simon was impulsive, unstable. Jesus doesn't see what he is, but what he will become.

## For Your Life

Jesus doesn't ask you to have all the answers before you follow him. He tells you: come and see. Faith isn't a leap into the void; it's a walk with someone who reveals himself along the way.

And look how the Gospel spread: a brother, a friend, a neighbor. Nobody gives a big sermon. Each person simply says: "I found someone, come see." You don't need to be a theologian to testify. You just need to have met Jesus and invite someone else to meet him too.

Today, think of someone in your life—a sibling, a friend, a coworker. And pray for a chance to tell them, in your own way: "Come and see."

pratique.texte: Jesus asks: "What are you seeking?" Write your honest answer today. What you're truly seeking says a lot about your heart.
Think of a secret prayer or a question you've carried for a long time. Remember that Jesus saw you there. Give him that specific matter.
Choose someone in your life and invite them simply: to a service, to watch a video, to read a Gospel with you. No debate, just an invitation.

days.question: Who in my life needs me to say in my own way: "Come and see"?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for seeing me before I even sought you. You know my fig trees, my questions and my secret prayers. I want to follow you, even without having all the answers. And give me the courage to invite others to come see you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus doesn't ask you to have all the answers: he says "come and see."

days.title: The Best Wine at Last
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus' first miracle does not take place in a synagogue, nor before a crowd, but in the middle of a wedding celebration in a small village called Cana. And he doesn't heal a sick person: he saves a party.

Back then, a wedding could last several days. Running out of wine was a public shame for the family, a humiliation that would be talked about for a long time in the village. Mary notices this and comes to Jesus. Then she says to the servants a sentence that deserves to be posted in every home: "His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'" (John 2:5)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus cares about what touches you. Not just your big spiritual crises: also your party that's going wrong, your embarrassment, your lack. Nothing is too ordinary for him.

And look at how the miracle happens. Jesus doesn't snap his fingers. He asks for something very simple, almost mundane: fill six large stone jars with water. Each one held about a hundred liters. It took back-and-forth trips to the well, carrying, pouring. Physical work, with no glory. But the servants fill them "to the brim" (John 2:7). Not halfway. To the brim.

The miracle came after obedience, not before. The servants poured water; as they carried it, it became wine.

And the result surprises everyone: "and said to him, 'Every man at the beginning sets out the good wine, and when the guests have well drunk, then the inferior. You have kept the good wine until now.'" (John 2:10)

## For Your Life

Maybe your life looks like this party: the wine has run out. Joy, energy, love in your marriage, passion for your work, fervor in your faith… Only empty jars remain.

Here are three lessons from Cana.

Bring your need to Jesus, as Mary did. She doesn't tell him what to do; she simply presents the problem to him: "They have no wine."

Do what he tells you, even if it seems ordinary. Sometimes God's answer starts with something simple: opening your Bible, asking forgiveness, going back to church, serving. Water in jars. Fill them to the brim.

And believe that God keeps the best for what comes next. The world serves the good wine at the beginning, then the lesser wine. With Jesus, it's the opposite. What comes is better than what has passed.

pratique.texte: Like Mary, present to Jesus what has run out in your life (joy, love in your marriage, energy, faith) in a simple sentence: "Lord, they have no wine here."

pratique.titre: Fill the Jar to the Brim
pratique.texte: What simple thing is Jesus asking you to do? Read his Word, go back to church, ask forgiveness, serve. Do it this week, fully, not halfway.
If the "wine" is missing at home, plan a time of quality this week with your spouse or children, and pray together, even two minutes.

days.question: In what area of my life has the "wine" run out? What simple thing is Jesus asking me to do?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you see my empty jars: what has run out in my life. I present them to you. I will do everything you tell me, even if it seems ordinary. I believe you have kept the best for what comes next. Change my water into wine. Amen.
days.aRetenir: With Jesus, the best wine is not behind you: it's ahead of you.

days.title: He Came by Night
days.meditation:
## The Story

Nicodemus is an important man: a Pharisee, a member of the Sanhedrin, the great Jewish council, and a recognized teacher. He has everything going for him: education, reputation, religion. Yet he comes to see Jesus… by night. Perhaps out of fear of what others will say, perhaps to have a real conversation in peace. He begins politely: "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God." But Jesus gets right to the point: "Jesus answered and said to him, 'Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.'" (John 3:3)

For Nicodemus, this is a shock. He thought he needed to improve; Jesus tells him he needs to start over. He thought he needed more religion; Jesus speaks to him of a new birth, of a life that comes from above.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

To help him understand, Jesus recalls a story that Nicodemus knows by heart: in the desert, when the people were bitten by serpents, Moses had lifted up a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived (Numbers 21:8-9). "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life." (John 3:14-15)

No need to heal the bite yourself. No need to earn healing. You simply had to look, with faith. And it is here that Jesus speaks perhaps the most well-known verse in all the Bible: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life. For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through Him might be saved." (John 3:16-17)

## For Your Life

The most beautiful part is the rest of Nicodemus' story. We find him twice more in John's Gospel. The first time, in the middle of the council, he dares to defend Jesus, timidly: "Does our law judge a man before it hears him and knows what he is doing?" (John 7:50-51). The second time, after the crucifixion, when the disciples are hiding, Nicodemus comes in broad daylight with about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury Jesus' body (John 19:39-40).

By night, then halfway, then in full light. Nicodemus' faith grew slowly, but it grew.

Maybe you are a Nicodemus. You believe, but in secret. You're afraid of what your family, your colleagues, your circle will say. Jesus doesn't reject you for that: he received Nicodemus by night. But he doesn't want to leave you in the night.

You can come to Jesus by night; he won't leave you in the night.

Today, ask yourself: what is the next step for me? Maybe to give your life to him for the first time, sincerely. Maybe to dare say around you that you believe in him. Take another step toward the light.

pratique.titre: Your Next Step Toward the Light
pratique.texte: Where are you at? By night, halfway, in full light? Choose a concrete step: give your life to Jesus, dare to say you're a Christian, get baptized, join a church.
As the people looked at the bronze serpent, take a moment to look at Jesus crucified for you. Read John 3:16, putting your name in place of "the world."

pratique.titre: If You're Afraid of What Others Think
pratique.texte: Choose just one trusted person to tell this week that you believe in Jesus. Courage grows step by step, as it did for Nicodemus.

days.question: Is there an area where I live my faith "by night," in secret? What step toward the light can I take this week?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for welcoming me even when I come by night, with my questions and my fears. I look toward you, lifted up on the cross for me, and I receive eternal life. Make me born from above, and make my faith grow into the full light. Amen.
days.aRetenir: You can come to Jesus by night; he won't leave you in the night.

days.title: The Woman at the Well
days.meditation:
## The Story

It is noon, the hottest part of the day. No one goes to get water at this hour: women go in the morning or evening, in the cool, together. But she comes alone, in the blazing sun. Why? Probably to avoid stares, whispers, comments. We discover later that she has had five husbands, and the man she is living with is not her husband.

And Jesus is there, sitting by the well, tired. He asks her for a drink. She is astonished: a Jew does not speak to a Samaritan woman, and a rabbi does not speak alone to a woman. Jesus has just broken three barriers with a single sentence: race, religion, and reputation.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus speaks to her of another water: "Jesus answered and said to her, 'Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst. But the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life.'" (John 4:13-14)

This woman had tried to quench her thirst in relationships, one after another. Five husbands, and always thirsty. Many people do the same today with other wells: money, success, pleasures, approval. You drink, and you're still thirsty. No person, no thing can fill a void that has the shape of God.

Then Jesus touches the sensitive point: "Go, call your husband." He knows her entire history. But notice: he doesn't humiliate her, he doesn't lecture her. He tells her the truth with a gentleness that sets her free instead of crushing her. Jesus knows your entire past, and he remains sitting by the well with you.

## For Your Life

What comes next is incredible: "The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and said to the men, 'Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did; could this be the Christ?'" (John 4:28-29)

She leaves her jar, what she had come for. She found something better. And she who fled stares now runs to the whole city. She who hid becomes Samaria's first evangelist. Her message is nothing complicated: "Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did." What was her shame becomes her testimony.

She who fled stares became the one who called the whole city.

What is your jar? The well where you keep returning, never satisfied? Today, Jesus waits for you by that well. Tell him your thirst, honestly. Let him touch your story. And let him turn your shame into testimony. What the enemy wanted to use to hide you, God can use to draw others to him.

pratique.texte: Where do you go to try to quench your thirst (relationships, approval, shopping, screens, alcohol)? Write it down, then tell Jesus: "Give me your living water."
Choose one specific thing to leave by the well this week: an unclear relationship, a habit, a dependency. If it's heavy, ask for help.
Think of a part of your story from which God has lifted you. When the right moment comes, dare to share it with someone going through the same thing.

days.question: What "well" do I keep returning to to fill my thirst? What do I want to leave by the well today?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you know my entire story, and you don't reject me. I have tried to quench my thirst at wells that don't satisfy. Give me your living water. I leave my jar. Turn my shame into testimony, so that others come to you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: What was her shame became her testimony.

days.title: The Spirit of the Lord Is Upon Me
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus returns to Nazareth, the village where he grew up. On the Sabbath, he enters the synagogue, as he usually does. Someone hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds the passage, and reads it before those who knew him as a child: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, Because He has anointed Me to preach the gospel to the poor; He has sent Me to heal the brokenhearted, To proclaim liberty to the captives, And recovery of sight to the blind, To set at liberty those who are oppressed, To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." (Luke 4:18-19)

Then he rolls up the book, sits down, and all eyes are fixed on him. He says simply: "Then He began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.'" (Luke 4:21)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

This is Jesus' program, his manifesto. Look at who he addresses: the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives, the blind, the oppressed. Jesus didn't come for people who are doing well, but for people who are broken. He didn't come to decorate the lives of those who already have everything, but to lift up those who have nothing left.

And notice where the power of this ministry comes from: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He has anointed Me." Even Jesus, the Son of God, exercised his ministry in the power of the Holy Spirit. If he needed it, how much more do we!

But the story takes a dark turn. At first, everyone is amazed. Then the questions come: "Is not this Joseph's son?" They know him too well. And when Jesus reminds them that God once blessed a foreign widow and a Syrian general rather than Israelites, the crowd becomes angry and wants to throw him off a cliff. Those who knew him best didn't recognize him.

## For Your Life

There are two lessons in this text.

First: if you feel poor, broken, captive, blind, or oppressed, this text is for you. You are exactly the kind of person Jesus came for. Your weakness is not an obstacle to his grace; it's the doorway in.

Second is a warning: familiarity is dangerous. The people of Nazareth were so used to Jesus that they saw nothing extraordinary in him anymore. It's a risk for those who grew up in church, who know all the stories by heart. You can know Jesus for so long that you stop marveling.

Today, ask the Lord to restore your sense of wonder. And reread this manifesto asking yourself: "Who around me is poor, broken, or captive?" Because what Jesus began, he continues to do today through his Church, filled with the same Spirit.

pratique.texte: If Jesus has become too familiar, read Luke 4:18-19 slowly as if for the first time, and thank him for one specific thing he has done for you.
Poor, brokenhearted, captive, blind, oppressed: which of these descriptions fits you today? Bring it to Jesus: this text is for you.
Choose one person around you who is poor, broken, or captive and do something concrete this week: a visit, a meal, help, a prayer.

days.question: Have I become too familiar with Jesus? Who around me needs to hear the good news of this manifesto?
