days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming for the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives. I bring to you what is broken in me. Forgive me when I've become too used to you. Restore my wonder, and fill me with your Spirit to continue your work around me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus didn't come for people who are doing well, but for people who are broken.

days.title: On Your Word
days.meditation:
## The Story

Simon has spent the entire night on the Lake of Gennesaret. He knows his trade: night is the best time to fish, when the fish come to the surface. And yet, nothing. Not a single fish. Early in the morning, exhausted, he washes his nets on the shore. The day is finished before it has begun.

That's when Jesus gets into his boat, teaches the crowd, and then says to him: "Launch out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch." Imagine the scene: a carpenter telling a professional fisherman how to fish. In broad daylight, in deep water, after a night of failure. Everything in Simon's experience tells him it's useless. And yet: "Simon answered and said to Him, 'Master, we have toiled all night and caught nothing; nevertheless at Your word I will let down the net.'" (Luke 5:5)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

"At Your word." That's the whole difference between experience and faith. Simon doesn't say, "I feel like this will work." He says, "I'm not so sure, but because it's you who says it, I'll do it." Faith isn't always a feeling; it's often a decision to obey.

The result exceeds everything: the nets begin to break, two boats are so full they start to sink. And Simon's reaction is surprising. He doesn't cry out for joy: he falls to Jesus' knees and says, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord!" Before Jesus' greatness, he sees his own smallness.

But Jesus doesn't leave. He answers him: "And so were also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon's partners. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid. From now on you will catch men.' So when they had brought their boats to land, they forsook all and followed Him." (Luke 5:10-11)

## For Your Life

Your experience tells you "it's useless"; his word tells you "launch out into the deep."

Maybe you feel like you've worked all night without catching anything. You've prayed about this situation, you've tried, you've persevered, and the nets are still empty. Your experience tells you: give up, it's over. But Jesus might be getting into your boat right now.

Notice that Jesus didn't choose people who had succeeded. He chose people who had just failed. And he used their failure as the place of a miracle and a calling.

Notice too the end of the story: "they forsook all and followed Him." On the day of their greatest catch ever, they leave the fish on the beach. Because they understood that the one who gives the catch is worth more than the catch itself.

Today, what is Jesus' word that seems illogical to you? Forgive, give, start over, dare? Simply tell him: "Lord, I don't understand everything, but on your word, I will let down the net."

pratique.texte: Write down the area where you feel like you've worked all night without catching anything. Bring it to Jesus just as it is.
What word of Jesus seems illogical in your situation (forgive, give, start over, wait)? Tell him: "On your word, I will do it," and take action this week.
If your job discourages you, pray before you start your workday: "Lord, get in my boat." Invite him into what you do most ordinarily.

days.question: In what area have I "worked all night without catching anything"? What word of Jesus am I going to dare to obey, even without understanding?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you see my nights without results and my empty nets. Today I'm not relying on my experience, but on your word. On your word, I will let down the net. And if you call me to follow you, give me the strength to leave everything for you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Faith is not always a feeling: it's often a decision to obey.

days.title: Four Friends and a Roof
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus is in Capernaum, in a house. The news spreads, and the crowd is so large that there's no room left, even outside the door. Then four men arrive carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. It's impossible to get in.

Most people would have given up: "We tried, we'll come back another time." Not them. They go up on the flat roof of the house, dig a hole through the roof made of earth and branches, and lower their friend right in front of Jesus. Imagine the dust falling on the guests, the homeowner seeing his roof torn open, the crowd looking up.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

And here's the sentence that moves me every time: "When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven you.'" (Mark 2:5)

"When Jesus saw their faith." Whose faith? The faith of the four friends. The paralyzed man said nothing, asked for nothing. It was his friends who believed for him, who carried him when he couldn't walk.

Then Jesus does something unexpected. Instead of healing the legs first, he forgives sins. He goes to the root, to the deepest need. The scribes are outraged: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" They're right on one point: only God can forgive. And that's exactly what Jesus is revealing. So, to prove his invisible authority, he performs a visible miracle: "But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins"—He said to the paralytic, "I say to you, arise, take up your bed, and go to your house." Immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went out in the presence of them all, so that all were amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!" (Mark 2:10-12)

## For Your Life

Some days you carry the stretcher; other days you're the one on it.

If today you're on the stretcher, paralyzed by fear, depression, grief, or sin, let yourself be carried. Accept that others pray for you, believe for you, carry you to Jesus. It's not weakness; it's the beauty of the Church.

If today you're standing, look around you: who is on a stretcher? Who can't move forward alone? You may not have the power to heal them, but you can carry them in prayer, invite them, walk with them, hold their hand. And sometimes you'll need to be creative and persistent: make a hole in the roof when all the doors seem closed.

Each of us needs four friends like those. And each of us is called to be one of the four.

Today, think of someone who can't move forward alone. Carry them before Jesus in prayer, and do something concrete for them: a call, a visit, a message. Jesus sees the faith of those who carry.

pratique.texte: Accept being carried: ask two or three people to pray for you this week. Tell them specifically what you're going through.
Choose one person who can't move forward alone and carry them: a call, a visit, a meal, daily prayer for a week.
Write the names of two or three people you could pray with regularly. Invite them for a prayer time this week, even over video call.

days.question: Am I the one carrying today or the one being carried? Who can I carry to Jesus this week?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for seeing the faith of those who carry. Thank you for the people who have carried me in prayer. Give me the strength to be a friend who carries others to you, with persistence and creativity. And when I am weak, teach me to let myself be carried. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Some days you carry the stretcher; other days you're the one on it.

days.title: The Physician of Sinners
days.meditation:
## The Story

Levi, also called Matthew, is sitting at his tax booth. He is a tax collector: he collects taxes for the Romans, the hated occupier. Tax collectors were often wealthy because they collected more than necessary and kept the difference. To the people, they were traitors and thieves. They were lumped together with prostitutes.

And Jesus passes by this booth. He doesn't take a detour. He looks at Levi and says two words to him: "As Jesus passed by, he saw a man named Levi sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And he rose and followed him." (Mark 2:14)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

No conditions first. Jesus doesn't tell him: "Pay back the money first, change jobs, go to the temple, and then we'll see." He calls him as he is, where he is. And Levi gets up, leaves everything, and follows him. A fisherman who leaves his boat can always go back to fishing; a tax collector who leaves his post will never get it back. Levi burns his bridges.

Then he throws a great feast at his house with all his friends: other tax collectors and people of ill repute. And Jesus sits at the table with them, eating, laughing, sharing. The religious leaders are scandalized: "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?" Jesus answers: "When Jesus heard this, he said to them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.'" (Mark 2:17)

Jesus presents himself as a doctor. A doctor doesn't run from the sick; he goes to them. Imagine a doctor who refused to enter a hospital because there were too many sick people. It would be absurd. Jesus goes where he is needed.

## For Your Life

This story has two messages, depending on where you find yourself.

If you feel like Levi, with a heavy past, a damaged reputation, things you're ashamed of, hear this: Jesus passes by your booth, and he calls you. Not when you become perfect: now. He doesn't ask you to be healthy to come to the doctor.

If you feel more like the religious leaders, ask yourself: do I see the Church as a museum for respectable people, or as a hospital for the wounded? Do I spend time with people who don't know Jesus, or do I stay only among Christians? Jesus wasn't afraid to be seen at the table with sinners. He didn't adopt their sin, but he shared their table.

Levi did the only thing he knew how to do: he invited his friends to meet Jesus over a good meal. And you? What table can you open this week so that someone might meet Jesus?

pratique.texte: Your past doesn't disqualify Jesus's call. Tell him today: "Here I am, just as I am." Then take one concrete step to follow him.
Like Levi, invite someone to your home or to a restaurant—someone who doesn't know Jesus. You don't need to preach: share a meal, listen, and let the conversation come naturally.
How do you welcome newcomers or those with a difficult past? This week, go greet someone who is alone at church or in your group.

days.question: Do I see the Church as a museum for respectable people, or as a hospital for the wounded? What table can I open this week?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, physician of my soul, thank you for calling me as I was. I had nothing to offer you, and you said: follow me. Give me your eyes for those far from you, and the courage to share their table so I can speak to them about you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus doesn't ask you to be healthy to come to the doctor.

days.title: Salt and Light
days.meditation:
## Part 3: His Word and His Power

Jesus goes up on a mountain, sits down, and begins the most famous sermon in history: the Sermon on the Mount. For several days, we will hear what he teaches and see what he does.

## The World Upside Down

Jesus's first words must have surprised the crowd: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." (Matthew 5:3-4)

Blessed are the poor, those who weep, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, those who are persecuted... The world says: blessed are the rich, the strong, those who never cry, those who crush others. Jesus says exactly the opposite. His kingdom is a world upside down, or rather, our world is upside down, and Jesus comes to set it right.

The Beatitudes are not a to-do list to earn blessing. They are declarations of happiness over people the world considers losers. If you're crying today, Jesus doesn't tell you "stop crying"; he tells you "you will be comforted."

## Salt and Light

Then Jesus looks at this crowd of simple people, peasants, fishermen, the sick, and says to them: "You are the salt of the earth." Not: "you will become," but: "you are."

Before the invention of refrigeration, salt was used to preserve meat and fish. Without salt, everything rotted in a few days. Salt also gave flavor. To be salt is to prevent decay around you and to give flavor to others' lives.

But salt is useless in the saltshaker. It must be spread, mixed, in contact. A Christian who stays only at church is salt in a saltshaker.

Then Jesus continues: "You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven." (Matthew 5:14-16)

## For Your Life

A light doesn't need to shout to be noticed. A lighthouse makes no noise; it shines, simply, and ships avoid the rocks because of it.

Notice the purpose of this light: so that people see your good works and "give glory to your Father." Not you. Your light isn't there to draw attention to yourself, but to show the way to God.

Where has God placed you? Your work, your school, your neighborhood, your family: that's where you must be salt and light. Today, ask yourself this question: if Christians disappeared from my surroundings, would anyone notice the difference? And choose one concrete act of kindness, honesty, or generosity so that someone sees the light of your Father.

pratique.texte: Where has God placed you (work, school, neighborhood, family)? Choose one specific place where you want to be salt this week.
Do one concrete act of kindness, honesty, or generosity that people will notice, so they glorify your Father, not you.
If you're going through a season of tears, reread Matthew 5:4 and write down what you expect from God's comfort. He doesn't ask you to hide your tears.

days.question: Where has God placed me to be salt and light? What concrete action will I take this week so my Father is glorified?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for saying I am the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Help me get out of the saltshaker. Where you've placed me, may my life prevent decay, give flavor, and show the way to you. May people see your works and glorify our Father. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Salt is useless in the saltshaker.

days.title: Seek First His Kingdom
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus continues his teaching and addresses a subject that concerns us all: worry. Money, food, clothes, the future. He begins with a question of the heart: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." (Matthew 6:21)

What you consider your treasure will always end up capturing your heart. Your bank statement and your calendar often say more about your faith than your prayers.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Then Jesus invites the crowd to look around them. He points to the birds flying over the mountain: "Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" (Matthew 6:26)

A bird makes no reserves for winter, doesn't worry about crisis, doesn't calculate retirement. It lives under the eye of the Creator, day after day. And Jesus adds: you are worth much more than them.

Then he shows them the lilies of the field, these wild flowers that no one planted: even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of them. If God clothes the grass of the field like this, which is here today and burned tomorrow, will he not care for you?

And Jesus asks a very practical question: "And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" Worry has never solved anything. A phrase often attributed to Corrie ten Boom says it this way: "Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength."

## For Your Life

Jesus's remedy is not "think of nothing," but "think of something else first": "But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble." (Matthew 6:33-34)

"First." Everything is in that word. It's not that your needs don't matter; Jesus even says the Father knows you need them. But order matters. When God is first, everything else finds its place.

It's like the buttons on a shirt: if you get the first one wrong, all the others will be misaligned. Put God on the first button, and the rest will follow.

And Jesus adds very practical wisdom: live one day at a time. God gives grace for today, not for imaginary problems three years from now.

Today, make a list of your worries. For each one, ask yourself: can I do something about this today? If yes, do it. If no, give it to the Father in prayer. Then make one concrete decision to seek God first: the first moment of your day, the first part of your money, the first place in your choices.

pratique.texte: Write down your worries. For each one: can I do something about this today? If yes, do it. If no, give it to the Father in prayer.
Choose one concrete way to seek God first: the first moment of your day, the first part of your money, the first place in a decision.
Tonight, before bed, thank God for three provisions of your day, and leave tomorrow to him. Do this every evening this week.

days.question: What worry occupies my mind the most right now? How can I concretely seek God "first" this week?
days.priere: Father, you feed the birds and clothe the flowers of the field: you will care for me. I give you my worries, one by one. I choose to seek you first, you and your kingdom. Give me the grace to live today, one day at a time, under your gaze. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength.

days.title: The House on the Rock
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus concludes his great sermon with a little story that every Sunday school child knows. Two men build a house. From the outside, you might see no difference: the same facade, the same walls, the same roof. The difference is hidden underground, in the foundations. "Therefore, whoever hears these sayings of Mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it did not fall, for it was founded on the rock." (Matthew 7:24-25)

"But everyone who hears these sayings of Mine, and does not do them, will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell. And great was its fall." (Matthew 7:26-27)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Notice this carefully: both men heard Jesus' words. They were both at the same sermon, maybe sitting side by side. The difference isn't between those who hear and those who don't hear, but between those who put it into practice and those who just listen.

And notice this too: the storm hits both houses. The rain, the floods, the winds. Jesus doesn't promise that the house on the rock will be spared from the storm. He promises that it will stand firm.

The Leaning Tower of Pisa is known throughout the world because it tilts. Why? Not because its walls are built poorly—its arches and columns are magnificent. But its foundations are shallow, laid on soil that's too soft. From the first floors upward, it began to lean. Beautiful construction never makes up for bad foundations.

## For Your Life

The storm doesn't create the cracks—it reveals them.

Sooner or later, a storm will come into your life: an illness, a loss, a betrayal, a financial crisis, a failure. This is not the moment to start digging foundations. Foundations are built in good weather, day by day, when everything is fine and it seems unnecessary.

Building on the rock isn't just reading the Bible, going to church, or listening to good messages. It's putting it into practice. Forgiving when Jesus says to forgive. Giving when he says to give. Being honest when no one is watching. Every act of obedience is another stone in your foundations.

Just before this story, Jesus speaks of two gates: a wide one that many take, and a narrow one that leads to life. Ease attracts crowds; truth demands courage.

Today, choose just one thing that you've heard in the Sermon on the Mount that you're not yet putting into practice. Not ten: one. And put it into practice this week. That's how you build a house that will stand in the storm.

pratique.texte: Choose just one thing from the Sermon on the Mount that you're not yet putting into practice (forgiving, not judging, praying in secret, giving) and practice it this week.

pratique.titre: Dig While the Weather Is Good
pratique.texte: If things are going well right now, this is the best time to strengthen your foundations: choose a spiritual habit to build before the next storm comes.
If a storm is here, ask yourself without shame: what crack is it revealing? Talk about it with God and with a mature believer.

days.question: Which word of Jesus am I hearing without putting it into practice? What step of obedience will I take this week?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you are my rock. I don't just want to hear your words; I want to put them into practice. Show me the cracks in my foundations, and help me build my life on you, day by day, so that I stand firm when the storm comes. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The storm doesn't create the cracks—it reveals them.

days.title: Say Only One Word
days.meditation:
## The Story

A Roman centurion lives in Capernaum. An officer of the occupying army, commanding a hundred soldiers. Normally, a man like him was despised by the Jews. But this one is different: he loves the Jewish people, and has even built their synagogue. And he has a servant whom he loves deeply, who is about to die.

He sends Jewish elders to beg Jesus to come. Jesus sets out. But as he approaches the house, the centurion sends friends to tell him: "Jesus went with them. Now when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof. Therefore I did not even think myself worthy to come to You. But say the word, and my servant will be healed.'" (Luke 7:6-7)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

The centurion understands something that many religious leaders have not grasped: Jesus' authority has no limit of distance. He explains: "For I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me. And I say to one, 'Go,' and he goes; and to another, 'Come,' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this,' and he does it." In the military, an order given by the one in authority is carried out, even if the officer is not present. The centurion has understood that sickness itself obeys Jesus.

And Jesus is amazed: "When Jesus heard these things, He marveled at him, and turned around and said to the crowd that followed Him, 'I say to you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel.'" (Luke 7:9)

There are only two times in the Gospels when it's said that Jesus is astonished: here, before the faith of a foreigner, and in Nazareth, before the unbelief of his own village (Mark 6:6). Jesus marvels at the faith of a man who did not grow up in religion, but who understood who Jesus was.

## For Your Life

Notice two things in the heart of this man.

First, humility: "I am not worthy." The elders had said of him: "He deserves that You do this for him." But he says: "I am not worthy." Faith is not built on our merit, but on Jesus' authority.

Second, trust in the word: "Say the word." No need to see, to touch, to feel. One word from Jesus is enough. The servant is healed from a distance, at that very hour.

Maybe you're praying for someone who is far away: a child who has drifted from God, a parent who is sick in another country, a friend in a desperate situation. You cannot be there. But Jesus' word has no limit of distance. No ocean, no hospital wall, no closed door can stop it.

Today, pray for a person who is far from you, with the faith of the centurion: "Lord, I am not worthy, but say only one word, and she will be healed, he will be saved, she will be set free."

pratique.texte: Choose a person who is distant (a child who has left, a parent who is sick in another country, a friend in crisis) and pray for them with the centurion's faith: "Say only one word."
Begin your prayer with: "Lord, I am not worthy," then present your request with confidence. The two go together.
The centurion interceded for his servant. Is there someone for whom you have responsibility and whom you could pray for this week?

days.question: For which person far from me will I pray with the centurion's faith?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof, but I know that Your word has all authority. No distance can stop it. Say only one word for those I love who are far from me. Give me faith that will amaze You. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus' word has no limit of distance.

days.title: Do You See This Woman?
days.meditation:
## The Story

Simon, a Pharisee, invites Jesus to dinner. In those days, guests reclined on cushions, with their feet turned outward, and homes often remained open—people from the village could come in to listen to conversations.

Suddenly, a woman enters. Everyone knows her: she's a sinner of the city, perhaps a prostitute. She approaches Jesus from behind, at his feet, and begins to weep. Her tears fall on Jesus' feet. She wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours precious perfume on them.

The silence must be terrible. Simon thinks to himself: "If this Man were a prophet, He would know who and what manner of woman this is who is touching Him, for she is a sinner."

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus has understood very well what Simon is thinking. He tells him a little parable: two men owe a creditor a debt, one owes five hundred denarii, the other fifty. The creditor forgives both debts. Which one will love him more? Simon answers: "I suppose the one whom he forgave more."

Then Jesus turns toward the woman and says to Simon: "So He turned to the woman and said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has washed my feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head.'" (Luke 7:44)

"Do you see this woman?" What a question! Of course Simon sees her. But he sees only her past, her reputation, her label. Simon saw her past; Jesus saw her love.

Jesus makes a list: Simon offered no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head. The most basic courtesies. She gave everything. And Jesus concludes: "Therefore I say to you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little.' Then He said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.'" (Luke 7:47-48)

## For Your Life

Simon's problem is not that he had sinned less. It's that he thought he needed less forgiveness. And the one who thinks he needs little forgiveness loves little.

The more you become aware of what Jesus has forgiven you, the greater your love for him grows. It's no accident that those who come from far away often have the most passionate praise.

And if you feel like this woman, rejected, judged, reduced to your past, listen to what Jesus says to her at the end: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." He lifts her up in front of everyone. He restores her dignity publicly, in the very place where she had been humiliated publicly.

Today, take a moment to remember all that Jesus has forgiven you. Not to sink into guilt, but to let gratitude rise up. Then ask yourself: is there someone I'm looking at the way Simon looked at this woman? Ask Jesus to give you his gaze.

pratique.texte: Write down everything Jesus has forgiven you, without staying locked in it. Then thank him, aloud or in song. Gratitude nourishes love.
Is there someone you're looking at the way Simon looked at this woman? Ask Jesus for his gaze and make a gesture of respect toward that person.
Reread Luke 7:50 and receive Jesus' word for you: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." Your past does not have the final word.

days.question: Am I aware of all that has been forgiven me? Is there someone I reduce to their past?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank You for all You have forgiven me. My debt was immense, and You erased it. May my love for You be measured by this forgiveness. Give me Your gaze on others, so that I see not their past, but what Your grace can do in them. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Simon saw his past; Jesus saw her love.

days.title: Let's Cross to the Other Side
days.meditation:
## The Story

It's evening, after a long day of teaching. Jesus says to his disciples: "That day, when evening came, he said to his disciples, 'Let us go over to the other side.'" (Mark 4:35) They get into the boat. Jesus, exhausted, falls asleep at the stern, his head on a pillow.

Then the storm breaks out. The Sea of Galilee is known for its sudden storms: it's surrounded by hills, and the wind can rush through with terrible violence. Waves fill the boat. And those who are afraid are not tourists: they are experienced fishermen who know this lake by heart. If they panic, it's because the situation is truly grave.

They wake Jesus: "And he was in the stern, asleep on a pillow. And they woke him and said to him, 'Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!' And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm." (Mark 4:38-39)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

"Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?" That's maybe the question you're asking God right now. "Does this matter to you? Why are you sleeping while I'm drowning?"

But look at Jesus's response. He gets up, and he speaks to the wind and the sea the way you'd speak to a barking dog: "Peace! Be still!" And everything stops. Not gradually: immediately, a great calm.

Then he turns to his disciples: "And he said to them, 'Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?' And they were filled with great fear, and said to one another, 'Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?'" (Mark 4:40-41)

Their fear changes its object. They were afraid of the storm; now they're in awe before the One who commands the storm. They're beginning to understand who is in their boat.

## For Your Life

There's a story about an airplane caught in severe turbulence. The passengers are terrified, some are screaming, others are praying. Only a little girl remains calm and keeps playing. After landing, someone asks her: "Weren't you afraid?" She answers: "No, my dad's the pilot."

Notice one essential detail: before the storm, Jesus had said "let us go over to the other side." Not "let's go into the middle of the lake to sink." His word already contained the destination. The storm didn't cancel his promise.

If Jesus is in your boat, the storm can shake the boat, but it cannot sink it.

What's the storm in your life today? Rather than letting fear speak, remember the word God has given you. And bring him your storm. He can calm it with a word. And if he doesn't calm it right away, he can calm your heart in the middle of it. Either way, you'll make it to the other side.

pratique.texte: Write down the storm you're going through. Just below it, write a promise from God that applies to your situation. Read it again when fear rises.
Like the disciples, cry out to him honestly. Then finish with: "I believe you're leading me to the other side."
Think of someone who's panicking right now. Call them, listen to them, and pray with them: your presence can be Jesus's calm for them.

days.question: What storm am I going through right now? What promise from God will I hold on to in the middle of it?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you're in my boat. You see the waves and the wind that frighten me. You command the storm: speak to mine too. Calm the waters, or calm my heart in the middle of them. I believe you're leading me to the other side. Amen.
days.aRetenir: If Jesus is in your boat, the storm won't sink it.

days.title: Sitting, Clothed, and in His Right Mind
days.meditation:
## The Story

After the storm on the lake, Jesus arrives on the other side, in the country of the Gerasenes. And as soon as he steps out of the boat, a man comes to meet him. A terrifying man: he lives in the tombs, naked, crying out day and night and cutting himself with stones. They've tried to chain him, but he breaks the chains. No one can control him. He's a man inhabited by a multitude of demons, who call themselves "Legion."

Notice one thing: Jesus crossed a storm at night to come to this one man. The entire journey had a purpose: one man, lost in the tombs.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

The demons tremble before Jesus. They beg him, they bargain. Jesus has total authority: he drives them out, and they enter a herd of about two thousand pigs that rush down into the sea.

Then the people of the town arrive, and here's what they see: "And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid." (Mark 5:15)

Sitting: the one who wandered day and night has found rest. Clothed: the one who lived naked has regained his dignity. In his right mind: the one who was tormented has regained peace of mind. That's what Jesus does with a life that everyone had given up on.

But the reaction of the townspeople is sad: they beg Jesus to leave their region. They've lost pigs, and that matters more to them than a man set free. Sometimes, someone's freedom disturbs the economy and comfort of others.

## For Your Life

The freed man wants to follow Jesus. But Jesus tells him: "Jesus did not permit him, but said to him, 'Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.'" (Mark 5:19)

He becomes the first missionary of this pagan region. He hasn't attended Bible school, he doesn't know much. But he has a story: "Here's what Jesus did for me." And the man goes and proclaims throughout the Decapolis all that Jesus has done for him (Mark 5:20). And when Jesus comes back to this region later, people will bring him the sick and the news will spread everywhere (Mark 7:31-37).

No one is too far, too chained, too broken for Jesus. The chains that no one could break, he breaks them. The man that everyone avoided, he crosses a storm to meet him.

Maybe you know someone who seems unreachable: addictions, violence, occultism, torment. Don't lose hope: Jesus has authority over all powers. Pray for this person with faith.

And your story? You don't need a complicated speech. Simply tell, in your own home, to those close to you, what the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.

pratique.titre: What Have You Been Set Free From?
pratique.texte: Write down what Jesus has broken in your life, even partially. Then tell someone close to you about it this week, simply.
Choose one person who seems too far gone (addiction, violence, occultism) and pray for them every day this week, with faith in Jesus's authority.
Is there a comfort or interest you're putting before someone's freedom? Ask God to give you his heart for people.

days.question: What has Jesus set me free from? Who will I tell this week what the Lord has done for me?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for crossing the storm to come find me. You broke chains that no one could break. I pray for those still in chains: show your authority in their lives. And give me the courage to tell those close to me what you have done for me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: No one is too far, too chained, or too broken for Jesus.

days.title: Don't Fear, Only Believe
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jairus is a respected man: a synagogue official. But that day, his title is useless to him. His twelve-year-old daughter is dying. He falls at Jesus's feet and begs him to come. Jesus goes with him. Every minute counts.

And suddenly, everything stops. In the crowd pressing around Jesus, a woman touches him. For twelve years, she's been suffering from constant bleeding. She's spent everything on doctors, and her condition has only gotten worse. According to the law, her illness made her unclean: she couldn't touch anyone or go to the temple. Twelve years without touch, without a hug, without community. She says to herself: "If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well." She touches him, and she's healed instantly.

Jesus stops: "Who touched my clothes?" The disciples think the question is absurd: everyone's touching him! But Jesus knows the difference between a crowd jostling him and faith touching him.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

The woman comes forward trembling and tells him everything. Jesus could have let her go healed in body. But he wanted to heal her heart too, before everyone: "And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.'" (Mark 5:34)

"Daughter." No one had called her that in twelve years. She came looking for healing; she leaves with an identity.

But meanwhile, Jairus is waiting. And the news comes: "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher anymore?" Imagine this father. That delay cost him his daughter. It's then that Jesus says to him: "But Jesus, overhearing what they said, said to the ruler of the synagogue, 'Don't be afraid, only believe.'" (Mark 5:36)

Jesus arrives at the house, takes the child's hand, and says to her: "Talitha koum," "Little girl, I say to you, get up." And she gets up.

## For Your Life

Jesus's delays are not refusals.

Twelve years of sickness for the woman, twelve years of life for the girl. The one is starting to live again at the moment the other seemed to be losing her life. And Jesus took care of both, in the right order, in his time.

Maybe you're like Jairus. You've prayed, and Jesus seems to have stopped for someone else. Others are answered, and you're waiting. And now you're being told: "It's too late. Don't trouble the Teacher anymore." Listen to Jesus's voice louder than the voice of bad news: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Maybe you're like that woman, exhausted, alone, after trying everything. Dare to reach out. Dare to make your way through the crowd. Jesus feels the difference between the crowd and faith.

Today, bring before Jesus what seems too late or too long to you. And repeat his word: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

pratique.titre: Set Down What Seems Too Late
pratique.texte: Write the situation where you hear: "It's too late, don't trouble the Teacher anymore." Then repeat Jesus's word: "Don't be afraid, only believe."
If you're exhausted like the woman, take a step toward Jesus today: a moment of prayer, attending a service, asking someone to pray for you.

pratique.titre: When Someone Else Gets Their Answer First
pratique.texte: If others are answered and you're not, rejoice for them and trust your waiting to Jesus. His delays are not refusals.

days.question: In what situation do I feel like it's "too late"? How can I reach out to Jesus today?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you feel the difference between the crowd and faith. I reach out to you today. When bad news says it's too late, help me hear your voice: don't be afraid, only believe. I trust you for your timing. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus's delays are not refusals.

days.title: Five Loaves and Two Fish
days.meditation:
## The Story

A massive crowd follows Jesus: about five thousand men, not counting the women and children. The day is wearing on, there's nothing to eat, and they're far from any villages. Jesus turns to Philip: "Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?" He already knew what he was going to do; he wanted to test him.

Philip does the math: two hundred denarii of bread—that's roughly eight months' wages for a worker—wouldn't even be enough. Philip sees the problem.

Then Andrew steps forward: "Here is a boy with five small barley loaves and two small fish, but how far will they go among so many?" (John 6:9)

Barley loaves: the bread of the poor. Two tiny fish. A child's meal. And Andrew himself says it: "How far will they go among so many?"

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus has the crowd sit down on the grass. Then: "Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated; so also the fish, as much as they wanted. When they had all had enough to eat, he told his disciples, 'Gather the pieces that are left over. Let nothing be wasted.'" (John 6:11-12)

Jesus takes what's given to him, he gives thanks, he distributes it. He doesn't despise the small basket. He doesn't say, "It's too little, I'll do without it." He could have made bread fall from heaven, like the manna in the desert. But he chooses to start with a child's meal.

And at the end, they gather twelve baskets of leftovers. More than they started with. God doesn't just give enough; he gives abundantly.

## For Your Life

What you give to Jesus is never too small; what he does with it is never small.

We're often like Philip: we calculate, we see the problem, we measure everything that's missing. Or like Andrew: we see a few resources, but we think they won't help. "What good is my little talent, my little time, my little gift, my little prayer, in the face of such a great need?"

The boy didn't calculate anything. He gave what he had. We don't even know his name. But two thousand years later, we're still talking about his meal.

Jesus doesn't ask you for what you don't have. He asks you for what you do have. Moses had a staff. David had a slingshot. The widow of Zarephath had a little flour and oil. This boy had five loaves and two fish. And you—what do you have in your hands?

Today, identify your "basket": a talent, some time, a skill, money, a house, a voice. Maybe it seems ridiculous compared to the world's needs. Give it to Jesus anyway. Let him take it, bless it, and multiply it. You'll be amazed at the leftovers.

pratique.texte: Write down what you have in your hands: a talent, time, a skill, money, a house, a voice. Nothing is too small.
Choose a concrete way to put it at His service: serve in your church, help a neighbor, give to a mission, lend your house for a group.
Face a need that's too big (finances, a project, family), do what Jesus did: take what you have, give thanks, and start with that.

days.question: What do I have "in my basket" that I could give to Jesus, even if it seems too small?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, I don't have much, but I give you what I have. My time, my talents, my resources, my life. Take them, bless them, and multiply them to feed many others. I don't want to keep counting what's missing—I want to trust you with what I have. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus doesn't ask you for what you don't have: he asks you for what you do have.

days.title: Get Out of the Boat
days.meditation:
## The Story

After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus has his disciples get into a boat and go ahead of him to the other side of the lake while he goes up on a mountainside by himself to pray. During the night, the boat is battered by the waves; the wind is against them. Between three and six in the morning, in the fourth watch of the night, Jesus comes to them... walking on the water.

The disciples cry out in fear: "It's a ghost!" And Jesus says to them: "Jesus immediately said to them: 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid!'" (Matthew 14:27)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Peter has a crazy idea: "Lord, if it's you, tell me to come to you on the water." And Jesus answers with one word: "Come!" "And he said, 'Come.' Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water and came toward Jesus. But when he saw the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, 'Lord, save me!' Immediately Jesus reached out his hand and caught him. 'You of little faith,' he said, 'why did you doubt?'" (Matthew 14:29-31)

We often talk about Peter sinking. But don't forget: Peter walked on water. He's the only human being besides Jesus to have done it. Eleven disciples stayed safe in the boat. Only one got out.

A Christian author, John Ortberg, wrote a book with a title that says it all: "If You Want to Walk on Water, You've Got to Get Out of the Boat." Miracles rarely happen in the comfort zone.

And what happened when Peter began to sink? The wind hadn't changed. The waves were the same as when he stepped out of the boat. What had changed was where he was looking: he looked at the wind instead of looking at Jesus.

And even then, Jesus doesn't let him sink. "Immediately," the text says, he reached out his hand and caught him. The rebuke comes after the rescue, not before.

## For Your Life

Better to sink after walking on water than to stay dry without ever trying.

What's your boat? What makes you feel secure but limits you? Maybe Jesus is saying "come" to you: for a calling, a service, a difficult conversation, a project, a step of faith. You're afraid of sinking. That's normal. But Jesus is on the water, and he's reaching out his hand.

And if you've already started to sink because you looked at the wind, circumstances, criticism, your weaknesses, it's not too late. Do what Peter did: cry out, "Lord, save me!" His hand is faster than the waves.

Today, spot one thing that's turning your eyes away from Jesus, a "wind" that impresses you. Then fix your eyes on him again, through his Word and worship. And dare to take a step out of the boat.

pratique.texte: Write down the comfort zone that protects you but limits you. What is Jesus saying "come" to? Write it down.

pratique.titre: One Step Out of the Boat
pratique.texte: Take a small step of faith this week: a difficult conversation, serving, signing up, witnessing. Start small, but get out.
Spot the "wind" that impresses you most (circumstances, criticism, numbers). Each morning, before you look at it, read a psalm and fix your eyes on Jesus.

days.question: What is my "boat," my comfort zone? What is Jesus saying "come" to right now?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you're walking on the waters that frighten me. If it's you calling me, I want to get out of the boat. Keep my eyes fixed on you, not on the wind. And when I start to sink, reach out and catch me by the hand. I trust you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Miracles rarely happen in the comfort zone.

days.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus takes his disciples far north to Caesarea Philippi, a city filled with pagan temples. In the midst of all these gods, he asks them a question: "Who do people say the Son of Man is?"

Answers come flying: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, one of the prophets. Respectful answers, even flattering. But all wrong. Today too, many say: "Jesus was a great teacher, a good prophet, a master of morality." That's nice, but it's not enough.

Then Jesus looks his disciples in the eye: "But what about you?" he asked. "Who do you say I am? Simon Peter answered, 'You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.'" (Matthew 16:15-16)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

What others say about Jesus won't save you; what you say about him changes everything.

Peter doesn't answer with an opinion, but with a revelation. And Jesus tells him: it's not flesh and blood that revealed this to you, but my Father. Then he adds: "And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it."

But right after, the same Peter goes too far. When Jesus announces that he must suffer, die, and rise again, Peter takes him aside and rebukes him: "Never, Lord! This shall never happen to you!" And Jesus answers him harshly: "Get behind me, Satan!" Just a few verses separate Peter's greatest declaration from his greatest error. You can have a true revelation and, the next moment, refuse the cross.

## For Your Life

And Jesus continues, speaking to all of them: "Then Jesus said to his disciples, 'If any of you wants to be my follower, you must give up your own way, take up your cross, and follow me. If you try to hang on to your life, you will lose it. But if you give up your life for my sake, you will save it.'" (Matthew 16:24-25)

Taking up your cross isn't about dealing with a bad back or a difficult coworker. In those days, the person who carried their cross was walking to their death. Jesus is talking about dying to yourself: to your ego, your rights, your own will, so you can live for him.

It's the paradox of the Gospel: those who cling to their life lose it; those who give it away find it. Like a seed: as long as it stays in the packet, it remains alone. Planted in the ground, it bears fruit.

Today, Jesus is asking you personally: "And you—who do you say I am?" Not what your parents, your pastor, or your church say. You. Take time to answer, write it down if you can. Then ask yourself: is there a cross I'm refusing to carry, an area where I say like Peter, "this won't happen to me"?

pratique.texte: Write your answer to the question: "And you—who do you say I am?" Not what others say: your answer.
Is there an area where you say like Peter: "This won't happen to me"? An obedience that costs, a surrender. Give it back to Jesus.
Choose an act of self-denial this week: give up your place, serve without being seen, don't need the last word in an argument.

days.question: If Jesus asked me today, "And you—who do you say I am?" what would I answer, honestly?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. You're not just a wise man or a prophet: you are my Lord and my Savior. I choose to deny myself, take up my cross, and follow you. I lose my life to find it in you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: What others say about Jesus won't save you; what you say about him changes everything.

days.title: Jesus Alone
days.meditation:
## The Story

Six days later, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. And there, before them, he is transfigured: his face shines like the sun, his clothes become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and talk with him. Moses, who represents the Law; Elijah, who represents the prophets. All of Israel's history is there, gathered around Jesus.

Peter, who can never seem to stay silent, suggests: "Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, I will make three shelters here—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." He wants to extend the moment, to hold it, to put Jesus on the same level as these two great men.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Before Peter even finishes speaking, a bright cloud covers them: "While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them; and suddenly a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Hear Him!'" (Matthew 17:5)

It's the same voice as at his baptism, with an addition: "Hear Him!" Moses and Elijah were great, but Jesus is unique. He is not a prophet among others—he is the Son.

The disciples fall facedown, gripped by great fear. Then: "But Jesus came and touched them and said, 'Arise, and do not be afraid.' When they had lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only." (Matthew 17:7-8)

Jesus alone. Moses and Elijah have vanished. The shelters will not be built. Only Jesus remains, touching them and saying: do not be afraid.

## For Your Life

You don't build shelters on the mountain; you take the light there and bring it back down into the valley.

There are moments of the mountain in the Christian life: a worship service where God's presence was so strong, a retreat, a camp, an encounter that shook you. And you want to stay there forever. But look what waits for the disciples at the foot of the mountain: a desperate father and a child tormented by a demon (Matthew 17:14-18). The mountain prepares you for the valley.

If you're in the valley today, remember the mountain. The glory you saw was not an illusion. The Jesus of the summit is the same one who walks with you down below.

And hold onto two words from this story. "Hear Him": among all the voices, opinions, advice, and influences, only one voice must have the final word. "Jesus alone": it's possible to stay attached to people, to experiences, to traditions—even good ones—to the point that they take Jesus' place.

Today, take ten minutes of silence simply to listen. Don't speak, don't ask—just listen. Open your Bible, read slowly, and ask: "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" Then go back down into your valley carrying his light.

pratique.texte: Take ten minutes of silence, Bible open, asking for nothing. Read slowly and ask: "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" Write down what touches your heart.
Is there a person, a tradition, or an experience that has taken Jesus' place? Restore it to its rightful place in prayer.

pratique.titre: Go Back Down Into the Valley
pratique.texte: After a powerful moment with God, choose one person who is suffering and serve them this week. The mountain prepares you for the valley.

days.question: What voices have taken up too much space in my life? How can I better listen to Jesus, and Jesus alone, this week?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you are the Father's beloved Son. I want to listen to you, above all other voices. Let nothing and no one take your place. Thank you for my mountaintop moments. Give me the strength to come back down into my valley with your light, to serve those who are suffering. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The mountain prepares you for the valley.

days.title: Who Is My Neighbor?
days.meditation:
## Part 4: On the Road to Jerusalem

Jesus sets his face firmly toward Jerusalem, where the cross awaits him. During this journey, he will tell some of his most beautiful stories.

## The Story

A teacher of the law wants to test Jesus: "What must I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns the question back to him, and the man answers very well: "He answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind'; and 'your neighbor as yourself.'" (Luke 10:27)

But he wants to justify himself, so he asks: "And who is my neighbor?" In other words: how far must I go? Whom must I love, and whom can I ignore?

Jesus answers with a story. A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, a road nearly twenty miles long, notorious for bandits. He is attacked, stripped, and left half dead. A priest comes by, sees him... and passes on the other side. A Levite does the same. Then comes a Samaritan—an enemy, despised by the Jews. He stops, bandages his wounds, puts him on his own beast, takes him to an inn, pays for him, and promises to return.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

The evening before his death, on April 3, 1968, Martin Luther King commented on this story in his final speech. He imagined that the priest and the Levite had asked themselves: "If I stop to help this man, what will happen to me?" The Samaritan, however, reversed the question: "If I do not stop to help this man, what will happen to him?"

That's exactly what Jesus does. The teacher was asking: "Who is my neighbor?"—that is, "Who deserves my love?" Jesus turns the question around: "Which of these three do you think was neighbor to him who fell among the thieves?" And he said, "He who showed mercy on him." Then Jesus said to him, "Go and do likewise." (Luke 10:36-37)

The question is no longer: "Who is my neighbor?" but: "Whose neighbor will I become?"

## For Your Life

The priest and the Levite weren't necessarily mean people. They probably had good reasons: a service at the temple, fear of becoming unclean by touching a half-dead man, fear of the bandits, their schedule. We too always have good reasons to pass on the other side of the road.

Love according to Jesus costs something: time (the Samaritan changes his plans), money (two denarii and the promise to pay more), and commitment (he will return). And it crosses barriers: a Samaritan helping a Jew.

And don't forget that in this story, Jesus is the first good Samaritan. We were wounded on the roadside, and he stopped, he paid the price, and he promised to return.

Today, ask God to open your eyes to someone "on the roadside": a lonely neighbor, a colleague in difficulty, a stranger in need. Don't pass on the other side. Do something concrete, even if it costs you a little.

pratique.texte: Ask God to show you someone "on the roadside" this week: a lonely neighbor, a struggling colleague, a stranger in need.
Set aside time, money, or energy for a concrete act of love. The Samaritan's love changed his plans.
Do an act of kindness toward someone different from you (different culture, opinion, generation, or someone you're in conflict with).

days.question: Who is "on the roadside" in my life right now? What concrete action will I take to become their neighbor?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you stopped for me when I was wounded on the roadside. Forgive me for the times I've passed on the other side. Open my eyes to those suffering around me, and give me a love that stops, that cares for wounds, and that pays the price. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The question is not "who is my neighbor?" but "whose neighbor will I become?"

days.title: One Thing Is Necessary
days.meditation:
## The Story

On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus stops in a village at the home of two sisters: Martha and Mary. Martha welcomes him into her house. Receiving Jesus and his disciples means welcoming at least thirteen hungry men at once. There's food to prepare, serving to do, cleaning up. Martha rushes around in all directions.

And Mary? "She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word. But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she approached Him and said, 'Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Therefore tell her to help me.'" (Luke 10:39-40)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

In that time, sitting "at the feet" of a teacher was the position of a disciple. And it wasn't the usual place for a woman. Mary takes a place that culture didn't give her, and Jesus welcomes her there.

Martha, on the other hand, is exhausted. She even reproaches Jesus: "Do You not care?" And Jesus answers her with great tenderness, repeating her name: "And Jesus answered and said to her, 'Martha, Martha, you are worried and troubled about many things. But one thing is needed, and Mary has chosen that good part, which will not be taken away from her.'" (Luke 10:41-42)

Jesus doesn't criticize Martha's service. The meal was necessary, the hospitality was beautiful. The problem wasn't what Martha was doing, but what it was doing to her: she was "worried and troubled." And in her anxiety, she ended up accusing her sister and doubting Jesus.

## For Your Life

You can be so busy serving Jesus that you forget to be with him.

That's the trap for many committed Christians. You do things for God, so many things, good things. Meetings, service, projects, phones ringing, notifications without end. And one day you realize you haven't spent real time alone with him in weeks. You serve the Master of the house, but you never sit at his feet anymore.

Imagine a wife whose husband works all the time to give her a beautiful house, but never spends an evening with her. She would eventually say: "I don't want your gifts—I want you." God doesn't first look for exhausted servants, but for present children.

Service must flow from presence. Martha without Mary is exhaustion. Mary sitting forever without getting up is spiritual selfishness. But Mary first, then Martha—that's balance.

Today, set a specific, protected time—even if it's short—when you'll sit at Jesus' feet. Phone on airplane mode, Bible open, heart available. That's "the good part," and no one can take it from you.

pratique.texte: Set a time each day at Jesus' feet, even if it's short: phone on airplane mode, Bible open. Put it on your calendar.
Write down what makes you "worried and troubled" in your service or life. Give it to Jesus before you keep serving.
If you're a busy parent, take five minutes with your children to read a verse and pray together. The good part can be shared as a family too.

days.question: Do I tend to be more like Martha or more like Mary? What protected time will I set aside to sit at Jesus' feet?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I've been so busy serving you that I forgot to be with you. I choose the good part. Teach me to sit at your feet, to listen to you, and then to serve with a heart at peace. Amen.
days.aRetenir: You can be so busy serving Jesus that you forget to be with him.

days.title: The Father Who Ran
days.meditation:
## The Story

It may be the most beautiful story ever told. A father had two sons. The younger said to him, "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In the culture of that time, many commentators point out, asking for your inheritance while your father is alive was almost like saying, "I wish you were dead."

The father agrees. The son goes to a distant country and squanders everything in wild living. Then comes the famine. He ends up keeping pigs, the unclean animal par excellence for a Jew, and he even envies their food. He has hit bottom.

That's when he "comes to himself." He prepares a speech: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired servants." And he takes the road home.

## What This Reveals About God

"And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." (Luke 15:20)

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him." That means the father was watching the road. Maybe every day. He had never stopped waiting.

And he runs. In that culture, an elderly, respected man did not run in public—he would have to lift his robe, and it was beneath his dignity. But this father doesn't care. He runs, throws his arms around his son, kisses him. The son starts his speech, but the father won't even let him finish. He calls his servants: the best robe, a ring on his finger, sandals on his feet, the fattened calf. A celebration.

The Father wasn't waiting for your speech; he was waiting for your return.

## For Your Life

But the story isn't over. There's a second son. The one who stayed, who always obeyed. When he hears the music, he gets angry and refuses to go in. "All these years I have been serving you…" He was at home, but his heart was just as far away as his brother's. He served his father like an employee, not like a son.

And the father comes out to him too: "My child," the father said to him, "you have always been with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this your brother was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." (Luke 15:31-32)

There are two ways to be far from the Father: by leaving home, or by staying at home with a hard heart. The first son loses himself in sin, the second in religion. And the Father runs toward both.

If you're the son who left, the road back is open. You don't need a perfect speech. The Father is already running toward you.

If you're the older son, ask yourself: Am I serving God with joy, like a son, or with bitterness, like an employee counting his hours? Do I rejoice when someone comes back, even if they've done anything wrong?

Today, come to yourself, no matter which son you are. And let yourself be embraced by the Father.

pratique.texte: Which son are you right now—the one who left or the one who stayed with a hard heart? Tell the Father honestly.
If you've wandered away, take a concrete step today: pray, go back to church, call a pastor or a Christian friend. The Father is already running toward you.
Think of someone who is coming back to God or to church. Welcome them warmly this week, without bringing up their past.

days.question: Do I see myself more in the younger son or the older son? What does the Father want to say to me today?
days.priere: Father, thank you for watching the road and running toward me. I come back to you, with my faults and without a perfect speech. Clothe me with your finest robe. And deliver me from the hardness of the older son: give me to serve you with joy, as your child, and to rejoice in every return. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The Father wasn't waiting for your speech; he was waiting for your return.

days.title: Roll Away the Stone
days.meditation:
## The Story

Lazarus, the friend of Jesus, brother of Martha and Mary, is gravely ill. The sisters send a message: "Lord, the one you love is sick." And Jesus… stays where he is for two more days. When he finally arrives in Bethany, Lazarus has been dead for four days.

Martha runs toward him: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." Then Mary arrives, falls at his feet, and says exactly the same thing. They must have repeated it for four days: "If only you had come…"

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus knew he was going to raise Lazarus. He had even announced it to his disciples. And yet, before the tomb, in the midst of weeping: "Jesus wept. So the Jews said, 'See how he loved him.'" (John 11:35-36)

It's the shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the most profound. Jesus weeps. He's not rushed to move on to the miracle. He doesn't say, "Stop weeping, you'll see!" He enters into the grief of his friends. He weeps with those who weep.

Your sorrow is not indifferent to Jesus. He knows the end of your story, and yet he weeps with you in the middle.

Then he gives an order: "Jesus said, 'Roll away the stone.' Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, 'Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.' Jesus said to her, 'Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?'" (John 11:39-40)

Martha has a very logical objection: "He already stinks." Everyone knows that after four days, it's over. But Jesus asks her to do her part: roll away the stone. He could have done it with a word. But he wants human hands to roll it.

Then he cries out: "Lazarus, come out!" And the dead man comes out, his feet and hands wrapped with burial strips. And Jesus gives one final order to the witnesses: "Unbind him, and let him go."

## For Your Life

Jesus can raise the dead, but he asks you to roll away the stone.

Maybe there's something in your life that has been dead for "four days": a dream, a marriage, a relationship, a calling, your joy. Everyone says, "It's over, it already stinks." And maybe you repeat, "Lord, if you had been here…"

Jesus weeps with you. But he also tells you: "Roll away the stone." The stone might be bitterness, refusal to forgive, a closed door, fear of believing again. He's not asking you to raise the dead; that's his job. He's asking you to roll the stone.

And look at the last word: "Unbind him." Lazarus was alive, but still wrapped in his burial cloths. It's the role of the community: to help those whom Jesus has brought back to life to free themselves from what still wraps them.

Today, name your "stone," and dare to roll it away before Jesus.

pratique.texte: Write down what's preventing God from acting in a situation that seems dead: bitterness, refusal to forgive, a closed door, fear of believing again.
Take a concrete step this week: forgive, make a first move, reach out again, dare to pray about this matter once more.
Think of someone who has known Jesus but remains trapped by their "burial cloths" (shame, habits, wounds). Walk alongside them: listen, pray, offer concrete help.

days.question: What "stone" is Jesus asking me to roll away today so he can act?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for weeping with me. You know what has died in my life and what everyone thinks is lost. I roll away the stone before you: my bitterness, my doubts, my closed doors. Cry out life again. And help me to unbind others. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus can raise the dead, but he asks you to roll away the stone.

days.title: I Must Stay at Your House
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jericho. Zacchaeus is not just a tax collector: he is the chief tax collector, and he is rich. In other words, he has grown wealthy by collaborating with the occupier and collecting more than required. The whole city hates him.

He wants to see Jesus, but there are two problems: the crowd, and his height. He is short. So he does something very undignified for a wealthy man: he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree. Imagine a bank manager perched in a tree in a suit.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus arrives at the tree. He stops, looks up, and calls him by name: "And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.'" (Luke 19:5)

Jesus knows his name. He doesn't say to him, "Come down, so I can lecture you." He says, "I must stay at your house today." "I must": as if it were the most important appointment of his journey.

The crowd murmurs, "He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner." But Jesus won't let public opinion dictate his friendships.

And yet, Jesus asks nothing of Zacchaeus. No list of conditions, no sermon on honesty. Zacchaeus himself stands up: "And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.' And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'" (Luke 19:8-10)

## For Your Life

Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus; he discovered that Jesus was seeking him.

Notice the order: first, Jesus welcomes Zacchaeus. Then, Zacchaeus changes. Change is not the condition for Jesus's love; it is the fruit of that love. No one forced Zacchaeus to give back the money. Grace did what shame and the reproach of an entire city had never been able to do.

And his repentance is concrete. He doesn't just say "I'm sorry." He gives half his possessions to the poor, and restores four times what he stole. The true encounter with Jesus always touches the wallet, relationships, and habits.

Maybe you feel small too: small because of your past, your reputation, what others say about you. Maybe the crowd is hiding Jesus from you. Do what Zacchaeus did: run ahead, climb a tree, do what it takes to see him. And you will discover that he stops under your tree, and that he knows your name.

And if Jesus comes to your house today, what needs to change? Is there something to repair, to restore, to give back? Grace doesn't ask it as a price to pay. It gives you the desire to do it.

pratique.texte: Make a concrete effort to see Jesus this week: wake up earlier, go to a prayer meeting, read an entire Gospel.
If Jesus came to your house today, what would need to change? A debt to repay, an apology, a wrong to make right? Do it, with joy.
Zacchaeus gave to the poor. Choose a concrete gift this week, within your means: money, a meal, your time.

days.question: If Jesus came to my house today, what would need to change or be made right?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for stopping under my tree and calling me by my name. I receive you with joy in my house and in my life. May your grace produce true change in me. Show me what I need to repair, and give me the joy of doing it. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus; he discovered that Jesus was seeking him.

days.title: The King on a Donkey
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus arrives near Jerusalem. The city is full of pilgrims who have come for Passover. He sends two disciples to find a young donkey that no one has ever ridden. When asked why they're untying it, they must answer, "The Lord needs it."

Then Jesus enters the city riding on this donkey. The crowd spreads their clothes on the road like a red carpet for a king. The disciples burst with joy: "They said, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!' " (Luke 19:38)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

When a king entered a city in those days, he arrived on a war horse, surrounded by soldiers. Jesus arrives on a donkey. He fulfills the prophecy of Zechariah: "Behold, your King is coming to you; He is just and having salvation, lowly and riding on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9). Jesus is a king, but not the kind many were expecting. They hoped for a political liberator who would drive out the Romans. He comes to free hearts.

And then there is this moving moment. In the midst of the cries of joy, Jesus looks at the city, and: "As He drew near, He saw the city and wept over it, saying, 'If you had known, even you, especially in this your day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. '" (Luke 19:41-42)

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem. He knows that the same city crying "Hosanna" today will cry "Crucify Him" in a few days. He also knows that, having rejected Him, the city will be destroyed—which happened in 70 AD. He weeps because it "did not know the time of your visitation."

## For Your Life

Jesus is not looking for fans; He is looking for disciples.

A crowd can cheer for Jesus on Sunday and reject Him on Friday. One day's enthusiasm is not enough. Fans applaud when everything is going well; disciples follow when it costs something. The question is not "Did I shout Hosanna?" but "Do I still follow Him when He takes the path to the cross?"

Notice too the little donkey. An animal of no value, never ridden, tied up somewhere. And yet: "The Lord needs it." That day, this donkey carried the King of kings. You may feel small, insignificant, tied down. But if the Lord needs you, He will come to untie you, and you will carry His presence wherever He wants to go.

And think of Jesus' tears. He still weeps today over cities that do not recognize Him. Over your city, your neighborhood, your family.

Today, do two things. Ask yourself whether your faith is that of a fan or that of a disciple. Then pray for your city as Jesus wept over Jerusalem: that it may recognize the time of its visitation.

pratique.texte: Write honestly what shows that you follow Jesus even when it costs something, and what shows that you follow Him only when everything is going well.
Ask God what He wants to use in you (your time, your car, your home, your talent) and say yes to Him this week.
Take ten minutes to pray for your city, walking if possible: its leaders, its families, those who don't know Jesus.

days.question: Does my faith look more like a fan's or a disciple's? For which city or place will I pray with Jesus' heart?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, humble and victorious King, I don't want to cheer for You only when everything is going well—I want to follow You all the way. Untie me and use me to carry Your presence. And give me Your heart for my city, that it may recognize the time of Your visitation. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus is not looking for fans; He is looking for disciples.

days.title: The King with a Towel
days.meditation:
## Part 5: The Cross

We enter the last days of Jesus before the cross. John devotes almost half his Gospel to this final week. Slow down, read carefully: this is the heart of everything.

## The Story

"Before the Feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that His hour had come that He should depart from this world to the Father, having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end." (John 13:1)

"He loved them to the end." And how? With a gesture no one expected. During the meal, Jesus rises, removes His outer garments, takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and begins to wash His disciples' feet.

In that culture, roads were dusty, people wore sandals, and feet were dirty. Washing guests' feet was the task of the lowest slave. Even a disciple was not required to wash his master's feet. That evening there was no slave, and none of the disciples offered to do it. Luke even tells us that during this meal they were arguing about who was the greatest (Luke 22:24).

So while they argue over first place, Jesus takes last place.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Peter refuses: "You shall never wash my feet." He cannot accept that his Lord would humble Himself this way. But Jesus answers him: "If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me." Before serving, you must accept being served by Jesus, being washed by Him. Pride can also hide in the refusal to receive.

And there is a detail that takes your breath away: Jesus knows that Judas will betray Him (John 13:2, 11). Yet He also washes his feet. He kneels before the one who will hand Him over for thirty pieces of silver, takes his feet in His hands, and washes them.

Then Jesus puts His outer garments back on and explains: "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that you should do as I have done to you." (John 13:14-15)

## For Your Life

The greatest is not the one who has the most people serving him, but the one who serves the most people.

In the world, greatness is measured by how many people are under your command. In the kingdom of God, it is measured by how many people you serve. Jesus didn't say, "Blessed are you if you know these things," but "Blessed are you if you practice them" (John 13:17).

Washing feet today may not be with a basin and water. It's doing the task no one wants to do. It's serving someone who can give you nothing in return. It's even serving someone who has hurt you, as Jesus did with Judas.

Today, take a towel, literally or figuratively. Find a humble, invisible service that no one will notice. And do it for Jesus.

pratique.texte: Find a humble and invisible service this week (dishes, cleaning at church, helping a neighbor) and do it for Jesus.
If you struggle to receive help, accept someone's assistance this week without making excuses. Receiving is also a form of humility.

pratique.titre: Serve the One Who Hurt You
pratique.texte: Think of a person who has hurt you. Without putting yourself in danger, do a small act of kindness toward them, as Jesus did with Judas.

days.question: What humble and invisible service can I render this week? Is there someone who has hurt me whom I could serve?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, You, the Master, took the towel and washed the feet of Your disciples, even the feet of Judas. Wash me first, and cleanse my heart of all pride. Then teach me to serve as You do, without seeking first place, even those who have hurt me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: While they argued over first place, Jesus took last place.

days.title: Do This in Remembrance of Me
days.meditation:
## The Story

It is the evening of Passover. For more than a thousand years, every Jewish family has celebrated this meal to remember the night when God freed Israel from Egypt. The blood of the lamb on the doorposts, the angel of death passing over, the exodus from slavery. Each element of the meal tells this story.

And that evening, Jesus says to His disciples a phrase full of emotion: "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer." Then He takes the bread and the cup and gives them new meaning: "And He took bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, 'This is My body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.'
