Likewise He also took the cup after supper, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you.' " (Luke 22:19-20)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus is saying: "Tonight, a new liberation is beginning, and I am the Lamb." The broken bread is His body that will be broken on the cross. The cup is His blood that will be shed. Not for Israel alone: "for you," for all who believe.

He speaks of a "new covenant." A covenant is more than a contract. A contract says, "I'll do my part if you do yours." A covenant says, "I give myself to you." Like in a marriage. Jesus seals this covenant with His own blood.

Yet at the same table there is Judas' betrayal, and right after, an argument over who is the greatest. Jesus answers them: "Let it not be so among you; on the contrary, he who is greatest among you, let him be as the younger, and he who governs as he who serves. For who is greater, he who sits at the table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at the table? Yet I am among you as the One who serves." (Luke 22:26-27)

Even on His last evening, the disciples don't understand. And Jesus doesn't reject them. He continues to love them, to teach them, to share bread with them.

## For Your Life

When you take communion, you're not just remembering—you're proclaiming a covenant.

When you take the bread and the cup, you are saying: "Jesus died for me. His body was broken in my place. His blood paid my debt. I am in the covenant." Paul adds that every time you do this, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). This is a proclamation looking to the past, but also to the future.

It's possible to take communion out of habit, thinking about something else, as if reciting a formula. This text invites us to rediscover it as a meal of love. Jesus "eagerly desired" this moment with His disciples. He desires it also with you.

Today, even if you're not taking communion, take a moment to remember. Thank Jesus for His broken body and shed blood, given precisely for you. And the next time you share the bread and cup at church, do it with awareness: you are proclaiming the covenant.

pratique.texte: Take a moment to thank Jesus for His broken body and shed blood, given precisely for you. Write a prayer of thanksgiving.
The next time you take it, prepare your heart the day before: confess what weighs on you, forgive, and live it as the proclamation of the covenant.
Organize a meal with brothers and sisters this week or with your family, and take a moment to remember what Jesus did.

days.question: How do I live communion: out of habit, or as the proclamation of a covenant? What could change?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for Your broken body and shed blood given for me. Thank you for this new covenant, sealed by Your love. Forgive me for the times I took this meal without thinking about it. I remember You, and I proclaim Your death until You come. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Communion is not just a memory—it's the proclamation of a covenant.

days.title: Gethsemane, the Wine Press
days.meditation:
## The Story

After the last meal, Jesus goes with his disciples to a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives: Gethsemane. The name means "oil press." This is where olives were crushed under heavy stones to extract their oil. And that night, it is Jesus' heart that will be crushed.

He takes Peter, James, and John a little further, and for the first time, he shows them his distress: "Then he said to them, 'My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with Me.' He went a little farther and fell on His face, and prayed, saying, 'O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.'" (Matthew 26:38-39)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus is not an unfeeling hero walking toward death without emotion. He is "exceedingly sorrowful, even to death." Luke even notes that his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke 22:44). He knows what awaits him: physical suffering, yes, but above all the cup—that is, to bear the sin of the world and God's wrath against that sin.

And he prays the same prayer three times, with disarming honesty: "If it is possible, let this cup pass from Me!" Then he adds: "Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will." He does not hide his struggle. But he submits his desire to the Father's.

Gethsemane teaches us that true prayer is not always the kind where we get what we want. Sometimes it is the kind where we end up wanting what God wants.

Meanwhile, the disciples are sleeping. Three times, Jesus comes back and finds them asleep. And he says to them: "Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." (Matthew 26:41)

## For Your Life

Olives never yielded their oil without being pressed. And it is often in our Gethsemanes that God causes something precious to flow through us.

Maybe you are going through a press right now: a trial that is crushing you, a decision that costs you, an obedience that hurts. Jesus understands you. He has been there before you. You have the right to tell him honestly: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." This is not a lack of faith. But also ask him for the grace to add: "Not what I want, but what You want."

It is through the "yes" of Gethsemane that we have the cross, and through the cross that we have the resurrection. Your "yes" in the press can also open the way to something you cannot yet see.

And do not sleep during the struggles of others. Someone around you may be in their own Gethsemane. Watch and pray with them.

pratique.texte: Write down what is crushing you right now. Tell it honestly to God, as Jesus did: "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me."
Then add, even if it's hard: "Not what I want, but what You want." If you cannot say it yet, ask for the grace to be able to say it.
Think of someone in their Gethsemane (illness, grief, trial). Do not sleep during their struggle: call them, pray with them this week.

days.question: What is the "press" I am going through right now? Am I able to say to God: "Not what I want, but what You want"?
days.priere: Father, you see what is crushing me right now. I tell you honestly: if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. But I choose to trust you: not what I want, but what You want. Let my life, even pressed, pour out the oil of your presence. Amen.
days.aRetenir: True prayer is not always the kind where we get what we want, but the kind where we end up wanting what God wants.

days.title: Jesus' Gaze
days.meditation:
## The Story

A crowd arrives in the garden with swords and clubs. Leading them, Judas. He approaches Jesus to kiss him: it is the agreed signal. Jesus simply says to him: "Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?"

Peter draws his sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. But Jesus stops him, touches the man's ear, and heals him. Even during his arrest, Jesus heals one of those coming to arrest him.

They take Jesus to the high priest's house. Peter follows at a distance. He enters the courtyard and sits by the fire with the servants. And three times, someone recognizes him. Three times, he denies it: "I do not know him." The third time, as he is still speaking, the rooster crows.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

"And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how He had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.' So Peter went out and wept bitterly." (Luke 22:61-62)

Jesus is being tried, beaten, humiliated. And in the midst of all this, he turns and looks at Peter. What kind of look? Not a look of anger, not "I told you so." I believe it was a look of wounded love, of compassion. A look that said: "I know. And I still love you."

Because Jesus had warned Peter a few hours earlier: "And the Lord said, 'Simon, Simon! Indeed, Satan has asked for you, that he may sift you as wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail; and when you have returned to Me, strengthen your brethren.'" (Luke 22:31-32)

Jesus knew Peter would fall. And he had already prayed for him. He had even already planned what comes after: "when you have returned to Me." Not "if," but "when."

## For Your Life

That night, two disciples betrayed Jesus. Judas delivered him, Peter denied him. Both felt remorse. But their stories end in opposite ways. Judas, crushed by his guilt, took his own life. Peter, on the other hand, wept bitterly, then came back. The difference was not the seriousness of their fall, but what they did afterward.

Remorse looks at the fault; repentance looks at Jesus.

Maybe you have denied Jesus in some way: out of fear, out of cowardice, out of a fall you never thought possible. You tell yourself: "I never would have thought I could do that." Peter had also said: "Lord, I am ready to go with You, both to prison and to death."

Listen carefully: your fall did not surprise Jesus. He had already prayed for you. And he looks at you today, not to crush you, but to bring you back. Do not do as Judas did, staying alone with his guilt. Do as Peter did: weep if you must, but come back. And when you are lifted up, you will be able to strengthen your brethren.

pratique.titre: Look at Jesus, Not Your Fall
pratique.texte: If you remain in the remorse of a fault, tell it to Jesus, receive his forgiveness, and read Luke 22:32. He had already prayed for you.
Judas stayed alone with his guilt. If guilt is crushing you, talk about it this week with someone you trust or with a pastor.
Your lifted-up fall can become strength for others. Think of someone who has fallen and encourage them: "Jesus lifted me up too."

days.question: Is there a fall for which I remain in remorse instead of returning to Jesus? What does his gaze tell me today?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you know my falls, even those I never thought possible. Thank you for praying for me before I even fell. I do not want to stay alone with my fault. I return to you. Lift me up, and make me someone who strengthens others. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Remorse looks at the fault; repentance looks at Jesus.

days.title: Father, Forgive Them
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus has been beaten, whipped, crowned with thorns, condemned. Too weakened to carry his cross all the way, they force a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, to carry it behind him. Then they arrive at the place called The Skull, Golgotha in Hebrew. "When they had come to the place called Calvary, there they crucified Him, and the criminals, one on the right hand and the other on the left. Then Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.' And they divided His garments and cast lots." (Luke 23:33-34)

Jesus' first words on the cross are not a curse. Not a cry for revenge. As they drive nails through his hands, he prays for his executioners: "Father, forgive them."

## What This Reveals About Jesus

All around, people mock him. The leaders: "He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ." The soldiers: "If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself!" And it is true: Jesus could have come down from the cross. But he could not save himself and save us at the same time. It was not the nails holding Jesus to the cross; it was love.

Two criminals are crucified with him. One insults him. The other rebukes him: "And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward of our deeds; but this Man has done nothing wrong." Then he turns to Jesus: "Then he said to Jesus, 'Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.' And Jesus said to him, 'Assuredly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.'" (Luke 23:42-43)

This man was never baptized. He never followed Jesus on the roads, never did good works to repair his faults. He has only a few hours left to live, nailed to a cross. He has nothing to offer except a prayer of faith. And Jesus promises him paradise, today.

There were three crosses on that hill: on one, a man died in his sin; on another, a man died to his sin; and on the one in the middle, a man died for sin.

## For Your Life

At Jesus' death, the veil of the temple tears in two from top to bottom (Luke 23:45). This veil separated the Holy of Holies, God's presence, from the rest of the people. Only the high priest could enter there, once a year. Now, the path to God is open to all.

Look at the cross today, and let it tell you three things.

You are forgiven. If Jesus could pray for those nailing him, there is no sin his blood cannot cover.

It is never too late. The criminal was saved in his final hour. While there is a breath, there is hope.

You can forgive. The one who said "Father, forgive them" lives in you. Think of someone you cannot forgive. You may not have the strength, but he does. Ask him to forgive through you.

pratique.texte: Read slowly Luke 23:34 and Isaiah 53:5. Say to Jesus: "Thank you, what you bore, you bore for me."

pratique.titre: Forgive in Light of the Cross
pratique.texte: Think of someone you cannot forgive. Pray: "Father, forgive them; and give me the strength to forgive." Repeat it every day of the week.
Think of someone who seems too far from God. Pray for them, and if possible, tell them gently that it is never too late to turn to Jesus.

days.question: What does the cross tell me personally today? Is there someone I need to forgive in light of the cross?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you were nailed to the cross for me, and it was not the nails holding you there, but your love. Thank you for your forgiveness. Remember me, as you remembered the criminal. And give me the strength to forgive as you have forgiven. Amen.
days.aRetenir: It was not the nails holding Jesus to the cross: it was love.

days.title: Mary!
days.meditation:
## Part 6: He Is Alive

The cross is not the end of the story. Over the next four days, we will discover how the Risen One encounters His own, one by one, and transforms their sorrow into joy.

## The Story

On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb. She came to weep, and no doubt to finish anointing the body. She loved Jesus deeply: He had delivered her from seven demons (Luke 8:2). When all the men fled, she remained at the foot of the cross.

But the stone had been rolled away, and the tomb was empty. She ran to tell Peter and John, who came, saw, and left. Mary stayed. She wept before the tomb. She saw two angels, and even that didn't stop her: "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid Him."

She turned around and saw Jesus, but did not recognize Him. "Jesus said to her, 'Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you seeking?' She, thinking He was the gardener, said to Him, 'Sir, if you have carried Him away, tell me where you have laid Him, and I will take Him away.' Jesus said to her, 'Mary!' She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, 'Rabboni!' (which means, Teacher!" (John 20:15-16)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

She was looking for a body; she found a living Lord who called her by name.

It took just one word. Not a sermon, not theological proof: her name. "Mary." And she recognized Him. Jesus had said: "My sheep hear My voice; I know them, and they follow Me" (John 10:27).

The Risen One, the victor over death, in the first moments of His victory, does not appear first to Pilate, the high priest, or the crowd. He appears to a weeping woman with a tormented past. And to her He entrusts the first message of the resurrection: "Jesus said to her, 'Do not cling to Me, for I have not yet ascended to My Father. But go to My brethren and say to them, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God."' Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that He had said these things to her." (John 20:17-18)

Notice Jesus's words: "My Father and your Father, My God and your God." For the first time, He calls His disciples "My brethren." The cross has made us the family of God.

## For Your Life

Perhaps you are like Mary: you are weeping before a tomb. Something has died, and you are searching in the wrong place. You are looking for a memory, a tradition, a past. Your tears prevent you from recognizing the One who is standing right beside you.

Listen: Jesus is alive, and He knows your name. He does not speak to you as to an anonymous crowd. He calls you personally, with the same tenderness He showed to Mary.

And note that Mary was the only one who remained at the tomb when the others left. Those who persevere in their search for Jesus, even through tears, end up meeting Him.

Today, take a moment of silence and listen to Jesus speak your name. Then do as Mary did: go tell someone "I have seen the Lord."

pratique.texte: Take a moment of silence and listen to Jesus speak your name with tenderness. Write down what you hear in your heart.
Is there a past, a tradition, or a memory where you are seeking Jesus instead of meeting Him alive today? Give it to Him.
Like Mary, tell someone this week: "Jesus is alive, and He has changed something in my life." Tell them one specific thing.

days.question: Am I seeking Jesus among the dead, in the past or in memories? What changes when I know He is alive and knows my name?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, You are alive! You have conquered death, and You know my name. Wipe away my tears and open my eyes to recognize You at my side. Thank You for calling me Your brother, Your sister. Give me the courage to go tell others: I have seen the Lord. Amen.
days.aRetenir: She was looking for a body; she found a living Lord who called her by name.

days.title: The Road to Emmaus
days.meditation:
## The Story

On the same day, two disciples left Jerusalem to return to Emmaus, about seven miles away. They walked with sad faces, talking about everything that had just happened. Jesus Himself approached and walked with them, but their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.

He asked them what they were talking about. And one of them, Cleopas, told Him everything. Then he spoke this sentence, one of the saddest in the Bible: "We were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel; and besides all this, it is the third day since these things happened." (Luke 24:21)

"We were hoping." In the past tense. They had hoped. Now it was over.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Jesus did not perform a spectacular miracle to make Himself known. He opened the Scriptures. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, He explained to them everything concerning Himself in the Old Testament. Imagine that Bible study: seven miles of walking with Jesus Himself explaining the Scriptures to you!

When they reached the village, Jesus acted as though He were going farther. He did not impose Himself. But they urged Him: "Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is far spent." And at the table, He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. "Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Him; and He vanished from their sight. And they said to one another, 'Did not our heart burn within us while He talked with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?'" (Luke 24:31-32)

"Did not our heart burn within us?" The Word had lit a fire in them before they even understood who was speaking to them.

## For Your Life

Jesus sometimes walks beside you in your disappointment, even when you do not recognize Him.

Perhaps you are on the road to Emmaus. You are leaving Jerusalem, the place of your faith, the church, your dreams. You say: "We were hoping..." I was hoping my marriage would hold together, that this healing would come, that this project would succeed, that God would intervene. And you walk on with a sad face.

These two disciples were disappointed because Jesus had not done what they expected. They hoped for a political deliverer; He had come for a far greater liberation. Their disappointment came from their expectations, not from Jesus's failure. Often, our greatest disappointments are the place where God prepares a revelation greater than our expectations.

Notice what changed everything: the Word that makes the heart burn, and the broken bread. The Bible and communion. These are still today the places where we recognize Jesus.

And the end of the story is wonderful: "And they rose up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem." At night, seven miles in the opposite direction. Disappointment had driven them away; meeting Him brought them back.

Today, tell Jesus what you "were hoping" for. Then open your Bible and ask Him to set your heart on fire again. Invite Him: "Stay with us, for it is toward evening."

pratique.titre: Tell What You Were Hoping For
pratique.texte: Write down the disappointment you carry: "I was hoping that..." Then present it to Jesus who walks with you.
Choose a passage of Scripture about hope (Romans 8, Psalm 42, Isaiah 40) and read it slowly each day this week.
If disappointment has driven you away from church or your brothers and sisters, take a step to return this week: a worship service, a phone call, a small group.

days.question: What were "we hoping" for that didn't happen as planned? How might Jesus be walking with me in this disappointment?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, You walk with me even when I do not recognize You. You know my disappointments, all that I was hoping for. Open the Scriptures to me, set my heart on fire, open my eyes. Stay with me, for it is toward evening. And bring me back to where You are calling me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Disappointment drove them away; meeting Him brought them back.

days.title: Do You Love Me?
days.meditation:
## The Story

After the resurrection, Peter went back to fishing. With six other disciples, he spent the whole night on the lake. And they caught nothing. Doesn't that remind you of something? It's exactly like the day he was called, three years earlier (Luke 5).

In the early morning, a man on the shore told them: "Cast the net on the right side of the boat." They obeyed, and the net was so full they couldn't pull it in: one hundred fifty-three large fish. John understood: "It is the Lord!" And Peter threw himself into the water to reach Jesus as quickly as possible.

On the shore, Jesus had kindled a fire of coals, with fish and bread. He prepared breakfast for them.

## What This Reveals About Jesus

Notice this detail: a fire of coals. The last time Peter had stood near a fire, in the courtyard of the high priest, he had denied Jesus three times (John 18:18). Jesus brings him back before a fire to rewrite the story.

After the meal, Jesus asks Peter a question: "So when they had eaten, Jesus said to Simon Peter, 'Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me more than these?' He said to Him, 'Yes, Lord; You know that I love You.' He said to him, 'Feed My lambs.'" (John 21:15)

Three times, Jesus asks him the question. Three times, like the three denials. The third time, Peter is grieved: "He said to him the third time, 'Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me?' Peter was grieved because He said to him the third time, 'Do you love Me?' And he said to Him, 'Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You.' Jesus said to him, 'Feed My sheep.'" (John 21:17)

Jesus does not reproach him. He does not ask: "Why did you deny Me?" or "Promise Me you'll never do it again." He asks one question: "Do you love Me?" What concerns Jesus first is not your past performance, but your present love.

And with each answer, Jesus entrusts him with a mission: "Feed My sheep." The one who failed is not benched; he is restored to service. Peter became a pillar of the Jerusalem church and preached at Pentecost to thousands of people.

## For Your Life

With Jesus, your failure is never the final chapter.

Perhaps you are like Peter: you have failed, you have disappointed, and you've gone back to your old nets. You tell yourself that God can no longer use you. That you've lost your place. But Jesus comes to find you on the shore of your life, kindles a fire, and prepares a meal. He does not want to condemn you; He wants to restore you.

Shortly before, Jesus had also restored Thomas, who doubted: instead of rejecting him, He had held out His hands (John 20:24-29). The Risen One rejects neither those who doubt nor those who have fallen.

Today, Jesus asks you the same question: "Do you love Me?" Take time to answer Him, honestly. Then listen to the mission He wants to entrust to you. You are not disqualified. You are called.

pratique.texte: Write your honest answer to Jesus. Not a heroic promise: the truth of your heart today.
If a failure has benched you, ask Jesus what mission He is entrusting to you now and take a first step this week.
Your love for Jesus is seen in how you care for others. Choose one person you will care for this week: a phone call, a visit, a helping hand.

days.question: Is there a failure that makes me believe God can no longer use me? How will I answer today the question "Do you love Me?"
days.priere: Lord Jesus, You know all things; You know that I love You. Thank You for not disqualifying me because of my failures. Restore me as You restored Peter. I receive the mission You want to entrust to me. May my love for You be seen in the care I take of others. Amen.
days.aRetenir: With Jesus, your failure is never the final chapter.

days.title: Go, I Am With You
days.meditation:
## The Story

The eleven disciples go to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated for them. They see him, and bow down before him. And Matthew adds a surprising note of honesty: "But some doubted." Even on that day, before the Risen One, some still doubted. And Jesus entrusts his mission to them anyway. He doesn't wait for everyone to be perfect before sending them out.

Then Jesus comes near and speaks his final words in the Gospel of Matthew: "Jesus came and told them, 'All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.'" (Matthew 28:18-20)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

It all begins with authority: "All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth." And it all ends with presence: "I am with you always." Between the two, the mission: "Go, make disciples." You are not sent with your own authority, nor alone. You are sent with his, and he walks with you.

Notice also that the mission is not just to make converts, but disciples: people who learn to "observe all that I have commanded you." For 40 days, you have followed Jesus. Now, it's your turn to help others follow him.

Before ascending to heaven, Jesus also promises the power to accomplish this mission: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." (Acts 1:8) The power of the Holy Spirit, to be his witnesses, from your city to the ends of the earth.

## For Your Life

There's an old story, a kind of parable. When Jesus went back to heaven, an angel asked him: "Lord, how will the world hear about what you've done?" Jesus answered: "I've entrusted the message to Peter, to John, to Mary, and to a few others." The angel worried: "What if they fail? What's your plan B?" And Jesus said: "I don't have a plan B."

God's plan to reach your coworker, your neighbor, your cousin, is you. You don't need to be perfect: the disciples doubted too. You don't need to be strong: the Spirit gives you power. You don't need to fear being alone: he is with you every day, to the end of the age.

For 40 days, you walked with Jesus. You saw him born, call, heal, forgive, weep, serve, die, and rise. This is not the end of the journey—it's the beginning of your mission.

To finish, do three things. Reread the key phrases from these 40 days and choose the three that touched you most. Write down the name of one person you want to tell about Jesus. And pray to be filled with the Holy Spirit, to be his witness where you are.

pratique.texte: Reread the "Key Phrases" from these 40 days and choose the three that touched you most. Write them down and display them.
Write down the name of one person you want to tell about Jesus. Pray for them each day, and ask God for the opportunity to speak with them.
Decide what you'll do tomorrow: start another plan, read an entire Gospel, join a group. The journey continues with him.

days.question: Who will I tell about Jesus in the coming days? What do I take away from these 40 days with him?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for these 40 days with you. You have all authority in heaven and on earth, and you are with me every day. I receive your mission: fill me with your Holy Spirit, and make me your witness where you have placed me. Here I am, send me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: This isn't the end of the journey: it's the beginning of your mission.

items.title: I Am Not Just Anybody
items.subtitle: 21 days to discover who God says you are, what you have received, and how to live in the power of the Spirit.
items.summary: Maybe you've been made to believe you were nothing much. Your failures, the way others looked at you, your wounds and bad days spoke loudly. But God has the final word, and he says: you are not just anybody. In 21 days, you'll discover who you really are (created, redeemed, adopted, forgiven, righteous, new), what you have received (the Spirit, access to the Father, freedom, authority, the baptism of the Holy Spirit and his gifts) and how to live it out every day: pray for the sick, cast out demons in the name of Jesus, overturn lies, dare to step into your calling. Each day: the verses first, then the exhortation, and concrete steps to put it into practice. Bible texts: ESV.

days.title: Created in the Image of God
days.meditation:
## Week 1: Who I Am

For three weeks, we're going to answer just one question—probably the most important one in your life: who am I? And to answer it, we need to start at the very beginning, before the fall, before your wounds, before your mistakes: in God's heart.

## What the Word Says

On the sixth day of creation, God does something different. For everything else, he said "let there be light," "let the earth bring forth." For the human being, he consults with himself: "Then God said, 'Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.' So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them." (Genesis 1:26-27)

You're not an accident of evolution, not a mistake of your parents, not a number in a statistic. You bear God's imprint. Like a coin bears the face of the king, your life bears the image of your Creator: your capacity to love, to create, to think, to choose, to govern, to connect with God.

And when God looked at the humanity he had just created, he didn't say "good." He said: "God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day." (Genesis 1:31)

Michelangelo is credited with saying something like this about his famous statue of David: "I simply removed the marble that wasn't David." God does something similar with you. He doesn't want to make you into someone else. He wants to remove everything that isn't you—everything that sin, lies, and wounds have added—to reveal the person he thought of before you were even born.

David, the king, understood this as he reflected on his own life: "I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well." (Psalm 139:14)

It's not pride to say that. Pride is boasting about what you've done. Here, we're praising God for what he has done. To despise the work is to despise the artist.

You may not be a finished masterpiece, but you are God's masterpiece in progress.

pratique.texte: Stand in front of a mirror and read aloud Psalm 139:14. Then thank God for three specific things about your body or character, even those you don't fully love yet.
Find the negative sentence you say most often about yourself ("I'm useless," "I never succeed"). Write down what God says instead, and every time it comes back today, replace it.

pratique.titre: If You Have Children or Young People Around You
pratique.texte: Tell one of them today a sentence that builds their identity: "You have value, God wanted you." What a child hears from their parents often becomes their inner voice.

days.question: What negative sentence about myself do I repeat most often, and what does God say instead?
days.priere: Father, thank you for creating me in your image. Forgive me for the times I've despised your work. I praise you that I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Remove everything that isn't me, and reveal the person you thought of. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I am not an accident: I bear God's imprint.

days.title: What Sin Has Broken, What the Cross Has Redeemed
days.meditation:
## The Context

Yesterday we saw the original design: the human being created in God's image, "very good." But something broke. The serpent planted a doubt in Eve's heart: "Did God really say...?" And the first sin didn't start with fruit, but with a question about God's goodness.

After disobedience, Adam and Eve's first reaction is to hide. "Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God as he was walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the garden. But the Lord God called to the man, 'Where are you?'" (Genesis 3:8-9)

## What the Word Says

Sin broke three relationships. With God: they hide from him. With themselves: they discover they're naked and feel ashamed. With others: Adam blames Eve, Eve blames the serpent. Shame, fear, and accusation entered the world, and they're still there in our lives.

And Paul leaves no one out: "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus." (Romans 3:23-24)

But look at the second part of the verse: "justified freely by his grace." From Genesis 3 on, God takes the initiative. He's the one who seeks the man: "Where are you?" It's not the question of a God who doesn't know, it's the call of a Father who wants his child to come out of hiding. And in that very chapter, God promises that a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent's head: it's the first promise of Jesus in the Bible.

Imagine a fifty-dollar bill. If I crumple it, step on it, soil it, how much is it worth? Still fifty dollars. Its value doesn't come from its condition, but from what's written on it. Sin has crumpled you, soiled you, damaged you. But your value has never disappeared, because God paid a price for you: "For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life handed down to you from your ancestors, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or defect." (1 Peter 1:18-19)

Your value is measured by the price God paid for you. And he paid it with the blood of his Son.

pratique.texte: Take ten minutes alone with God and honestly answer his question: "Where are you?" Tell him what you're hiding, what you're ashamed of, without justifying yourself or blaming anyone else.
Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent. Is there a situation where you're putting all the blame on others? Take your share of responsibility before God, and if possible before the person involved.
Write on a piece of paper: "I have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18-19) and slip it into your wallet. When you feel worthless, look at the price paid for you.

days.question: Is there an area of my life where I still "hide" from God out of shame or fear?
days.priere: Lord, you call me as you called Adam: "Where are you?" I come out of hiding. I confess what shames me. Thank you for redeeming me, not with gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Jesus. Amen.
days.aRetenir: My value is measured by the price God paid for me.

days.title: Born Again
days.meditation:
## The Context

Nicodemus is an impressive man: a Pharisee, a teacher of the law, a member of the Sanhedrin, the great council of Israel. If anyone thinks they're in good standing with God, it's him. He comes to see Jesus at night, maybe so he won't be seen, and starts with a polite compliment. Jesus gets straight to the point: "Jesus replied, 'Very truly I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again.'" (John 3:3)

## What the Word Says

Nicodemus doesn't understand: "How can someone be born when they are old?" Jesus explains that it's not a physical birth but a spiritual one: "Jesus answered, 'Very truly I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless they are born of water and the Spirit. Flesh gives birth to flesh, but the Spirit gives birth to spirit.'" (John 3:5-6)

What Jesus is announcing is not an improvement, it's a birth. Religion tries to make a man better; Jesus makes him new. You don't become a Christian by adding a few good habits to your life, but by receiving a new life that comes from God.

Think of a caterpillar. No matter how hard it tries, it will never fly by flapping its legs faster. To fly, it needs a transformation it cannot produce itself: in the chrysalis, its entire being is reorganized, and a butterfly emerges. Being born again is the work of the Spirit, not your effort.

Peter clarifies how this life comes to us: "For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God." (1 Peter 1:23) God's Word is like a seed. When it's received in faith, it produces a life that cannot die.

And at the heart of this night-time conversation, Jesus speaks the most famous verse in the Bible, John 3:16: God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son. Being born again is not a reward for the good, it's a gift for those who believe.

You don't need a new resolution, you need a new birth.

pratique.texte: If you have any doubt, settle it today: tell Jesus in your own words that you believe he died and rose again for you, that you turn from your sin, and that you receive him as your Savior and Lord. Then tell a trusted Christian.
Write in a few lines how you met Jesus: before, the encounter, after. This little testimony will often help you share your faith simply.
A baby needs milk every day. Choose a realistic rhythm for the week: one chapter from the Gospel of John daily, for example, and a church where you can grow with others.

days.question: Am I certain that I've been born again? What is my certainty based on: my efforts, or God's work?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for being born again. I don't just want an improved life, I want your life in me. I receive you as my Savior and my Lord. May your Word, incorruptible seed, bear fruit in my heart. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Religion tries to make man better; Jesus makes him new.

days.title: Adopted as God's Child
days.meditation:
## The Context

When Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, he uses an image that everyone understands in the Roman Empire: adoption. For the Romans, adoption was a very strong legal act. The adopted child received the name of his new family, all the rights of a legitimate son, a share of the inheritance, and his former debts were erased. He literally began a new life.

## What Scripture Says

John announces it at the very beginning of his Gospel: "But as many as received Him, to those who believe in His name, He gave the right to become children of God, who were born" (John 1:12). This is not an honorary title. It is a change of status, of family, of name.

And Paul adds that this is not only a legal truth, it is a lived experience: "The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. Now if we are children, then we are heirs—heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with Him, that we may also be glorified together with Him" (Romans 8:16-17). The Holy Spirit whispers deep inside you: "You are mine." He is the one who makes you cry out "Abba, Father!" Not a slave trembling in fear, but a child running into the arms of his Father.

Notice also the word "heirs." Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to you in Christ. You are not a tolerated guest in God's house, nor a servant: you are family, with the same table, the same name, the same inheritance.

There is an enormous difference between an orphan and a child. An orphan lives with the fear of lacking, fights for his place, constantly seeks approval, and protects himself. A loved child rests, dares, asks, and knows that his father's door is always open. Many Christians are adopted on paper but still live with an orphan's heart.

God did not save you to make you a weary servant, but a beloved son and daughter.

## For Your Life

Test yourself honestly: in your relationships, your prayers, your service at church, are you acting like an orphan who must earn his place, or like a child who already knows he is loved?

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to bear this witness in your heart. Take some time in silence, and simply say: "Abba, Father." Let Him answer you: "You are My child."

And if you grew up without a father, without affection, or rejected by your family, hear this truth: God chose you. Paul says He predestined us "in love to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:5). You were not adopted by default; you were wanted.

pratique.texte: Take five minutes of silence and simply say: "Abba, Father." Let the Holy Spirit remind you that you are His child. Write down what you feel or what comes to you.
Do you feel obliged to earn your place at church, at work, in your family? Choose a situation from this week and live it as a loved child: without trying to prove yourself, without fear of rejection.
If this word is painful, tell God without hesitation and read Psalm 27:10. If the wound is deep, talk to a pastor or someone you trust: healing also comes through relationships.

days.question: In my relationship with God, do I live more like an orphan who must earn his place, or like a loved child?
days.priere: Abba, Father, thank you for adopting me. Thank you for Your name, Your house, and Your inheritance. Holy Spirit, bear witness with my spirit that I am a child of God. Heal my orphan heart and teach me to live as a loved child. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I am not an orphan who must earn his place, but a loved child who already has one.

days.title: Forgiven, Without Condemnation
days.meditation:
## The Context

Romans 7 ends with a cry of despair: Paul describes the internal struggle between what he wants to do and what he actually does, and cries out: "O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" (Romans 7:24). And just after, like a sunrise, he writes: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).

## What Scripture Says

"No condemnation." Not "less condemnation," not "condemnation on probation": no condemnation. For the one who is in Christ Jesus, the case is closed.

Paul explains how this is possible: "And you, being dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, He has made alive together with Him, having forgiven you all trespasses, having wiped out the handwriting of requirements that was against us, which was contrary to us. And He has taken it out of the way, having nailed it to the cross" (Colossians 2:13-14). In ancient times, when a condemned man was crucified, sometimes the charge against him was nailed above him. Above Jesus's cross was written "King of the Jews." But spiritually, it was your list of faults that was nailed there. Your debt was paid, in full.

David had already glimpsed this reality: "As far as the east is from the west, So far has He removed our transgressions from us" (Psalm 103:12). He did not say "from north to south" because north and south meet at the poles. East and west never meet.

Corrie ten Boom, who had known concentration camps and God's immense forgiveness, loved to say that God casts our sins into the deepest sea, then posts a sign: "No Fishing." Many Christians return to fish out what God has already thrown away.

You must distinguish between conviction and condemnation. Conviction comes from the Holy Spirit: it is specific, shows you a sin, drives you toward God, and stops when you repent. Condemnation comes from the accuser: it is vague, crushes you, makes you flee from God, and never stops. One lifts you up; the other pulls you down.

God does not forgive you halfway: when He erases, He erases everything.

## For Your Life

Is there a fault for which you continue to punish yourself, though you have already confessed it to God? You pull it out at night, you recall it when you want to serve God, and a voice says: "You cannot do this."

Today, refuse that voice. Not by denying your fault, but by proclaiming what Jesus did. Say out loud: "There is now no condemnation for me, because I am in Christ Jesus." And if an accusation returns, answer it with this verse. You do not have to go back and fish out what God has drowned.

pratique.texte: When a fault you've already confessed haunts you again, say Romans 8:1 out loud. Memorize this verse today so you have it ready in the middle of the night or when you want to serve.

The conviction of the Holy Spirit is specific and brings you back to God; accusation is vague and drives you away from Him. This week, every time you feel guilty, ask yourself: Is this pushing me toward Jesus or away from Him?

pratique.titre: If You Need to Make Repair
pratique.texte: God's forgiveness is complete, but sometimes a relationship needs healing. If you have hurt someone, take a step this week: a message, an apology, a restitution.

days.question: Which fault I've already confessed do I keep "fishing back up" in my mind, and how am I going to answer the accusation?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for nailing to the cross the charge that condemned me. I receive Your complete forgiveness. I refuse the voice of the accuser and listen to the voice of Your Spirit. There is now no condemnation for me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God does not forgive me halfway: when He erases, He erases everything.

days.title: Declared Righteous
days.meditation:
## The Context

Yesterday, we saw that forgiveness erases the debt. Today, we go further. Being forgiven is like leaving the courtroom with a clean record. Being justified is leaving the courtroom declared righteous, as if you had never committed the fault, and even as if you had always done what was right.

## What Scripture Says

Paul sums up the Gospel in one breathtaking sentence: "For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him" (2 Corinthians 5:21).

This is what theologians call the "great exchange." At the cross, Jesus took what was mine—my sin—and gave me what was His—His righteousness. He was treated as I deserved, so that I would be treated as He deserved.

And the consequence is immediate: "Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1). Peace with God. Not a fragile truce that depends on your week, but peace founded on what Jesus did once and for all.

Think of the parable of the prodigal son. The son returns in rags, reeking of pigs, with a little prepared speech: "Treat me as one of your hired servants." But the father does not even let him finish. He cries to his servants: "Bring out the best robe and put it on him." The robe was the sign of restored dignity. The son did not have time to wash, to redeem himself, to prove he had changed. He was clothed.

Isaiah sang of this reality: "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, My soul shall be joyful in my God; For He has clothed me with the garments of salvation, He has covered me with the robe of righteousness, As a bridegroom decks himself with ornaments, And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels" (Isaiah 61:10).

God's righteousness is not a wage you earn; it is a garment you receive.

## For Your Life

Many Christians live like employees on probation: they feel they must prove every day that they still deserve their place. When they have prayed well, they feel close to God. When they have fallen, they feel rejected.

But your standing before God does not depend on your performance today. It depends on the righteousness of Jesus, which never fluctuates. That does not mean sin does not matter: you do not live in sin when you wear the King's robe. But your holiness becomes a response of love, not an attempt to be accepted.

Today, when you pray, do not enter God's presence hanging your head like a beggar. Enter clothed in the robe your Father has given you. You are righteous before Him, in Christ.

pratique.texte: Tonight, instead of rating your day on a scale of 10 to see if God is pleased with you, say: "I am accepted because of Jesus's righteousness." Then thank Him for something specific from your day.

pratique.titre: Serve Out of Love, Not Fear
pratique.texte: Choose a service at church or home that you often do out of obligation. This week, do it while saying inwardly: "I do this because I am loved, not to be loved."
Romans 5:1 speaks of peace with God. When spiritual anxiety rises ("Is God angry with me?"), reread this verse and breathe slowly while meditating on it.

days.question: Do I live my relationship with God like an employee on probation, or like a child clothed in the righteousness of Christ?
days.priere: Father, thank you for the great exchange. Jesus took my sin and gave me His righteousness. I receive the robe You hold out to me. I want to live in peace with You, not because of my efforts, but because of the cross. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God's righteousness is not a wage I earn; it is a garment I receive.

days.title: A New Creation
days.meditation:
## The Context

This first week ends with one of the most liberating verses in the Bible: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. Old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Paul writes these words to a church in Corinth full of people with heavy pasts. In another letter, he reminds them that before knowing Christ, some were thieves, drunkards, sexually immoral… then he adds: "And such were some of you. But you were washed."

## What Scripture Says

Notice the word "creation." Paul doesn't say "a repaired creature" or "an improved version." He uses the same word as for the creation of the world. What God did on the first day with light, he does in you through the Spirit: he creates something that never existed.

Centuries earlier, God had promised it through Ezekiel: "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." (Ezekiel 36:26)

In 1967, in South Africa, surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant. For the first time, a man lived with another person's heart. What medicine learned to do in the twentieth century, God had been promising spiritually for millennia: he removes the stone heart, hard and insensible, and puts in a new one, capable of love, repentance, and obedience.

That doesn't mean you'll never struggle with old habits again. But those struggles no longer define who you are. Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it no longer dictates your future.

Your past is no longer your prison—it's your testimony.

## For Your Life

Maybe you've worn labels for a long time: "the troubled kid," "the divorcee," "the former addict," "the one who had an abortion," "the worthless one." People have stuck them on you, or you've stuck them on yourself. But if you're in Christ, these labels belong to "old things."

Today, write down on a sheet the labels that stick to your skin. Then, one by one, cross them out and write next to each what God says about you: child of God, forgiven, righteous, loved, new creation. Keep this sheet. It sums up this first week.

Here's what you are now: created in God's image, redeemed, born again, adopted, forgiven, declared righteous, new creation. Next week, we'll discover everything you received with this new identity.

pratique.texte: Write down the labels that stick to your skin, cross them out one by one, and write next to each what God says about you. Keep this sheet: you'll use it again on the last day of the plan.
Is there someone you reduce to their past (a brother, an ex, a colleague)? This week, say or write something that sees them the way God sees them.
Write down one thing that has already changed in your life since you've known Jesus, even if it's small. Thank God and share it with someone: gratitude strengthens the new creation.

days.question: What label from my past am I still letting define who I am, and what does God say instead?
days.priere: Lord, thank you for making me a new creation. Old things have passed away. I renounce the labels my past has stuck on me, and I receive the new heart you have given me. Let my past become a testimony of your grace. Amen.
days.aRetenir: My past is no longer my prison—it's my testimony.

days.title: The Temple of the Holy Spirit
days.meditation:
## Week 2: What I Have in Christ

Last week, we discovered who you are. This week, we're opening the treasure chest: everything God has given you in Christ. And we start with the greatest gift: God himself, coming to live in you.

## What Scripture Says

In the Old Testament, God's presence lived in the Temple in Jerusalem, specifically in the Holy of Holies, a room only the high priest could enter, just once a year, with the blood of a sacrifice. Imagine the shock of the early Christians when Paul writes to them: "Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16)

The Temple is no longer a stone building in Jerusalem. The Temple is you. The presence that Moses saw in the cloud, that priests could only approach with trembling, now lives in every believer.

Paul draws a very concrete consequence: "Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's." (1 Corinthians 6:19-20) Your body is not an unimportant detail. What you watch, what you do with your sexuality, how you eat, rest, and take care of yourself—it all matters to God's house.

And he adds elsewhere that the Holy Spirit is like a seal on your life: "In him you also trusted, after you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation; in whom also, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, to the praise of his glory." (Ephesians 1:13-14) In ancient times, a seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. The Spirit in you is God's signature on your life: "This one is mine."

You are never alone: you are God's portable house.

## For Your Life

This truth has two sides. First, immense comfort: in the hospital room, at work, in your solitude, in the night when you can't sleep, God is not far away. He is in you. You can talk to him anytime, in a whisper, and he hears.

Second, a call to holiness. Not the holiness of cold rules, but that of someone who knows they're hosting an honored guest. If Jesus were coming to sleep at your house tonight, you'd tidy up certain things, wouldn't you? He already lives with you.

Today, walk through your "house" with the Holy Spirit. Ask him: "Is there a room I've closed to you?" And invite him to fill every space.

pratique.texte: Ask the Holy Spirit: "What in my life doesn't honor you?" Listen, then act on one thing today (content, a habit, words, a relationship).
Your body is the temple of the Spirit: sleep, food, rest, and movement matter too. Choose one small, realistic change for this week.
If you feel alone (in the hospital, at night, far from your family), speak softly to the Holy Spirit who lives in you. Tell him: "You are here." Then reread John 14:16-17.

days.question: If I truly took seriously the fact that I am God's house, what would I change in how I live or treat my body?
days.priere: Holy Spirit, thank you for living in me. I am your temple. I open to you every room of my life, even those I had closed. Fill me with your presence, and teach me to live and care for my body as your house. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I am never alone: I am God's portable house.

days.title: Free Access to the Father
days.meditation:
## The Context

At the moment Jesus dies on the cross, Matthew reports an extraordinary detail: the veil of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom. This veil separated the holy place from the Holy of Holies, where God's presence was manifested. According to Jewish tradition, it was a thick and enormous curtain. It said to everyone: "No entry."

And it was torn from top to bottom. Not from bottom to top, as if men had ripped it: from top, as if God himself had opened it.

## What Scripture Says

The author of Hebrews explains what this means: "Therefore, brethren, having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way which he consecrated for us, through the veil, that is, his flesh;" (Hebrews 10:19-20) The way to God's presence is open, permanently, through Jesus's sacrifice.

And he draws an invitation: "Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need." (Hebrews 4:16) Notice the word "boldly." Not with fear, not crawling, not wondering if you have the right. Boldly. And notice the name of the throne: not the throne of judgment, but "the throne of grace."

Paul adds that this access is given to us by the Spirit: "for through him we both have access by one Spirit to the Father." (Ephesians 2:18)

Imagine the President gives you a permanent access badge to his office with this message: "Come whenever you want." Maybe you wouldn't dare use it. That's exactly what many Christians do with prayer: they have the badge, but they stay in the hallway.

The veil is torn: you don't need to wait in the hallway anymore.

## For Your Life

What's holding you back from coming to God boldly? The feeling of not being holy enough? Fear of bothering him? The impression he has better things to do? Remember: your access doesn't rest on your holiness, but on Jesus's blood. And the throne you're approaching is one of grace, specifically "to help in time of need."

Today, go in. Don't pray at the edge of your lips, like someone who stays on the threshold. Tell him: "Father, I enter boldly through Jesus's blood." Then present to him what weighs on you, without detour.

pratique.texte: Start your prayer with: "Father, I enter through Jesus's blood." Then present to him without hesitation what weighs on you most today, like a child knocking on his father's door.
Hebrews 4:16 speaks of help "in time of need." Write down one specific need (a job, a child, health, a decision) and present it each day this week, noting the date.
You have access to the Father: use it for others. Pray today for someone who no longer dares come to God, and tell them you prayed for them.

days.question: Do I pray like someone staying in the hallway, or like someone entering boldly?
days.priere: Father, thank you for tearing the veil. Through Jesus's blood, I enter your presence boldly. I approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and help. Thank you for always welcoming me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The veil is torn: I don't need to wait in the hallway anymore.

days.title: Free from Sin
days.meditation:
## The Context

After proclaiming grace, Paul anticipates an objection: "If God forgives everything, why not keep on sinning?" His answer is emphatic: "Absolutely not!" And he explains that grace doesn't just make us forgiven—it makes us free.

## What the Word Says

"knowing that our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves of sin" (Romans 6:6)

Paul doesn't say that sin has disappeared from the world, or that you'll never be tempted again. He says that sin is no longer your master. Before Christ, you were enslaved: you sinned because you couldn't do otherwise. In Christ, you are free: you can still sin, but you're no longer forced to.

There's a story from India about young elephants that used to be tied with a simple rope to a stake. When small, they'd pull with all their strength without managing to break free, and eventually they'd give up. As adults, strong enough to uproot a tree, they'd remain tied with the same fragile rope because they were convinced they couldn't leave. Many Christians live this way: freed, but still convinced they're tied down.

That's why Paul asks us to change how we see ourselves: "Likewise you also, reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts." (Romans 6:11-12) "Reckon yourselves dead to sin." It's not pretending—it's believing what God has done. Your freedom begins with how you see yourself.

And Jesus made a promise without reservation: "Therefore if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed." (John 8:36) Free indeed. Not halfway, not in theory.

The rope is no longer tied: stop believing you can't leave.

## For Your Life

Is there a sin that keeps coming back into your life, to the point that you've finally told yourself: "I'm just like this, I'll never get free"? Pornography, anger, lying, alcohol, gossip, an addiction?

Today, change your declaration. Stop saying "I'm just like this" and start saying "I was enslaved, and Jesus set me free." Then take action: Paul says to stop "presenting your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin." Concretely: cut off access, change the habit, talk to a trusted brother or sister, ask for help and prayer. Freedom is already won; now you need to live in it.

And if you fall, get back up immediately. A child learning to walk falls often; his father doesn't disown him. He lifts him up.

pratique.texte: Stop saying "I'm just like this." Say instead: "I was enslaved, Jesus set me free." Write this sentence down and say it out loud each time temptation returns this week.
Make one concrete, visible decision: add a filter to your phone, delete a contact, stop keeping alcohol at home, change your route. Freedom is protected by choices.
Choose someone you trust who you can give an account to once a week. If it's a serious addiction, also ask for help from a professional: that's not a lack of faith.

days.question: What sin have I ended up considering as "part of me," and what concrete decision will I make to walk in my freedom?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for crucifying my old self. I am no longer enslaved to sin. I reckon myself dead to sin and alive to God. Give me the strength to walk in the freedom you won for me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The rope is no longer tied: I stop believing I can't leave.

days.title: More Than a Conqueror
days.meditation:
## The Context

Paul is not writing these words from a comfortable living room. Just before, he lists everything Christians of his time went through: "tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword." He knows these trials firsthand: he's been beaten, stoned, imprisoned, shipwrecked. And yet, he concludes: "Yet in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us." (Romans 8:37)

## What the Word Says

Notice the phrase: "in all these things." Not "by avoiding all these things," nor "once all these things are over." Right in the middle of the trial, you can be more than a conqueror.

And what does "more than a conqueror" mean? There's a story about a boxer who wins a championship. He comes home exhausted, his face swollen, and gives his victory check to his wife. He is a conqueror; she is "more than a conqueror": she enjoys the victory without taking the blows. Jesus took the blows at the cross. He conquered sin, death, and the devil. And you receive His victory.

Paul begins this passage with a question that changes everything: "What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?" (Romans 8:31) He doesn't say no one will be against you. He says: what opponent could win if God is on your side?

And he ends with a staggering list: "For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." (Romans 8:38-39) Nothing. Not your sickness, not your failures, not the devil, not the future that worries you. Nothing can separate you from God's love.

I don't fight to win the victory; I fight from the victory.

## For Your Life

What battle are you walking through right now? A diagnosis, a crisis in your marriage, debt, depression, a lawsuit, a spiritual attack? The enemy wants you to believe that this trial proves God has abandoned you. Paul says the exact opposite: nothing can separate you from His love.

Today, name your battle before God. Then speak Romans 8:31 and 8:37 out loud, putting your own name in: "If God is for me, who can be against me? In all these things, I am more than a conqueror through Him who loved me."

This isn't positive thinking. It's God's truth, spoken in the middle of the storm.

pratique.texte: Write in one sentence the battle you're walking through. Then speak Romans 8:31 and 8:37, putting your own name in them. Do this morning and evening for a week.
Write down three times when God brought you through a trial. Read them again when you doubt: the One who did it yesterday will do it again.
Think of someone who is fighting (illness, divorce, grief, job loss). Send them Romans 8:38-39 today with a personal word, or offer to pray with them.

days.question: What battle am I waging as if I had to win it alone, instead of leaning on Jesus's victory?
days.priere: Father, if You are for me, who can be against me? In all these things, I am more than a conqueror through Him who loved me. I trust You with this battle. Thank You that nothing can separate me from Your love in Jesus Christ. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I don't fight to win the victory; I fight from the victory.

days.title: Seated with Christ: The Authority of the Believer
days.meditation:
## The Context

In his letter to the Ephesians, Paul doesn't pray for Christians to receive more power. He prays that they would understand the power they already have: "and what is the exceeding greatness of His power toward us who believe, according to the working of His mighty power which He worked in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power and might and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in that which is to come." (Ephesians 1:19-21)

After the resurrection, Jesus was raised to the highest position there is: at the right hand of the Father, above all spiritual authority, above every name.

## What the Word Says

And just a few lines later, Paul makes a stunning claim: "and raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 2:6) Not only is Jesus seated above all power, but you are also seated there, in Him. Your spiritual position is not down below, struggling to survive; it's up above, with Christ.

Jesus had already given this authority to His disciples: "Behold, I give you the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt you." (Luke 10:19) And after His resurrection, He declared: "All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore..." He received all authority, then He sent us in His name.

We must distinguish between power and authority. A police officer directing traffic cannot stop a 40-ton truck with his muscles. But when he raises his hand, the truck stops. Why? Because behind him stands the State. It's not his strength; it's his authority. When you speak in Jesus's name, it's not your strength that acts—it's the authority of the Son of God who sent you.

This authority is not exercised over people to dominate or manipulate them. It's exercised over the enemy and his works: disease, oppression, fear, the forces of darkness.

The enemy doesn't fear your strength; he fears the name you bear.

## For Your Life

Many Christians pray like victims: "Lord, the devil is attacking me, do something." God invites us to also pray as sons and daughters who have received authority: "In the name of Jesus, I resist fear. In the name of Jesus, I refuse this lie. In the name of Jesus, I declare that this house belongs to God."

This authority doesn't come from pride but from submission: you have authority only if you yourself are under Jesus's authority. Today, start by submitting to Him. Then identify one area of your life where the enemy has set up: fear, division, oppression. And speak with authority, in Jesus's name.

pratique.texte: Before you resist, submit (James 4:7). Start your prayer with: "Jesus, You are my Lord, I place myself under Your authority." Spiritual authority comes from submission.

pratique.titre: Take Authority Over One Specific Area
pratique.texte: Identify one domain where the enemy has established himself (fear, conflicts, nightmares, discouragement). Pray with calm: "In the name of Jesus, I resist... and I declare that this domain belongs to God."
If you live with family, take a moment to pray in each room of your home and declare God's peace. Do this with your children if possible: they'll learn that prayer has authority.

days.question: In what area am I still praying like a victim, when Jesus has given me authority?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank You for seating me with You in the heavenly places. I submit myself to You, and I take the authority You have given me. In the name of Jesus, I resist the enemy in my life, my family, and my home. All power belongs to You. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The enemy doesn't fear my strength; he fears the name I bear.

days.title: Baptized with the Holy Spirit
days.meditation:
## The Context

Before ascending to heaven, Jesus gives His disciples one final command: don't start the mission right away. Wait. "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be My witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the remotest part of the earth." (Acts 1:8)

Yet these men had spent three years with Jesus. They had seen the miracles, heard the teachings, seen the empty tomb. They believed. And Jesus told them: you're still missing something—power from on high.

## What Scripture Says

Ten days later, on the day of Pentecost, as they gathered and prayed: "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit was giving them utterance." (Acts 2:4)

The result was spectacular. Peter, who had denied Jesus before a servant girl just weeks earlier, stands before thousands and preaches with incredible boldness. That day, about three thousand people converted. The difference between the Peter of the denial and the Peter of Pentecost is the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

And this experience wasn't just for the apostles. Peter makes it clear to the crowd: "Peter said to them, 'Repent, and each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God will call to Himself.'" (Acts 2:38-39) "For you, your children, and all who are far off." That means you, today.

In the book of Acts, this experience repeats: in Samaria, at Cornelius's house, in Ephesus. Paul meets disciples there and asks them a question: "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" They said to him, "We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit." (Acts 19:2) Then he laid his hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came upon them: they spoke in tongues and prophesied.

In 1906, in Los Angeles, in a modest building on Azusa Street, a group of believers around an African-American preacher, William Seymour, began to pray to receive the Holy Spirit as on the day of Pentecost. What happened there marked the beginning of the Pentecostal movement, which today counts hundreds of millions of Christians around the world. The same Spirit, the same promise.

The Holy Spirit is not an option for special Christians: it's the power promised to every believer.

## For Your Life

Have you been baptized in the Holy Spirit? This isn't a question to judge you—it's an invitation. Jesus made a simple promise: "If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him."

Today, ask Him. Simply, with faith, like a child asking his father. Open your mouth to praise God, and let the Spirit give you new words. Don't be afraid: your Father won't give you a serpent when you ask Him for a fish.

And if you've already received it, remember that Paul urges: "be filled with the Spirit." You can be filled again and again. The disciples, filled at Pentecost, are filled again a few chapters later.

pratique.texte: If you haven't yet received the baptism of the Holy Spirit, take time alone or with a leader from your church. Read Luke 11:13, ask simply, then open your mouth to praise God without fear.
Paul says "be filled"—it's continuous. This week, take five minutes each day to pray in the Spirit and praise God, even in your car or while walking.
The baptism of the Holy Spirit gives power to be a witness (Acts 1:8). Ask God for an opportunity this week to speak about Jesus, then seize it, even if awkwardly.

days.question: Have I already asked for and received the baptism of the Holy Spirit? What's keeping me from asking today, or from being filled again?
days.priere: Heavenly Father, You have promised to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask You. I ask You today, with faith. Baptize me, fill me with Your Spirit and Your power, so that I may be Your witness. I receive Your promise. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The Holy Spirit is not an option for special Christians: it's the power promised to every believer.

days.title: Equipped with Spiritual Gifts
days.meditation:
## The Context

The church at Corinth was a living church, where spiritual gifts were manifesting frequently, sometimes in disorder. Paul doesn't tell them to stop. He teaches them how to exercise them properly, with love. And he begins with a fundamental principle: "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." (1 Corinthians 12:7)

## What Scripture Says

"To each one." Not just the pastor, the elders, or "spiritual" Christians. Every believer receives a manifestation of the Spirit. And why? "For the common good." Gifts aren't medals to show off—they're tools to serve.

Paul gives a list: "To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the distinguishing of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues." (1 Corinthians 12:8-10)

And he clarifies who decides: "But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually just as He wills." You don't need to envy someone else's gift, nor despise your own.

Elsewhere, Paul mentions other gifts: serving, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, showing mercy. Peter sums it up: "As each one has received a special gift, employ it in serving one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God." (1 Peter 4:10)

Are these gifts still for today? The Bible never says they ceased with the apostles. On the contrary, Paul writes that we await Jesus's return without lacking any gift, and he urges: "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy." (1 Corinthians 14:1) To desire earnestly means to long for them intensely. God doesn't distribute His gifts to those who mock them, but to those who desire them to bless others.

And at the heart of this passage, Paul places the famous chapter 13: love. Without love, even the most spectacular gifts are just noise. Gifts are the means; love is the goal.

Imagine at Christmas someone leaves their gifts wrapped under the tree for years, afraid to open them or use them wrongly. Many Christians have God's gifts still wrapped up.

An unopened gift blesses no one.

## For Your Life

What is your gift? If you don't know yet, ask yourself these questions: What makes me come alive when I serve God? When have I seen God work through me? What do others recognize in me? And most importantly, ask God, as Paul recommends.

Then take action in a healthy setting: your local church, a prayer group, a service team. If you feel God giving you a word of encouragement for someone, dare to share it humbly. If you feel compassion for a sick person, offer to pray for them. Gifts grow when you use them with love.

pratique.texte: Answer three questions in writing: What makes me come alive when I serve God? When have I seen God work through me? What do others recognize in me? Then pray over your answers.
Offer your help in a service at your church or a prayer group. Gifts develop through serving, and they're protected when you stay in fellowship and under the guidance of leaders.
Ask God for a word of encouragement for a person. If something comes to you, share it humbly: "I believe God is putting on my heart to tell you…" and let them judge.

days.question: What gift has God placed in me, and how can I start using it this week to bless someone?
days.priere: Holy Spirit, thank You for the gifts You distribute as You will. I earnestly desire spiritual gifts to bless others. Reveal to me what You have placed within me, and give me courage to use it with love, for the common good. Amen.
days.aRetenir: An unopened gift blesses no one.

days.title: Laying Hands on the Sick
days.meditation:
## Week 3: Living Out My Identity

The first two weeks, we discovered who you are and what you've received. This final week, we put it into practice: how to live out this identity concretely. And we start with a mission Jesus entrusted to all who believe.

## What Scripture Says

After His resurrection, Jesus announces the signs that will accompany His disciples: "These signs will accompany those who have believed: in My name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues; they will pick up serpents, and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover." (Mark 16:17-18) Notice well: "those who have believed." Not just the apostles, not just pastors. Believers.
