The first disciples took this seriously. Peter and John go up to the temple to pray. At the gate, a man crippled from birth begs. Peter has no money, but he has something else: "Then Peter said, 'I do not possess silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene—walk!'" (Acts 3:6) And the man gets up, walks, leaps, and praises God.

Where does this boldness come from? The cross. Isaiah had announced: "But He was pierced through for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; The chastening for our well-being fell upon Him, and by His scourging we are healed." (Isaiah 53:5) And Matthew shows that Jesus fulfilled this prophecy when He healed the sick: "He Himself took our infirmities and carried away our diseases." Jesus hasn't changed—He's the same yesterday, today, and forever.

James also gives a framework for the church: "Is anyone among you sick? Then he must call for the elders of the church and they are to pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him." (James 5:14-15)

In the early twentieth century, in England, a former plumber who was almost illiterate, Smith Wigglesworth, became a preacher known worldwide for his healing ministry. What struck people wasn't his eloquence, but his simple faith: he believed Jesus did what He promised.

Let's be honest: not everyone is healed immediately when we pray, and we don't always understand why. Praying for the sick doesn't mean refusing doctors; God uses medicine too. But these mysteries should never make us stop obeying. We don't heal anyone; Jesus heals. Our part is to believe and obey.

You may have neither silver nor gold, but you have the name of Jesus.

## For Your Life

This week, dare to pray for a sick person. It could be a family member, a coworker, a neighbor. Ask them first: "Can I pray for you?" Most people say yes.

Then pray simply, without theatrics: place your hand on their shoulder if they're comfortable with it, and say for example: "In the name of Jesus, I command this pain to leave. Be healed." Ask them afterward how they feel. If nothing changes, don't be ashamed: thank them, and keep praying. And if something happens, give glory to God.

pratique.titre: Pray for a Sick Person This Week
pratique.texte: Choose someone sick (family, coworker, neighbor) and ask them: "Can I pray for you?" Pray briefly, in Jesus's name, then ask them how they feel.
Praying for healing doesn't replace medical care. Always encourage the person to continue their treatment and see their doctor: God heals also through medicine.
If nothing changes, thank the person, never make them feel guilty about their faith, and keep praying in the following days. If something changes, give glory to God together and tell others.

days.question: Who around me is sick and needs me to pray for them this week? What's keeping me from offering?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, You bore our diseases and You are the same today. Give me the boldness of Peter and John. I have neither silver nor gold, but I have Your name. Use me to lay hands on the sick, and confirm Your Word with healings, for Your glory. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I may have neither silver nor gold, but I have the name of Jesus.

days.title: Casting Out Demons in Jesus's Name
days.meditation:
## The Context

Jesus sends seventy disciples two by two into the cities where he will go. These are not apostles, not "super-Christians": ordinary disciples. He tells them to heal the sick and announce that the kingdom of God is near. They return overjoyed: "The seventy returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name.'" (Luke 10:17)

## What Scripture Says

Jesus confirms their experience: "I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning." Then he adds: "Behold, I give you the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt you. Nevertheless do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven." (Luke 10:18-20)

Spiritual warfare is a reality in Scripture. John sums up Jesus' mission in one sentence: "He who sins is of the devil, for the devil has sinned from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that He might destroy the works of the devil." (1 John 3:8) About a third of Jesus' ministry in the Gospels concerns delivering people who are tormented. And he entrusted this mission to his disciples: "In My name they will cast out demons."

In the book of Acts, at Philippi, a slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination follows Paul for several days. Finally: "This she kept doing for many days. But Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And he came out that very hour." (Acts 16:18) Notice how Paul acts: he doesn't cry out for hours, he doesn't dialogue with the spirit, he doesn't make a show. He gives a clear command, in the name of Jesus Christ, and the spirit leaves.

Three principles of wisdom. First, don't see demons everywhere: many difficulties come from our choices, our wounds, or our health, and they demand other answers, like repentance, support, or care. Next, don't be afraid: the one in you is greater than the one in the world. Finally, don't exalt yourself: Jesus says to rejoice first that our names are written in heaven. Authority is a tool, not an identity; your identity is being a child of God.

And be wise: deliverance is best experienced with the support of mature leaders in faith, within the context of the church.

Darkness does not flee before the volume of your voice, but before the authority of the name of Jesus.

pratique.texte: If you or your family have touched occultism (fortune telling, horoscopes, witch doctors, spiritism, "lucky" objects), renounce it clearly in the name of Jesus and get rid of the objects connected to it.
Pray aloud, without shouting or being afraid: "In the name of Jesus, I cast out every spirit of fear, torment, and oppression from my life and my house." Then fill your home with praise.
If the oppression is strong or long-standing, don't face it alone: ask leaders from your church to pray with you. Deliverance happens in the body of Christ, with wisdom and love.

days.question: Is there a door open to the enemy in my life (occultism, fear, unforgiveness, hidden sin) that I need to close in the name of Jesus?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you came to destroy the works of the devil. I close every door I have opened to the enemy, and I renounce it. In the name of Jesus, I cast out all oppression from my life and my house. Thank you especially that my name is written in heaven. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Darkness does not flee before the volume of my voice, but before the name of Jesus.

days.title: Unmask the Lies
days.meditation:
## The Context

Just before being tempted in the wilderness, Jesus has just been baptized. The heavens opened, the Spirit descended on him, and the Father spoke: "and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon Him. And a voice came from heaven which said, 'You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.'" (Luke 3:22)

And what does the devil do, right after? "Then the tempter came to Him and said, 'If You are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.'" (Matthew 4:3)

## What Scripture Says

Did you notice? The devil's first attack is not about food, it's about identity. "If You are the Son of God…" The Father just said "You are My Son," and the enemy replies: "Prove it." That's always his strategy: to sow doubt about what God has said. Just like in the Garden of Eden: "Did God really say…?"

Jesus makes it clear: "You are of your father the devil, and the desires of your father you want to do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, for he is a liar and the father of it." (John 8:44) The enemy really has no other weapon than the lie. He can't tear you from the Father's hand, so he tries to make you believe you're not in it.

His lies often sound like our own thoughts: "God can't love you after what you've done." "You'll never change." "You're alone." "You have no value." They sometimes settle in from childhood, like strongholds in our minds.

Paul gives us the strategy: "For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty in God for pulling down strongholds, casting down arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:4-5) Pulling down strongholds, bringing every thought into captivity. That means you're not obligated to accept every thought that comes into your head. You can examine it, confront it with Scripture, and if it's a lie, reject it.

And notice how Jesus responds: not with arguments, not with emotions, but with Scripture. Three times: "It is written."

You don't drive out the lie by fighting it in the dark; you turn on the light of truth.

pratique.texte: Write three lies you believe about yourself on the left, and on the right three truths from Scripture with their references. Keep the paper with you this week.
Each time a lie returns, respond like Jesus: "It is written…" and proclaim the truth. Do it even if you don't feel it yet: the truth eventually sinks into the heart.

pratique.titre: If a Lie Comes from a Wound
pratique.texte: Some lies were born from a hurtful word ("you'll never amount to anything"). Forgive the person who said it, and ask God to heal the wound.

days.question: What are the three lies about myself that I have believed the longest, and what truth from Scripture answers each one?
days.priere: Lord, I thank you for calling me your beloved child. I refuse the enemy's lies about my identity. I pull down strongholds in my mind, and I bring every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ. It is written… and I believe what you say. Amen.
days.aRetenir: You don't drive out the lie by fighting it in the dark; you turn on the light of truth.

days.title: Renew My Mind, Align My Words
days.meditation:
## The Context

Yesterday, we unmasked the lies. Today, we go deeper: filling the empty space. Because an empty mind doesn't stay empty for long. Paul writes: "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God." (Romans 12:2)

## What Scripture Says

The word "transformed" translates the Greek verb that gave us the word "metamorphosis." The same transformation as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. And Paul says it happens through the "renewing of your mind," that is, your way of thinking.

Imagine a field of tall grass. The first time you cross it, it's hard. But if you always pass through the same spot, a path forms, and soon you walk it without thinking. Our thoughts work a bit like that. Old thoughts of fear, shame, or anger have worn deep paths. Renewal is tracing new paths with God's truth, day after day, until they become natural.

Paul also tells us where to direct our thoughts: "Finally, brethren, whatever things are true, whatever things are noble, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report, if there is any virtue and if there is anything praiseworthy—meditate on these things." (Philippians 4:8)

And what fills the heart eventually comes out of the mouth. The book of Proverbs affirms it: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, And those who love it will eat its fruits." (Proverbs 18:21) Your words are not neutral. They build or they destroy, you and others. "I'm worthless," "it will never work," "my children are disasters": these sentences, repeated, become prophecies over our lives.

God gave Joshua a key to succeeding in his mission: "This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate in it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success." (Joshua 1:8) "This Book shall not depart from your mouth." To meditate on Scripture is not only to read it, but to whisper it, repeat it, declare it.

Change your thoughts, and you will change your words; change your words, and you will change your direction.

pratique.texte: Note for one day what you feed your mind (social media, shows, conversations, news). Choose one thing to reduce this week and replace that time with Scripture, praise, or a good book.
For 24 hours, monitor your words. Every negative word about yourself or someone else—catch yourself and replace it with a word of faith or blessing.
Choose someone you tend to speak negatively about, and decide to speak at least one positive and true word about them today.

days.question: What negative words do I speak most often about myself or others, and what word of life will I replace them with?
days.priere: Lord, transform me by the renewing of my mind. Fill my thoughts with what is true, pure, and worthy of praise. Guard my lips: let my words give life, not death. Let Your word not depart from my mouth. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Change your thoughts, and you will change your words; change your words, and you will change your direction.

days.title: My Value Is Neither My Performance Nor Others' Gaze
days.meditation:
## The Context

God sends the prophet Samuel to Jesse in Bethlehem to anoint the future king of Israel. Jesse has his sons pass by. The first, Eliab, is tall and impressive; Samuel immediately thinks: "It must be him." But God stops him: "And the Lord said to Samuel, 'Do not look at his appearance or at the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the Lord does not see as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.'" (1 Samuel 16:7)

Seven sons pass by, and God chooses none of them. There remains one, the youngest, whom they hadn't even thought it necessary to call: David, who was tending the sheep. The one his own family had forgotten—he was the one God had chosen.

## What Scripture Says

We live in a culture that measures your worth by two things: what you produce and what others think of you. Degrees, salary, followers, "likes," appearance. And many Christians bring this system into their relationship with God: I'm worth something if I pray a lot, if I serve a lot, if people notice me at church.

Look at Jesus's baptism. The Father declares: "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased." At that moment, Jesus had not yet performed any miracle, preached any sermon, healed any sick person. The Father loves him before any performance. He doesn't serve to be loved; he serves because he is loved.

Paul, who had been a very ambitious and highly recognized man, had to choose: "For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I trying to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." (Galatians 1:10) You cannot serve two masters, and the regard of others is a demanding master. It changes its mind every day, it's never satisfied, and it makes you a slave.

Jesus put his finger on the root of the problem: "How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"

When you live for the approval of men, their criticism kills you and their compliments puff you up; when you live for God's approval, you are free.

## For Your Life

Ask yourself honest questions. Does my mood depend on what people think of me? Do I post, speak, serve to be seen? Do I feel worthless when I fail or when I rest?

Today, do something good in secret, that no one will see: an act of help, a gift, a prayer for someone. And say to God: "This is for you." Then receive, as Jesus did at the Jordan, the Father's word over your life, before any performance: you are his beloved child.

pratique.texte: Ask yourself: does my mood depend on what people think of me? Write down a recent situation where others' regard took up too much space, and give it to God.
Perform an act of kindness today that no one will see, and tell God: "This is for you." Do it again this week without posting about it.
If you feel worthless when you produce nothing, take real time to rest this week and thank God for being loved even when you do nothing.

days.question: Does my sense of worth depend more on my performance and others' regard, or on what God says about me?
days.priere: Father, you look not at appearance but at the heart. Free me from the slavery of others' regard and the race for performance. I receive your word over my life: I am your beloved child, before anything I could ever do. Amen.
days.aRetenir: I don't serve God to be loved; I serve him because I am loved.

days.title: Called and Sent
days.meditation:
## The Context

Gideon is hiding in a winepress, threshing wheat in secret so that the Midianite enemies won't steal it from him. He is a frightened man in a humiliated people. And it is there that the Angel of the Lord appears to him and says: "And the Angel of the Lord appeared to him, and said to him, 'The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor!'" (Judges 6:12)

Mighty man of valor? Gideon must have looked behind him. He answers: "Gideon said to Him, 'O my lord, if the Lord is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all His miracles which our fathers told us about, saying, "Did not the Lord bring us up from Egypt?" But now the Lord has abandoned us and delivered us into the hands of the Midianites.'" (Judges 6:15)

## What Scripture Says

God doesn't call Gideon for who he is, but for who he will become with him. "The Lord is with you"—that's the key. It's not Gideon's strength that will make him a hero; it's God's presence.

You are not only saved to go to heaven one day. You are called and sent right now. Paul says: "For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them." (Ephesians 2:10) God has prepared good works for you in advance. There are people only you can reach, places only you have access to.

After his resurrection, Jesus said to his disciples: "Jesus said to them again, 'Peace to you! As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.'" (John 20:21) As the Father sent him—with the same mission, the same presence of the Spirit, the same authority. And he made this staggering promise: "Most assuredly, I say to you, he who believes in Me, the works that I do he will do also; and greater works than these he will do, because I go to My Father." (John 14:12)

The greatest works don't come from great talents, but from ordinary people who say yes to an extraordinary God. Moses stammered, Jeremiah thought he was too young, Peter was impulsive, Gideon was afraid. God doesn't look for capable people; he makes capable those who make themselves available.

God doesn't call you for what you see in the mirror, but for what he sees in you.

## For Your Life

What is your "Midian"? The area where you hide, where you feel too small, too weak, not qualified enough? Maybe God has been speaking to you for a while about a calling: to witness to a coworker, to start a prayer group, to serve in the church, to go on a mission, to write, to sing, to build something for the kingdom.

Today, listen to what God says about you: "The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor." Then take one step, just one, even if small, in the direction of your calling. Share your faith with a person this week. Dare to say: "May I pray for you?" You are a messenger of Jesus where you live, and he promised: "Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age."

pratique.texte: Write down the area where you hide or feel too small. Then read Judges 6:12 putting your name in it: "The Lord is with you, O mighty [your name]."
Choose a concrete step toward your calling this week: offer your help at church, talk about Jesus to a coworker, start a project God has put on your heart, ask advice from a leader.

pratique.titre: Pray for Someone Where You Are
pratique.texte: At work, school, or in your neighborhood, dare to ask a person: "May I pray for you?" You are a messenger of Jesus where you live.

days.question: In what area do I feel "the smallest," when God calls me "mighty man of valor"? What concrete step will I take this week?
days.priere: Lord, like Gideon, I sometimes feel the smallest. But you are with me. I receive your calling: as the Father sent you, you send me. I make myself available. Use me to do the works you have prepared beforehand for me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God doesn't call me for what I see in the mirror, but for what he sees in me.

days.title: Abiding in Him
days.meditation:
## The Context

We've reached the last day of this journey. In 21 days, you've discovered your identity: created in God's image, redeemed, born again, adopted as a child, forgiven, declared righteous, a new creation. You've opened the treasure chest of all you have in Christ: the Spirit who dwells in you, access to the Father, freedom, victory, authority, the baptism of the Holy Spirit, his gifts. And you've begun living from this identity: praying for the sick, driving out oppression in Jesus's name, overturning lies, aligning your thoughts and words, serving without seeking approval, answering your calling.

But how can you keep all this just weeks from now? Jesus gives the answer in one word: abide.

## What Scripture Says

"As the Father loved Me, I also have loved you; abide in My love." (John 15:9)

Identity is not a teaching you learn once and for all; it's a relationship in which you remain. Everything you are, you are "in Christ." Not outside of him, not beside him: in him.

Paul expresses it this way: "As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him and established in the faith, as you have been taught, abounding in it with thanksgiving." (Colossians 2:6-7) As you received Jesus, through faith, through grace, walk in him the same way. Don't start with grace and continue by your own efforts.

And he sums up the entire Christian life in one magnificent verse: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me." (Galatians 2:20)

A tree doesn't work hard to develop deep roots. It develops them day after day, reaching down deep to find water. Trees whose roots are shallow fall at the first storm. Those who are deeply rooted hold firm, even when the wind blows hard.

What defines a Christian is not having met Jesus one day, but abiding in him every day.

## For Your Life

To finish this journey, I invite you to do three things.

Reread your list. Go back to the sheet you made on day seven, with the crossed-out labels and God's truths. Add everything you've discovered since. Keep it somewhere you'll see it often.

Choose your rhythm. Abiding in Jesus comes through simple habits: a daily time in Scripture and prayer, fellowship in a local church, worship, service. Concretely choose what you'll keep after this plan.

Declare your identity. Read aloud, in conclusion: "I am created in God's image, redeemed by the blood of Jesus, born again, adopted child of the Father, forgiven and declared righteous, a new creation, temple of the Holy Spirit, free, more than a conqueror. I have the authority of Jesus's name, I am filled with the Spirit and equipped with his gifts. I am called and sent. And I abide in him."

This is not the end of the road; it's the beginning of a life lived out of who you truly are.

pratique.texte: Go back to your sheet from day seven (crossed-out labels and God's truths). Add what you've discovered since, and post it somewhere you'll see it often.
Decide concretely what you'll keep after this plan: a daily time in Scripture, a local church, a home group, a service. Write it down and share it with someone who will encourage you.
Think of someone who needs to discover who they are in Christ. Invite them to do this plan, or do it together as a "two-person plan" in the app.

days.question: What concrete habits will I keep after this plan to continue abiding in Jesus every day?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for these 21 days. Thank you for revealing to me who I am in you. I choose to abide in your love, rooted and founded in you. It is no longer I who live, but you who live in me. May my entire life flow from my identity in you from now on. Amen.
days.aRetenir: What defines a Christian is not having met Jesus one day, but abiding in him every day.

items.title: Announce, Free, and Heal
items.subtitle: 21 days to rediscover the three mandates Jesus entrusted to his disciples, and live them today.
items.summary: When Jesus sends his disciples, he gives them more than a message: he entrusts them with a mission. Announce the good news of the kingdom, heal the sick, free the captives. This wasn't reserved for the twelve, nor for pastors, nor for the first century: every disciple is called to live it. In 21 days, you'll see how Jesus and the first Christians lived these three mandates, and how you too, where you live, can announce, lay hands on the sick, and see lives set free, with a concrete challenge each day of the week "Heal." Each day: the verses first, then the exhortation, and concrete steps to put it into practice. Bible texts: Louis Segond 1910.

days.title: Sent as He Is
days.meditation:
## Part 1: The Mandate

For 21 days, we're going to look closely at a mission. Not a mission invented by a church or organization, but one that Jesus himself entrusted to his disciples. It comes down to three verbs: announce, heal, free.

## What the Word Says

Jesus gathers the twelve. They are neither priests nor theologians nor public figures. Fishermen, a tax collector, a political activist. Ordinary people. And here's what he does: "Jesus called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. He sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick." (Luke 9:1-2)

Notice the order. First, Jesus gives: power, authority, strength. Only then does he send. He never sends anyone empty-handed. And the mission is clear: proclaim the kingdom of God, heal the sick, and authority over demons to free those who are tormented. Three mandates, one mission: to show that the reign of God has come.

To announce is to speak the good news. To heal and free is to demonstrate it. The message and the signs go together. A word without demonstration can seem theoretical; a demonstration without a word can seem like magic. Jesus unites the two.

And this mandate didn't stay on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. After his resurrection, Jesus says to his disciples: "Jesus said to them again, 'Peace be with you! As the Father has sent me, I also send you.'" (John 20:21)

## Ambassadors

An ambassador is not at home. He lives in a foreign country, but he represents his own. When he speaks officially, it's not his personal opinion: it's the voice of his country. And behind him stands all the authority of his government. Paul uses exactly this image: "We are therefore Christ's ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us" (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Jesus didn't just send a message: he sent messengers.

## For Your Life

Maybe you've always thought these things were for pastors, evangelists, missionaries. But look at who Jesus entrusted them to first: ordinary people, who weren't finished with their training, who often made mistakes, who even argued about who was the greatest.

You don't need to be perfect to be sent. You need to be with Jesus and receive what he gives. During these three weeks, let him show you how these three mandates can take shape in your life: in your home, at work, in your neighborhood, in your church.

pratique.texte: Honestly note what scares you or troubles you about these three words: announce, heal, free. Present this list to Jesus; he doesn't send you without equipping you.
Pray simply: "Lord, as the Father sent you, send me. Give me what I need for this mission." Date this prayer in your Bible or journal.
Jesus sent his disciples two by two (Luke 10:1). Invite someone to do this plan with you and pray together once a week during these 21 days.

days.question: What makes me think these three mandates aren't "for me"? What does Jesus answer to that?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for entrusting your mission to ordinary people like me. As the Father sent you, send me. Give me your power and authority, and teach me during these 21 days to announce, to lay hands on the sick, and to see lives set free in your name. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus didn't just send a message: he sent messengers.

days.title: Moved With Compassion
days.meditation:
## What Jesus Did

Before sending his disciples, Jesus showed them the model. Matthew sums up his entire ministry in one sentence: "Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom and healing every disease and sickness." (Matthew 9:35)

Teaching, proclaiming, healing. And, as we see throughout the Gospels, freeing those who were tormented. Peter will summarize it later to a Roman official: "How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and how he went around doing good and healing all who were under the power of the devil, for God was with him." (Acts 10:38)

## The Engine: Compassion

But what strikes most is the reason for all of this: "When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd." (Matthew 9:36)

The Greek word translated "compassion" refers to the viscera, the gut. It's not a polite emotion, it's something that grabs you from the inside. Jesus sees a crowd that is tired, lost, sick, and beaten down, and it hurts him inside.

Jesus' miracles were never demonstrations of power to impress. When the devil offered him to throw himself from the top of the temple to make a sensation, he refused. But before a leper, a widow burying her son, a hungry crowd, he would stop. Compassion was the engine; power was the means.

Compassion without action remains an emotion; action without compassion becomes a performance.

## Prayer Before Sending

Then Jesus says something astonishing: "Then he said to his disciples, 'The harvest is plentiful but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into his harvest field.'" (Matthew 9:37-38)

He doesn't say "go" first, but "pray." And a few verses later, in chapter 10, those he asked to pray for workers... become themselves the workers sent out. Often, when you really pray for a need, God ends up saying to you: "And you?".

## For Your Life

Before asking God for his power, ask him for his heart. Many people would like to see miracles, but few accept to see the suffering of others up close. The two go together.

Look around you with the eyes of Jesus. In your apartment building, at your work, in your family, on your social feed, there are "sheep without a shepherd": people who are tired, lost, sick, alone. The harvest is not just in Africa or Asia. It's often two meters away from you.

The first step to announce, heal, and free is to let God break your heart for what breaks his.

pratique.texte: Pray today: "Lord, give me your compassion for the people around me." Then stay attentive all day: who do you notice that you didn't notice before?
Write down five names of people in your circle who are tired, sick, lost, or far from God. Pray for them every day during this plan.
Choose one of these people and take a concrete action this week: a phone call, a visit, a meal, help. Compassion becomes real when it moves.

days.question: Who makes my heart "move with compassion" today? And for whom should it move even more?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you were moved with compassion for the crowds. Give me your heart. Break my heart for what breaks yours. I prayed for workers in your harvest; here I am, send me too. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Compassion without action remains an emotion; action without compassion becomes a performance.

days.title: For Today Still
days.meditation:
## The Last Mandate

Before ascending into heaven, Jesus gives his final instructions. And he doesn't limit them to the twelve: "Then he said to them, 'Go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation.'" (Mark 16:15)

Then he adds a promise that concerns "those who have believed," that is, all those who would believe through the testimony of the apostles—so you and me: "These signs will accompany those who have believed: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover." (Mark 16:17-18)

Announce, free, heal: the three mandates are there, for the whole Church.

## What History Says

Some think miracles stopped with the apostles. But history tells a different story. Around the year 180, Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, wrote that in the Church of his time, some still cast out demons, others healed the sick by laying hands on them. More than a hundred years after the death of the apostles, in Lyon, in France, the Church was still living these mandates.

And these days, in many countries of Africa, Latin America, and Asia, the rapid growth of the Church is often accompanied by healings and deliverance. What Jesus began has never stopped.

Jesus had announced it: "Very truly I tell you, whoever believes in me will do the works I have been doing, and they will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father;" (John 14:12)

## A Relay

Think of a relay race. The first runner doesn't run the whole race. He carries the baton, then passes it on. The second doesn't start over: he continues the same race. Jesus ran the first part; he passed the baton to the apostles, who passed it to others, generation after generation, until you.

A mandate doesn't expire with the one who received it first.

## For Your Life

Notice the end of the chapter: "Then the disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them and confirmed his word by the signs that accompanied it." (Mark 16:20) The disciples go out, and the Lord works with them. They preach; he confirms. It's not you who heals or you who frees. You, you obey: you announce, you lay on hands, you command in the name of Jesus. He does the miracle.

That takes away a lot of pressure. You don't have to produce results. You have to be faithful. The results belong to God.

Today, the question is not: "Am I spiritual enough for this?" But: "Do I believe that Jesus told the truth?"

pratique.texte: Reread Mark 16:17-18 replacing "those who have believed" with "I who believe." Note what that does in you: faith, fear, doubt, joy? Tell God about it.
Ask Christians in your church if they've ever seen God heal or free someone. Listen to their stories: faith grows by hearing what God does.
If you prayed for someone who wasn't healed, or if you've seen abuse in this area, tell God about it honestly. Ask him to heal your disappointment without quenching your faith.

days.question: Do I really believe that the promises of Mark 16 are for today, and for me? What makes me hesitate?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, I believe you told the truth. I receive the baton you passed on to your Church. I don't want to produce results; I want to obey you. Work with me, and confirm your word by the signs that accompany it. Amen.
days.aRetenir: A mandate doesn't expire with the one who received it first.

days.title: Good News, Not Good Advice
days.meditation:
## Part 2: Announce

The first mandate is to announce. But announce what, exactly? Many Christians are afraid to talk about their faith because they don't know where to start. So let's begin with the heart of the message.

## What the Word Says

Paul writes to the Corinthians to remind them of what is essential, what he taught "first and foremost": "For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4)

There's the Gospel in four statements: Christ died, for our sins, He was buried, He rose again. Not a philosophy, not a list of rules, not a method to be happy: facts. Something that happened in history, with witnesses. Paul even mentions over five hundred people who saw the risen Jesus, most of whom were still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:6).

The word "gospel" means "good news." In the Roman Empire, this word was used to announce a military victory or the birth of an emperor: an event that changed everyone's life. The early Christians took it up to announce the greatest victory in history: death has been defeated.

The Gospel is not good advice; it's good news.

Advice tells you what you should do. News tells you what has been done. "Try harder, be better, and maybe God will accept you": that's advice, and it crushes. "Jesus paid for you, He's alive, and He offers you a new life": that's news, and it sets you free.

## The Power

Paul adds elsewhere: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and also for the Greek" (Romans 1:16)

The Gospel is not just information; it's power. When you announce it, even awkwardly, something happens in people's hearts, because God works through His Word.

## For Your Life

To announce, you don't need to know all theology. You need to know the news, and be able to say it simply. Try: can you explain the Gospel in one minute to a ten-year-old? God loves us; sin has separated us from Him; Jesus died in our place and rose again; if we put our trust in Him, we receive forgiveness and a new life.

And don't be ashamed. Paul, who was beaten, imprisoned, mocked for this message, says he is not ashamed of it. Sometimes we're afraid of bothering people. But if you had found a cure for a deadly disease, would you keep it secret out of politeness?

pratique.texte: Write out the Gospel in five simple sentences, in your own words. Read it aloud until you can say it without notes in one minute.
Explain it to a Christian friend or your child, and ask them what was clear and what wasn't. You learn to announce by announcing.
Think of someone who doesn't know Jesus. Pray each day this week for an opportunity to open up and talk to them, and for you to recognize it when it comes.

days.question: If someone asked me tomorrow "what is the Gospel?", what would I say in one minute?
days.priere: Lord, thank you for the good news: You died for my sins, You were buried, You rose again. I am not ashamed of the Gospel. Give me simple words to announce it, and the power of Your Spirit to touch hearts. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The Gospel is not good advice; it's good news.

days.title: Peter's Boldness
days.meditation:
## The Story

Fifty days after Passover, the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit. A crowd gathers. And Peter stands up to speak. Peter—the one who, just a few weeks earlier, had denied Jesus before a servant girl, by a fire. That same man now stands before thousands of people, in the very city where Jesus was crucified, and he boldly announces: this Jesus whom you crucified, God has raised Him.

## What Changed

What happened between the Peter who trembled before a servant girl and the one preaching to the crowd? Two things: he saw the risen Jesus, and he was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Boldness is not the absence of fear; it's the presence of the Spirit.

And the result is stunning: "Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the other apostles, 'Men and brethren, what shall we do?' Then Peter said to them, 'Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'" (Acts 2:37-38) That day, about three thousand people join the disciples.

Notice how Peter announces. He starts from what the people just saw and heard (the tongues, the sound). He quotes the Scriptures they know (Joel, the Psalms). He speaks about Jesus: His life, His death, His resurrection. And he calls them to respond: repent, be baptized, receive the Spirit. Announcing is not just informing; it's inviting.

## Ordinary People

Some time later, Peter and John are arrested for healing a crippled beggar and announcing Jesus. The religious leaders are amazed: "Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated and untrained men, they marveled. And they realized that they had been with Jesus." (Acts 4:13)

"Uneducated": they had no formal religious training. But it was clear they had been with Jesus. Their strength didn't come from their degrees; it came from their relationship with Him.

## For Your Life

Maybe you feel like the Peter of before: you've already been ashamed of Jesus, you've stayed silent when you should have spoken, you've even denied your faith in one way or another. That's not the end of your story. The same Spirit who transformed Peter wants to fill you with boldness.

Boldness doesn't mean being aggressive or forcing people. It's daring to say what you believe, with love, when the opportunity comes. It's no longer hiding your faith as if it were something to be ashamed of.

And remember: you're not responsible for people's response. Peter spoke; it was the Spirit who touched hearts. Your part is to open your mouth. God's part is to open hearts.

pratique.texte: Pray each morning this week: "Holy Spirit, fill me with boldness today." Then stay alert for opportunities to talk about Jesus, even with just a small sentence.
When someone asks how your weekend was, simply mention church or what God is doing in your life. One sentence is enough to open a door.
If you have a chance to talk about Jesus with someone this week, don't forget the invitation: offer to pray with them, suggest they read a Gospel, or invite them to church.

days.question: In what situation do I struggle most to talk about my faith? What does Peter's story tell me about that situation?
days.priere: Holy Spirit, You transformed fearful Peter into bold Peter. Fill me with Your boldness. I don't want to hide my faith anymore. Open my mouth when I need to speak, and open the hearts of those who hear me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Boldness is not the absence of fear; it's the presence of the Spirit.

days.title: Philip on the Desert Road
days.meditation:
## The Story

Philip is in the midst of a revival. In Samaria, crowds are listening to him, the sick are healed, demons come out screaming, and there is great joy in the city. And it's precisely at this moment that an angel tells him: leave all this, go down the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza.

Why? For one person. A high-ranking Ethiopian official, minister of finance to the queen, sitting in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah without understanding.

For God, one person is worth a journey into the desert.

## How Philip Announces

"The Spirit said to Philip, 'Go near and overtake this chariot.' So Philip ran to him, and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, 'Do you understand what you are reading?'" (Acts 8:29-30)

Notice first that Philip obeys the Spirit. He runs. He doesn't think about how to "place" the Gospel; he follows a direction.

Next, he starts with a question. He doesn't give a sermon: he asks the man what he's reading and if he understands it. He shows genuine interest in him. The man invites him to climb up into his chariot.

Finally, he starts from where the person is: "Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning at this Scripture, preached Jesus to him." (Acts 8:35)

"Beginning at this Scripture." The Ethiopian was reading Isaiah 53, the lamb led to slaughter. Philip doesn't change the subject; he takes the man's question and brings him to Jesus. And a few miles down the road, the man asks to be baptized and continues on his way filled with joy.

## For Your Life

Evangelizing is not reciting a ready-made speech to just anyone. It's listening to the Spirit, taking genuine interest in the person, and starting from their question, their story, their pain, to bring them to Jesus.

The people around you are already "reading" something: a trial, a question about death, a search for meaning, a TV show that talks about redemption, a song. These are their "passages of Isaiah." Ask questions, listen carefully, and you'll often find a bridge to Jesus.

Peter writes: "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts, and always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear" (1 Peter 3:15). With gentleness and respect. Not by crushing them, not by mocking them, not by trying to win a debate.

And perhaps God will sometimes ask you to leave the crowd for one person. One conversation on an ordinary road can change a life, and even a nation: tradition holds that the Church of Ethiopia traces its history to this man who returned home with the Gospel.

pratique.texte: This week, in a conversation with someone who doesn't know Jesus, ask a question about their life ("What gives you hope?" "How are you holding up through this trial?") and really listen.
Note what concerns the people around you: grief, illness, the future, loneliness. Prepare a verse or a small testimony that could answer that particular question.
Ask each morning: "Holy Spirit, who do You want me to go to today?" If someone comes to mind, send them a message or give them a call.

days.question: What questions are the people around me asking right now? How could I start there to talk to them about Jesus?
days.priere: Holy Spirit, teach me to listen to Your voice like Philip. Send me to those who are searching. Give me genuine interest in them, help me ask the right questions, and help me start from their story to announce Jesus to them, with gentleness and respect. Amen.
days.aRetenir: For God, one person is worth a journey into the desert.

days.title: Paul in Athens
days.meditation:
## The Story

Paul arrives in Athens, the intellectual capital of the ancient world. Philosophers, temples, statues at every corner. His spirit is "provoked" when he sees the city full of idols. But instead of shouting his anger, he reasons: in the synagogue, in the marketplace, with everyone he meets. Eventually he's brought to the Areopagus, where thinkers like to hear new ideas.

## How Paul Announces

"Then Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in all things you are very religious; for as I was passing through and considering the objects of your worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore, the One whom you worship without knowing, Him I proclaim to you.'" (Acts 17:22-23)

Paul doesn't start by condemning. He starts by observing and finding a point of contact: that altar "to an unknown god." He says in effect: "You're already seeking something. I've come to tell you who it is you're seeking."

Then he quotes their own poets: "We are also His offspring." He speaks their language, starts from their culture, uses their references. And he brings them to Jesus and His resurrection.

You don't change the message; you change the way you say it.

Paul explains it himself: "To the weak I became as weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." (1 Corinthians 9:22)

## The Results

And what are the reactions? Some mock. Others say: "We will hear you again on this matter." And a few believe, including a member of the Areopagus named Dionysius and a woman named Damaris.

Not a crowd of three thousand like at Pentecost. A few conversions, mockery, polite indifference. Yet Luke deems this story worth telling. Because obedience matters more than statistics.

## For Your Life

Your "Athens" might be your office, your university, your friend group, your social media. People who don't know the Bible, who have their idols (money, success, appearance, comfort), and yet are seeking something.

You don't need to start by condemning them. Find their "altar to an unknown god": the need for meaning, the longing for love, the fear of death, the desire for justice. Speak their language. Use examples from their lives, movies they watch, music they listen to.

And accept that not everyone will respond. Some will mock, others will say "later." That's not your failure. Your responsibility is to sow faithfully. God takes care of the harvest.

pratique.texte: Think of a person you know well who is not a believer. Write down what they're really searching for (meaning, love, peace, security). That's where you can begin to talk to them about Jesus.
Prepare a way to explain your faith using words and images from their world (sports, work, music, family)—without church jargon like "sanctification" or "anointing".
If someone mocks you or says "another time", don't get discouraged. Keep praying for them and loving them. Write their name on your prayer list.

days.question: What is my "Athens"? What are the "altars" of these people—what they're searching for without knowing it?
days.priere: Lord, give me a vision like Paul's: to see what people are really searching for without realizing it. Teach me to speak their language without changing your message. And when they mock me or put it off, keep me faithful and full of love. Amen.
days.aRetenir: You don't change the message—you change the way you say it.

days.title: I Know One Thing
days.meditation:
## The Story

Jesus meets a man who has been blind from birth. He spits on the ground, makes mud, applies it to the man's eyes, and tells him to go wash at the Pool of Siloam. The man goes, washes, and comes back seeing.

Everyone should rejoice. Instead, an investigation begins. The neighbors question him, the Pharisees question him, then his parents, then the man again. They want him to say that Jesus is a sinner, because he healed on the Sabbath.

The man doesn't know theology. He can't answer all their questions. But he says one sentence that no one can dispute: "He answered, 'Whether he is a sinner I don't know. One thing I do know—that though I was blind, now I see.'" (John 9:25)

## The Power of Testimony

The Pharisees have degrees, arguments, authority. The man has only one thing: what Jesus did for him. And it's unstoppable. You can debate a doctrine; you can't debate a blind man who now sees.

No one can dispute what Jesus has done in your life.

Revelation shows how believers overcame the accuser: "And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death." (Revelation 12:11) The blood of the Lamb, and the word of their testimony. Your story with Jesus is a weapon.

Notice also that the man's understanding grows as he testifies. First, he talks about "the man they call Jesus." Then he says, "He is a prophet." Then he defends Jesus before the authorities. And at the end of the chapter, he bows down before him, saying, "I believe, Lord." Testifying strengthens your own faith too.

## For Your Life

You may have never been born blind. But if you know Jesus, you have a story. Maybe he brought you out of depression, restored your family, freed you from addiction, gave you peace through grief, or simply gave your life meaning.

A simple testimony has three parts: what my life was like before I knew Jesus (or before he intervened); how I met him (or how he stepped in); what has changed since. No need to exaggerate or tell every detail. The truth is enough.

And don't be afraid of questions you can't answer. You can say, like this man: "I don't know that. But I know one thing."

pratique.texte: In three short paragraphs: before, the encounter, after. No more than a page. Read it over, remove the jargon, and keep what matters most.

pratique.titre: Practice Saying It in Two Minutes
pratique.texte: Tell it out loud, with a timer. Then tell it to a Christian friend and ask them what touched them most.
Choose one person and tell them what Jesus did for you, in the course of a conversation. If they ask hard questions, simply say: "I don't know everything, but I know one thing."

days.question: What is "the one thing I know"—what Jesus has done in my life that no one can dispute?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for what you have done in my life. I was blind, and now I see. Give me the courage to tell my story simply, without shame, and let my testimony lead others to you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: No one can dispute what Jesus has done in your life.

days.title: Praying for Boldness
days.meditation:
## The Story

Peter and John have just been released by the religious leaders with a strict order: stop speaking in the name of Jesus. They return to the other believers and tell them everything. And what does the church do? It prays.

But listen carefully to what it asks for: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus. And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness." (Acts 4:29-31)

They don't ask for persecution to stop. They don't ask to be protected, or for the leaders to be punished. They ask for boldness to keep speaking, and for God to stretch out his hand to heal and perform miracles in the name of Jesus. All three mandates are in their prayer.

The early church didn't pray for persecution to end—it prayed for boldness to increase.

And God answers immediately: the place shakes, they are all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they speak God's word with boldness.

## Prayer, the Engine of Mission

Throughout the history of the church, great missionary movements have almost always been born in prayer. In 1727, in a small village in Germany called Herrnhut, a community of Moravian Christians began a continuous prayer chain, day and night. It lasted about a hundred years. And from that village went missionaries to the Caribbean, Greenland, Africa, and America—ordinary men and women, often craftspeople, who went to live among the poorest to announce Jesus to them.

Before going to the people, they went to God.

## For Your Life

Paul asks a series of questions that show what's at stake: "How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!'" (Romans 10:14-15)

If no one speaks, how will people hear? And if no one prays, where will the boldness to speak come from?

Today, pray like the church in Acts. Not just "Lord, protect me," but "Lord, give me boldness, and stretch out your hand." Pray for the five people on your list. Pray for your church, that it would be a community that speaks, heals, and sets free.

And if you can, pray with others. That day, it wasn't one believer alone who prayed, but a whole community, "with one accord." There's a special power when brothers and sisters pray together for the mission.

pratique.texte: Copy Acts 4:29-30 and pray it every day this week, adding the names of the people on your list and the name of your city.

pratique.titre: Join or Start a Prayer Time
pratique.texte: Attend a prayer meeting at your church this week. If there isn't one, invite two or three people to pray together for 20 minutes about the mission, even by phone.

pratique.titre: If You Face Mockery for Your Faith
pratique.texte: Don't just pray that it stops—ask God for boldness and love for those who mock you, and pray for them by name.

days.question: When I pray, do I mainly ask for comfort, or also for boldness for the mission?
days.priere: Lord, see the difficulties around us, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness. Stretch out your hand so that healings, signs and wonders may be performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus. Fill us with your Spirit. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Before you go to the people, go to God.

days.title: The God Who Heals
days.meditation:
## Part 3: Heal

The second mandate is to heal the sick. Over the next six days, you'll discover that this mandate isn't reserved for a few pastors or famous evangelists. It's given to every disciple of Jesus. To you too. And each day, you'll have a concrete challenge to put it into action. But before we talk about what we do, let's look at who God is.

## The Story

The people of Israel have just crossed the Red Sea. Less than three days later, joy has given way to thirst. They arrive at Marah, but the water is bitter. The people complain. Moses cries out to God, and here is the answer: "Then Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a log; he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the Lord issued a ruling and instruction for them and put them to the test. He said, 'If you listen carefully to the Lord your God and do what is right in his eyes, if you pay attention to his commands and keep all his decrees, I will not bring on you any of the diseases I brought on the Egyptians, for I am the Lord, who heals you.'" (Exodus 15:25-26)

"I am the Lord, who heals you." In Hebrew, Yahweh Rapha. God doesn't say "I can heal" or "I heal sometimes," but "I am the one who heals you." Healing is part of his identity, like love, holiness, or faithfulness.

God doesn't just heal—healing is part of who he is.

And notice how the water becomes sweet: God shows Moses a log, which he throws into the water. Many Christians have seen in this an image of the cross, the log thrown into the midst of our bitterness to make it sweet. It is through the cross that God heals the heart, soul, and body.

## This God Lives in You

David sang: "Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not all his benefits—who forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases;" (Psalm 103:2-3) Forgiveness and healing, side by side. The God who forgives all your iniquities is the one who heals all your diseases.

And here's the good news that changes everything for the rest of this journey: this Yahweh Rapha no longer just speaks to Moses from a cloud. Through Jesus, he came to dwell in those who believe. The God who heals is not far from you, waiting for you to convince him—he lives in you through his Spirit. When you lay your hand on a sick person, you are not alone—it is the one whose name is "I am the one who heals."

## For Your Life

Maybe you're going through your own "Marah"—an illness, chronic pain, depression. Don't stop crying out to God like Moses did: he is still Yahweh Rapha. And start looking at those around you with a new conviction: the God who heals wants to show himself through you.

God sometimes also uses means: a doctor, treatment, rest. Healing that comes through medicine comes from him too; prayer and medical care go together. But never forget that behind all means, there is a God whose name is "the one who heals."

pratique.titre: Healing Challenge, Day 1: Start at Home
pratique.texte: Pray today for yourself if you have pain or illness, then for someone in your home or family. A short prayer: "In the name of Jesus, the Lord who heals, I ask for healing for…"
Write "Yahweh Rapha: the Lord who heals" on a note or as your phone wallpaper. Every time you see it this week, thank him for being the one who heals and for living in you.

pratique.titre: Pray and Take Care of Yourself
pratique.texte: Continue following your treatments and medical appointments, and pray for your doctors. Always encourage those you pray for in the same way: faith and medical care don't conflict.

days.question: Do I believe that healing is part of who God is, and that this God lives in me?
days.priere: Lord, you are the one who heals. I do not forget any of your benefits: you forgive all my sins, you heal all my diseases. Thank you for dwelling in me through your Spirit. Show your healing power in my life, and through me, in the lives of others. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God doesn't just heal—healing is part of who he is.

days.title: By His Wounds
days.meditation:
## What the Word Says

Seven centuries before Jesus, the prophet Isaiah describes a suffering servant who bears upon himself what belonged to us: "Yet it was our infirmities that he bore, and our sorrows that he carried; but we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed." (Isaiah 53:4-5)

He bore our sins and our iniquities, yes. But also our sorrows and our suffering. And the result: peace, and healing.

Matthew, recounting an evening when Jesus was healing the sick, quotes this very passage: "When evening had come, they brought to him many who were demon-possessed. And he cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were sick, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, saying: 'He himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.'" (Matthew 8:16-17)

## Healing Is Part of the Gospel

For Matthew, Jesus's healings fulfill Isaiah 53. Healing is therefore not an optional bonus to the Gospel, reserved for a few "specialized" Christians: it is part of the work of the cross. Jesus came to save the whole human being—soul and body.

This changes how you pray. When you pray for someone who is sick, you are not praying on shaky ground, hoping God might be in a good mood today. You are praying on the basis of a price already paid. Imagine someone going to pick up a package that has already been paid for: they don't beg the shopkeeper, they present the receipt. The cross is your receipt.

Paul says that the Holy Spirit is "the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:14), like a down payment given right now on what is promised to us. Every healing today is a down payment on the world to come, where there will be no more sickness or pain. And God wants to distribute this down payment through the hands of his children.

## For Your Life

It is not your holiness, your experience, or your title that gives weight to your prayer: it is what Jesus bore. A new convert who prays on the basis of the cross has the same basis as a pastor with thirty years of ministry.

So pray with confidence. Not "Lord, if it's your will, maybe…" as if the cross had settled nothing. But: "Jesus, you bore this sickness. By your stripes, I declare healing on this person."

And if healing doesn't appear right away, don't question the cross, and never make the sick person feel guilty. Keep praying, loving, walking with them. The receipt remains valid.

pratique.titre: Healing Challenge, Day 2: Make a Call
pratique.texte: Call someone sick today (family, friend, church member). Check in with them, then offer: "Can I pray for you right now, over the phone?" Pray for a minute, with confidence, on the basis of Isaiah 53:5.
Memorize Isaiah 53:5 today. It's the foundation you will pray from for the sick throughout this journey.
Replace "if it's your will, maybe" with a prayer that relies on the cross: "Jesus, you bore this pain; in Jesus's name, be healed." Practice praying for yourself this evening.

days.question: Am I praying for the sick on the basis of what Jesus bore on the cross, or on the basis of my impressions?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, thank you for bearing our sins and our sufferings. By your stripes, we are healed. I no longer want to pray timidly, as if the cross had settled nothing. Teach me to pray with the confidence of one who knows what you paid. Amen.
days.aRetenir: The cross is your receipt: don't plead, present it.

days.title: Greater Works
days.meditation:
## What the Word Says

On the evening of his last meal, Jesus makes to his disciples a promise that seems almost too great: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father;" (John 14:12)

"Whoever believes in me." Not "whoever is an apostle," not "whoever is a pastor," not "whoever has a special gift." Whoever believes. If you believe in Jesus, this promise is for you.

And what are "the works that I do"? The disciples had just spent three years watching Jesus heal the sick, open the eyes of the blind, raise up the paralyzed, cast out demons. Jesus tells them: you will do these works. And even greater ones.

## Why "Greater" Ones?

"Because I am going to the Father." While Jesus was on the earth, he was in one place at a time, in one body. In rising to the Father, he sends the Holy Spirit, who comes to live in every believer. Jesus says this just after: the Spirit "dwells with you and will be in you" (John 14:17). From now on, it is not two hands healing in Galilee, but millions of hands, in every city of the world.

Paul sums up this mystery in three words: "God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory." (Colossians 1:27) "Christ in you." The same Jesus who touched the lepers lives in you. The same Spirit that raised Jesus from the dead lives in you (Romans 8:11).

You do not carry a religion: you carry a Person. And that Person heals.

## Not an Exclusive Club

Healing has sometimes been made the business of a select few: the great evangelists, the pastors, the elders, those who have "the gift." It is true that Paul speaks of gifts of healings that the Spirit gives to some in a particular way (1 Corinthians 12:9). But the mandate is given to all: "those who believe will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover" (Mark 16:18). The particular gift does not cancel the general call.

## For Your Life

Today, stop looking at yourself: your weaknesses, your lack of experience, your doubts. Look at who lives in you. You don't need to become someone else to pray for the sick: you need to believe that Christ is in you.

And start. The disciples didn't become disciples who heal by reading books about healing, but by obeying: by laying on hands, one person at a time.

pratique.titre: Healing Challenge, Day 3: Pray Face to Face
pratique.texte: Choose someone sick in your circle today and pray for them face to face (at home, at work, at church). Ask their permission, pray briefly in Jesus's name, then ask how they feel.
Each morning this week, before you start your day, say aloud: "Christ is in me. He who believes in Jesus will do the works he did. I believe." (John 14:12, Colossians 1:27)

Write down what makes you think this "isn't for you" (your past, sin, lack of training). Opposite it, write: "Whoever believes in me." The promise doesn't rest on your background, but on your faith in Jesus.

days.question: What changes in how I see the sick around me if I truly believe that Christ lives in me?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you said: whoever believes in me will do the works that I do. I believe in you. Thank you for living in me by your Spirit. I no longer want to look at myself, but at you, who are in me. Use my hands to heal the sick around me. Amen.
days.aRetenir: You do not carry a religion: you carry a Person. And that Person heals.

days.title: I Am Willing
days.meditation:
## The Story

A leper comes to Jesus. In those days, leprosy was a sentence of exile: living apart, wearing torn clothes, crying out "Unclean!" when anyone approached. Years without a hand touching you.

He falls to his knees and says: "A leper came to him, begging him on his knees and saying, 'If you are willing, you can make me clean.' Moved with compassion, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, and said to him, 'I am willing; be clean.'" (Mark 1:40-41)

## What This Reveals About Jesus

The leper doesn't doubt that Jesus can heal him. His question is: does he want to? That's often our question too. And Jesus's answer is unambiguous: "I am willing."

Three actions: he is "moved with compassion," he stretches out his hand and touches him, he speaks. Jesus could have healed with a word, from a distance. But this man needed to be touched. Jesus touched the one no one else touched.

Matthew says it again elsewhere: "When he stepped ashore, he saw a large crowd, and out of compassion for them he healed their sick." (Matthew 14:14) With Jesus, compassion always ends in action.

## The Hands of Jesus Today

In the nineteenth century, a Belgian priest, Father Damien, volunteered to live on the island of Molokai, in Hawaii, where lepers were exiled. He cared for them, he built houses, he buried the dead, until he contracted the disease himself. He then began one of his sermons with these words: "We lepers…"

Jesus no longer has physical hands on the earth except ours. When you place your hand on a sick person's shoulder and pray, it is Jesus's hand reaching out still, and it is his voice saying still: "I am willing."

Also notice the beginning of the passage: before this healing, Jesus rose early to pray in a solitary place (Mark 1:35). His compassion and power came from his intimacy with the Father. It's the same for you.

## For Your Life

When you pray for someone who is sick, start with this certainty: Jesus loves this person, and he wants them healed. You don't come to convince a reluctant God; you come to bring the will of a God who has already said "I am willing."

And look around you: who are the "lepers" of today? The elderly living in isolation, the chronically ill whom we no longer visit, those suffering from mental illness, the homeless. Praying for them is good. Drawing near them, sitting with them, touching them with respect and praying with them—that's even better.

pratique.titre: Healing Challenge, Day 4: "Can I Pray for You?"
pratique.texte: Ask this question today of someone in pain (a coworker with a sore back, a neighbor, a family member). If they agree, place your hand on their shoulder and pray in one sentence: "In Jesus's name, I command this pain to leave."
Visit this week someone sick, elderly, or isolated whom people often forget. Sit down, listen to them, and pray with them.
Rise a little earlier one day this week to pray alone, as Jesus did. Ask the Father for his compassion for the sick you will encounter.

days.question: Do I doubt Jesus's willingness to heal? Who are the "untouchables" around me whom Jesus wants to touch through my hands?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you said to the leper: I am willing. Give me this certainty when I pray for the sick, and your compassion to draw near those others avoid. Let my hands become yours, and my voice, yours. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Jesus touched the one no one else touched. Today he does it through your hands.

days.title: Ananias, an Ordinary Disciple
days.meditation:
## The Story

In Damascus, there is a man about whom we know almost nothing. Not an apostle, not an elder, not a pastor. Luke simply introduces him: "a disciple named Ananias." And to him, Jesus entrusts an impressive mission: to lay hands on Saul of Tarsus, the persecutor of Christians, who has become blind on the road to Damascus.

Ananias is afraid, and he says so: "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much harm he has done to your saints." But he obeys: "Ananias went away and entered the house. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, 'Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.' Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized" (Acts 9:17-18)

## What It Reveals

The greatest apostle in history, Paul, was healed and filled with the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands by an anonymous disciple. No one knows about Ananias's ministry before that day, or after. He simply obeyed, with his fear, at a specific moment.

God is not looking for celebrities: he is looking for available disciples.

Also notice that Ananias doesn't perform a long ceremony. He lays on hands, he says why he is there, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and healing comes.

## What If It's Not Complete Right Away?

Mark's Gospel tells a precious detail. Jesus laid his hands on a blind man at Bethsaida, then asked him if he could see anything. The man answered: "He looked up and said, 'I see people; they look like trees walking around.' Once more Jesus put his hands on the man's eyes. Then his eyes were opened, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly." (Mark 8:24-25)

Even Jesus prayed twice! He laid on hands, asked a question, noticed progress, and did it again until complete healing came. This is a very liberating lesson: praying a second time is not a lack of faith, it is following Jesus's example.

When you pray for someone, ask them afterward: "What are you feeling? Is there any change?" If it's better but not complete, thank God and pray again. If nothing changes, don't get discouraged and never make the person feel guilty: thank them, and keep praying in the days ahead.

## For Your Life

Maybe you feel like Ananias: unknown, without title, and a little afraid. That's exactly the profile of people God loves to use. Your obedience today could change someone's life, maybe even that of a future "Paul."

Dare to step outside your circle of close friends. Jesus's disciples prayed for people they didn't know: in streets, in marketplaces, in homes where they were welcomed.

pratique.titre: Healing Challenge, Day 5: Beyond Your Close Circle
pratique.texte: Pray today for someone you know less well (coworker, neighbor, shopkeeper, classmate). Ask permission, pray briefly in Jesus's name, then ask the question: "What are you feeling?"
If the person says there's an improvement but it's not complete, do as Jesus did at Bethsaida: thank God and pray again. Write down what happens in your journal.
If God puts a person on your heart and you're afraid, tell him: "Lord, I'm afraid, but I'm going." Like Ananias, obedience doesn't wait for fear to disappear.

days.question: Am I waiting to have a title or to stop being afraid before I pray for the sick? What does Ananias's example tell me?
days.priere: Lord, thank you for using simple disciples like Ananias. Here I am, Lord. Even with my fear, I want to obey you. Send me to those who need you, give me the grace to lay on hands in your name, and teach me Jesus's perseverance—to keep praying until complete healing comes. Amen.
days.aRetenir: God is not looking for celebrities: he is looking for available disciples.

days.title: The Seventy: All Sent Out
days.meditation:
## The Story

We often talk about the twelve apostles. But Luke tells of another sending, much less known: "After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of him to every town and place where he was about to go." (Luke 10:1)

Seventy disciples whose names we don't even know. Anonymities. And here is their mission: "When you enter a town and are welcomed, eat what is offered to you. Heal the sick who are there and tell them, 'The kingdom of God has come near to you.'" (Luke 10:8-9)

Heal the sick and announce the kingdom. Exactly the same mission as the twelve. The mandate to heal was not already reserved for Jesus's apostles of that time. And when they return, they are full of joy: "The seventy-two returned with joy and said, 'Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name'" (Luke 10:17).

## All Called

James, in his letter, asks the sick person to call the church elders so they can pray for him. That's a beautiful practice. But he adds right away, for the whole church: "Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). Pray for each other: everyone.

Praying for the sick is not the work of the pastoral team, it is the normal breath of the whole body of Christ.

## How to Pray for a Sick Person

Here is a simple way to do it, which you can use everywhere, at work as at home.

First, ask: "Can I pray for you?" Then listen: "Where does it hurt? How long have you had this?" Next, pray briefly, with authority, in the name of Jesus: one or two sentences are enough, eyes open, one hand on the shoulder if the person agrees. For example: "In Jesus's name, I command this pain to leave. Be healed." Then check: "What are you feeling?" If it's better but not complete, pray again. Finally, whatever the result, bless the person, and tell them in one sentence why you believe in Jesus.

No need to shout, make a long speech, or make the person uncomfortable. The power is not in the form, it is in the name of Jesus.

## For Your Life

Jesus sent his disciples two by two. Why not do the same this week? With a friend, a brother, a sister, go out with the intention to pray for sick people: in your neighborhood, at the hospital (respecting the establishment's rules), in the home of an elderly person, at work.

You have had six days of challenges. This is not the end, it is a beginning: praying for the sick can become a reflex of your disciple life.

pratique.titre: Healing Challenge, Day 6: Go Out Two by Two
pratique.texte: Organize a time this week with a brother or sister to pray for at least three sick people (visits, neighborhood, work, calls). Use the method: ask, listen, pray briefly, check, pray again, bless.

Write down everything that happened during these six days of challenges: the prayers, the changes, even small ones. Share a testimony with your church or a friend: testimonies build the faith of others.
Make a simple commitment for what comes next: for example, offering to pray for at least one sick person each week. Write it down, and ask someone to remind you of it.

days.question: What is still keeping me from praying for the sick around me? With whom could I go out "two by two" this week?
days.priere: Lord Jesus, you sent seventy anonymous disciples to heal the sick and announce your kingdom. Send me too. Make praying for the sick a reflex of my life, and make my church a family where everyone prays for one another. May many be healed and come to know you. Amen.
days.aRetenir: Praying for the sick is not the work of a few: it is the normal breath of the whole body of Christ.

days.title: Come to Destroy the Works of the Devil
days.meditation:
## Part 4: Setting Free

The third mandate is to set captives free: to cast out demons and deliver those who are bound. This is perhaps the most forgotten mandate in our Western churches, and yet it occupies an enormous place in Jesus's ministry.

## The Story

Jesus is teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. And in the assembly, a man possessed by a demon begins to cry out. Notice: he was in the synagogue. The place of worship didn't prevent his captivity.
